All this under the constant threat of eviction from her own apartment. Oh, modern life, modern life, how inescapable is the feeling of powerlessness? The only thing I ask is the dignity of a rental contract that will reduce on the purchase of the property in the future and with a rent that is no more than the national minimum wage. It shouldn’t be too much to ask. (Rui Mendes)

An animated film in which the question is why get over a broken heart if you can just remove it? Ornatos Violeta and Vitor Espadinha had already sung “love is a disease when we think we see our cure in it”. Which is easier? Stop loving or remove the heart? Broken heart syndrome is also known as takotsubo cardiomyopathy. In turn, tako tsubo means, in Japanese, an octopus trap, which is a pot shaped like the heart in the acute phase of this syndrome. And this is also a trap movie. At first, we find the object strange. Then we get trapped inside it and can’t escape its charm. The ending is apotheotic in Mary Orcher’s voice, flying over a pool of blood. (Carlos Ramos)

Recent archaeological findings in Lagos, southern Portugal, unearthed the forgotten past of Portugal’s role in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved African people. Invoking the distance between what we want to forget and the urgency of memory, Tales of Oblivion is a territory of revelation of the past in the present. Tales of Oblivion takes us through a process of revisiting facts from a historical memory, brought to light by recent archaeological excavations in Lagos, Portugal. What is discovered belongs to the past of slavery, revealing Portugal’s role in the transatlantic trafficking of Africans. A 15th century rubbish dump, and all the details that are presented in the list of the collection of the remains, inform us and tell us more and more. The timing of the image, the sound and the narration set a rhythm that leads our gaze and perception on a sensitive discovery that plunges into various media, texts, illustrations, scattered materials and meticulous descriptions. A temporal interplay is established between present and past, where we are placed at the center of this remembered and projected memory. It is also a pretext for reflecting on time, the mark of death and its inexorable disappearance. We must remember, we must not forget. – Carlota Gonçalves

Melgaço, Parada do Monte. The memory of a chance encounter on the border between the real and the imagined, the affection and superstition, has been passed down from generation to generation. The courage of the people of a quiet village in Melgaço, Parada do Monte, is put to the test in an encounter with the devil, known there as Tanganhom. This episode told through time transcends the limits between the real world and the imaginary. The narrative, passed down from generation to generation using oral tradition, takes on fascination and intrigue as it reveals details about this unique experience. The protagonists’ boldness in exploring the unknown mixes with the ancient superstitions of the place, creating a scene of suspense and reflection on the mysteries of everyday life. (Margarida Moz)

aw: Novissimos Prize - Special Mention

films.syn: In Damien Chazelle’s Babylon , someone tells an actor that 100 years from now he will come back to life whenever a reel of his work is projected. In this film, countless actors from all over the world, who are now dead, come back to life, creating a cast of angels and ghosts. The film has a single 35mm print, incorporating natural wear and tear in each viewing, until it erodes definitively — this will be the 56th screening of the film and Shackleton’s fifth film at IndieLisboa.

Romance and dystopia often go hand in hand. Léa Seydoux is Gabrielle, a woman who lives in a futuristic society that abhors emotions that exalt human beings. To this end, a DNA purification process is carried out that leads the individual to travel through all their previous lives, separating themselves from all the things that have affected them. On these journeys, Louis (George MacKay) appears, in an encounter that jeopardizes the whole process. To what extent is it really possible to get rid of our affections? Can artificial intelligence end up blurring and erasing the remnants of what constitutes us as humans? Bertrand Bonello decides to focus on one face, that is Léa Seydoux’s, to venture to search for some of the deepest and most disturbing mysteries of our own humanity. Throughout a three-stage journey, Gabrielle will navigate the abyss of being human and dealing in the same time with other human beings. Inspired by Henry James’ The Beast in the Jungle, Bertrand Bonello gives us what is probably his best film to date. – Miquel Escudero Diéguez

Lisbon, 2027. Marta and Miguel are both researchers that are part of a scientific group and a couple in their private lives. Their relationship will be put to the test on one decisive night when the parameters that Marta is analyzing point to the very high probability of a major earthquake hitting Lisbon. The group splits, debating whether or not to warn the population of the possible impending tragedy. There is a general consensus in the scientific community that a major earthquake will happen again in Lisbon. The question is not so much whether it will happen, but when. Rita Nunes suggests that this could happen as early as 2027. In the not-too-distant future, a group of scientists, led by a confident and convinced Sara Barros Leitão, are faced with the possibility of being able to predict the unpredictable. Data from new submarine cables installed in 2025, a real fact on which the film is based, indicates the likelihood of an imminent earthquake. The group is torn between the possibility of saving many lives or creating unjustified widespread panic, which could be even more catastrophic. But even before this earthquake shakes the city of Lisbon, it has already shattered personal convictions and ruined intimate relationships. -Carlos Ramos

The Golem didn’t do it on purpose, but he turned out to be a bridge linking cliffs in a peaceful forest and, thus, allowed all the animals to cross the path without a second thought. An unexpected community service.

Creating things out of nothing involves a lot of imagination, but the truth is that turning imagined things into concrete things is no easy task. And these Creators, in their own dimension, aren’t having an easy time of it.

A film about finding the courage to leave our comfort zone, here following a lion seed that is afraid to blossom. But when the wind takes him to meet a gardener, the flowers he meets give him the strength to bloom.

Lawrence Abu Hamdan reveals veiled tactics when he notices that, during the pandemic, even though air traffic over Lebanon was at a standstill, the noise caused by Israeli planes became a strong and constant hum in the lives of citizens, creating atmospheric violence. Lawrence Abu Hamdan is already a well-known and prolific name in international short films at IndieLisboa. His work is very political and focuses on capturing and interpreting audio. Due to Covid, airplanes have left the skies of Beirut, but noise pollution has increased. Israeli fighter jets fly over the city around 50 times a day. Lawrence Abu Hamdan investigates, archives all these records and systematically shows us the neighboring country’s unconventional levels of oppression. The Israel-Palestine conflict is finally getting the global spotlight it should have had decades ago, but Palestine is not the only country to suffer the repercussions of Israel’s absurd and unnecessary war capabilities. Lawrence Abu Hamdan makes us look to the skies over Lebanon with ears wide open to the inescapable levels of noise violence committed against the people of Beirut. (Rui Mendes)

Bruno Dumont takes an incredibly operatic premise — an invasion of our planet by interstellar forces that represent themselves as, fundamentally, Good and Evil — while setting it in an absolutely ordinary place, a French seaside town where nothing out of the ordinary could happen. There’s room for lightsabers, explosions and forbidden love, and a vision of the apocalypse that’s as satirical as it is amusing. Bruno Dumont’s reserves of imagination seem to be inexhaustible and a renewable energy. L’Empire , winner of the 2024 Jury Prize at the Berlinale, seeks to somehow retake the successful strategy of P’tit Quinquin (2014) and the sequel Coincoin et les Z’inhumains (2018) which deconstructed the crime and mystery thriller genre, set in the peaceful region of Pas-de-Calais, requesting local inhabitants for their characters. Dumont realizes that the fusion between burlesque (or “typically” French) with universes coded by genre cinema are a source of comedy. But more than that. This kind of “gallic version” of Star Wars ends up pushing the burlesque to its limits, as if telling us that seriousness begins only when the foundations of science fiction’s verisimilitude crack and when everything is taken less seriously. Perhaps only then can good finally glimpse victory against evil. Or its opposite. (Carlos Natálio).

films.t: The Feeling That the Time for Doing Something Has Passed
films.syn: Joanna Arnow won’t be able to escape comparisons to Lena Dunham, not only because this is an entry in the sexual girl canon with humour and some perversity, but also because Arnow directs, stars in, writes and edits the film — her first feature. The film, a comic mosaic of Ann’s, her character, experiences, shows us her corporate job, her belligerent family and her casual relationships involving BDSM.

films.ot: Les Premiers Dinosaures Étaient des Pommes
films.syn: Between puppets and animation, two little sisters try to decipher the beginning of History on Earth. If it was the dinosaurs, how it all happened. But what if everything happened a little… differently? Perhaps the first dinosaurs had a more curious beginning.

films.t: The Girl with the Occupied Eyes
films.ot: A Menina com os Olhos Ocupados
films.syn: Once upon a time, there was a little girl who, even when out and about, was always distracted. Eyes fixed on her phone, she didn’t notice the world around her or anyone who wanted to play. What could be done to “disoccupy” her eyes?

films.t: The Girl With the Red Beret
films.syn: The girl travels through the Montreal underground with her beret on and encounters musical adventures and hilarious characters, where nothing is what you would call “normal”. There are even horses carrying a sofa into the carriage.

A ritual involving the preparation of wool, dyed red, to cover a stone. The symbolism is linked to the protection of a shepherd who takes care of his sheep before he becomes obsolete. The growth of large cities swallows the surrounding countryside and forces rural lifestyles into formats subjugated to urban needs. Only the stubborn dedication of some to rural life gives them the necessary courage to maintain their professions despite the strength of a centripetal urbanity. In “The Good Omen” a sheepherder continues his activity even when nearby you can hear the major motorways and the deafening noise of a city like Barcelona. The sheep’s rattles are not enough to drown out the noise of the engines, and in an attempt to guarantee the continuity of his livelihood, the shepherd counts on the help of an ecofeminist collective that works with wool from the flock, artistically intervening in the Sacrificial Stone from Collserola. The extraordinary beauty of this film, which follows both processes, the activity of the pastor and that of the artistic collective, lies in the subtlety with which the director places this story “in a kind of undefined temporality” to show “the traces of the past and the threats of the future.” (Margarida Moz)

films.t: The House Is On Fire, Might As Well Get Warm
films.syn: A film that begins with a character getting away from Algeria to Paris. Money is saved and the departure is imminent. When a friend dies, Yanis visits the wake only to be robbed. A road mission ensues in order to catch the culprit. Yanis is leaving for a journey of uncertain dreams. On the last day in Algeria, before heading to France, he dedicates himself to the final preparations in the neighboring village and ends up involved in a series of unforeseen events that fuel the anguish of departure. Will there be a destiny? Will it make sense to try to counter it? There will always be doubts about the reports of the success of those who have already left, but let no one question the courage of those who invest everything in the departure, leaving a part of themselves behind. In this beautiful story, pensive and melancholic, there is an idea of emigration in the opposite direction to success. What awaits us on the other side might just be an imposed, sublimated and silent detachment. Based on his own story of emigration, director Mouloud Aït Liotna makes his film debut saying that this film is a kind of disillusioned tribute, paid to those who like him are uprooted in fact or in spirit. (Margarida Moz)

aw: Special Jury Prize (International Short Film Competition)

films.syn: Watching this film, you have to wonder if what you’re seeing is really the pinnacle of being human, and if it is, despite the cheeky wink, you have to think twice about what you want to do when you leave the theater. We are shown people — living in a reality that is almost-the-same-as-ours — trying to pass the time, together, by telling discouraging stories about their work. Filmed with a 360-degree camera and adapted for the cinema, the restlessness emanates from this film. It’s understandable that the viewer feels lost. You will be invited into a mutant universe that provokes imaginative observation through the bodies of Taiwan, Peru and Sri Lanka – these spaces are recognisable but need to be interpreted, as the recording apparatus is a 360º camera. We are connected to a network without borders, of relationships both physical and virtual, of a shared world that is constantly nearing its end. But that end never comes – and so it’s a patient journey to extinction The Human Surge 3 is a test of our role as observer-observed, because ultimately you get the feeling that it could be you and your search for ways to pass the time in a labour-centered life to appear in Eduardo Williams’ next film. (Bianca Dias)

aw: Special Mention (International Feature Competition)

films.t: The Illusion of an Everlasting Kiss
films.syn: A November day in Porto, in a square where skaters jump up a flight of stairs. Three characters share a moment, which is divided into three subjective shots and which, without dialogue, are intended to characterize them emotionally. The idea of shared love is called into question. As in rococo painting (by Marguerite Gérard, for example), where several characters occupy a space and draw multiple glances between them (from which all kinds of speculations can be plotted), in The Illusion of an Everlasting Kiss Marta Sousa Ribeiro (whose Simon Chama was shown at IndieLisboa in 2020) stages a realm of crossed glances in permanent circulation, based on a small episode of everyday life. Following the narrative scheme of Rashomon , we return again and again and again to the same situation, and with each repetition we discover it from a new point of view. But the director literalises this idea using three subjective cameras that are attached to three different bodies. This subjectivation therefore operates according to schemes of desire and repulsion that translate ways of understanding others from different positions of gender, sexuality, class and age. Starting from the banal, Sousa Ribeiro rehearses an intriguing reflection on the furtive power of the gaze and on the social theatre of reality. – Ricardo Vieira Lisboa

films.t: The Little Bird and the Squirrel
films.ot: Der kleine Vogel und das Eichhörnchen
films.syn: Autumn arrives and the scene is set for animal playtime. A small bird is tending to the leaves on a tree, but then a squirrel arrives and usurps the watering can. And so begins an exciting squirrel chase. But watch out for the sly fox, always on the lookout.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Cinema at the Pool)

films.syn: A pair of directors who often combine dance, performance and cinema, this film is part of a trilogy. Here the “lodge” of the title is not in Twin Peaks, but focuses on a group of people who get together in a country cottage to see how they react to each other.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: European Short Film Network)

films.syn: Nothing spoils a romantic dinner like unexplained transformations in the face of one of the members of the couple. But that doesn’t mean that the romance is extinguished. Sometimes you just need a change of wig. Carolina Sandvik uses the stop motion animation technique for a deadpan exploration, as existential as it is amusing, of what happens when you mix horror and romance, the decomposition of the body and the mundane life of a couple. Here, the growing bodily transformations are a clear but exquisite metaphor for a relationship falling apart. Yet, Sandvik’s gaze is always humorous, punctuating the growing poignancy of the story. (Ana Cabral Martins)

Pity and Dido are married, but that doesn’t prohibit extramarital relationships; on the contrary, they are encouraged. The film questions rigid cultural standards and what a woman is allowed to do. Directed by Tereza Trautman when she was just 22, a film banned by the Brazilian military dictatorship for its inclusion of sexual and feminist content, presented in a new digital print restored by the Cinemateca Brasileira.

The animation in this film results in a touching metaphor about trauma, both physical and emotional, and reconciliation. Eric is an animation artist who literally has no mouth, so he communicates through a frame around his neck. Too introverted to confess his feelings to his co-worker, he lives in isolation, despite his mother’s attempts to bring him closer to the outside world. Until the day she asks him to visit his uncle Rogelio. Directed by Filipino Carl Joseph Papa, The Missing is a feature film with animation done using rotoscoping. If rotoscoping allows us to preserve expressiveness, Papa quickly makes room for the surreal. The mouth of Eric, the main character, is erased. In a pause (or in a dream?), the film migrates to science fiction. The filmmaker establishes an interesting dialogue between ultra-realistic appearance and fantastic tension. The animation in The Missing is free, inventive and particularly expressive: parts of the face erased, visible grids, pencil scratches… each element seems to be chosen in direct connection with the expression of emotions and the inner world. Genre is also a means of expression, with fantasy here talking about queer traumas, as in Gregg Araki’s Mysterious Skin . (Michaël Gaspar)

Directed by and starring Buster Keaton, this film is a comedy about Rollo Treadway’s mistaken voyage on a ship sold to a warring country. Initially intending a honeymoon cruise, Rollo boards the wrong ship when his proposal to neighbour Betsy O’Brien is rejected. The ship belonged to Betsy’s father’s and she comes looking for him. Eventually, both find themselves trapped there. Movie accompanied by live music. Live music by Catherine Morisseau on the piano.

Documentary about education in Cuba, highlighting the educational revolution in rural secondary schools, where theory and practice merged. Fidel Castro is a prominent figure in this film by Jorge Fraga.

An innocent start, a granddaughter revisiting her grandmother’s story with archive footage. A fantastic revelation about the past that is turned into a fable in the film. Luz Emilia García is not just the grandmother, but also the woman who pioneered pornographic cinema in Colombia. In The Night of the Minotaur , we plunge into a fantastic tale set in this enchanted environment. In a village in the middle of the mountains, where a lighthouse stands out among its tops, a forest is home to a variety of mystical creatures – and it is in this setting that the birds find the place where they will die. Among the archive footage, we discover the story of Luz Emilia García, the precursor of pornographic cinema in Colombia. Her extraordinary journey, intertwined with the imaginary world presented to us by her granddaughter, is a unique narrative that transcends the limits of time and space. (Jéssica Pestana)

Films playing with the integrated use of Artificial Intelligence are beginning to proliferate and in this short film we navigate through a world of images created in this way, but also through conversations with a chatbot that reveals all the tendencies and prejudices of human beings. Artificial intelligence is not something new, but in recent years there has been a dominance of the subject in culture that has been impossible to deny or avoid. Society is permeable, and should be, to new technologies, but it is inevitable that we talk about what is lost with their introduction. AI, like many other technologies before it, replaces human resources, but in this case it also replaces psychological and emotional resources. This is where Replika comes in, a chatbot where we can create romantic or friendly relationships with an artificial intelligence. Our Replika won’t criticize us; on the contrary, it will comfort us in any moment of emotional turmoil. Humanized by some, mistreated by others, Inès Sieulle’s film uses Replika not to talk about the machine’s dominance over human beings, but rather to hold up a mirror to humanity itself. (Rui Mendes)

aw: Grand Prize for Short Film EMEL

films.syn: In late 1920s Chile, an economic crisis hits peasants and displaced nitrate workers. El Traje Cruzado and José Durán meet and discuss revolution and land occupation, ending up establishing a town in Palmilla. They arm themselves for socialist revolution but fail, facing eviction and violence.

Nostalgia can be paralysing and that’s what is examined in this short film that explores the relationship with the Portuguese Revolution of 1974, animating an archive photograph to understand what lies between the weariness of the past and the vigour of struggling for a country.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: European Short Film Network)

films.syn: Meditation and a familial and personal portrait. This documentary takes Kamal Aljafari, who lived in Germany at the moment, to visit relatives in Palestine. He walks through his father’s family’s Ramla and his mother’s family’s Jaffa, weaving the history of the country with that of his parents, the memories of 1948 with the conversations with his sister who, like him, also holds an Israeli passport.

Two friends escape their problems by going on a party cruise. When they disembark in Australia, the lack of funds to continue travelling leads to the need for temporary work. They both land in a village in the middle of nowhere, a small society made up of bored miners and alcoholics. They stay for a few weeks, tending bar. Tension grows between the outsiders and the locals. Driven by alcohol, dust and paranoia, The Royal Hotel may evoke the Australian outback of classics like Wake in Fright, but the proposal here is more politically pertinent and astute: two young American friends travelling around Australia agree to work in a remote pub serving a mining town. Mostly frequented by men, the atmosphere in the pub is marked by casual sexism, misogynistic jokes and veiled hostility, and the girls deal with this differently – Hanna is uneasy; Liv thinks it’s normal. The film, which could easily have descended into an empty, classist exercise, is skilfully directed by Kitty Green, who explores excellently the psychological tension and microaggressions of everyday life in the pub. An urgent feminist thriller. (Bruno Pereira)

A queer comedy that begins on a gay cruising Greek beach, but where the idea is no longer to relax but to work. Work on an idea for a film, a first feature. This is the premise for an exploration of the world of two best friends, Demosthenes and Nikitas (the director in search of inspiration), in which the past becomes inspiration and the plot of the future film is tied to a dog called Carmen.

In the mid-19th century, a group of survivors from a wrecked slave ship, both black and white, end up on a deserted island, lost somewhere in the Atlantic Ocean. The fight for survival and power will flip the moral and social values of those days. The Survivors tells the story of how masters and enslaved people may or may not coexist under extreme circumstances. The Survivors is about a group of men and women [black and white] who survive the sinking of a slave ship in the middle of the Atlantic. What starts out as salvation and a celebration of life quickly turns into a nightmare in which hierarchies weigh heavily, money still counts and so does status. But a journey of reconnaissance around the island, after overcoming immeasurable obstacles, leads to a turning point. The island’s new society has created new hierarchies, new powers and many new ways of living together. The film, beautifully photographed in black and white by Hugo Azevedo, perhaps to avoid narrative distractions, places everyone in the same penumbra of (dis)integrity, leading us to question our history and its permanent lie. Now, finally, in Portugal, the debate seems to be emerging about what Portuguese colonisation was, the massacre of slaves and the horrendous crimes committed. The Survivors touches on this in a very sharp and fair way, putting its finger on the wound, finally moving away from black and white to look for a grey area with answers. The educated man turns out to be the weakest link in the balance. And with this power, Barahona brings to light the possible debate in the hope that the ‘reparation’ debate can follow. – Miguel Valverde

An emissary from the Crown gets lost in a forest. He is taken in by a family who are waiting for a father they fear dead, until a figure shrouded in death appears, claiming to be the long-awaited patriarch. The myth of a vampire figure emerges and is realised within this family, where our unsuspecting Marquis d’Urfé is found. Artifice and theatricality are the threads that sew together this fascinating adaptation of the vampire’s folkloric cousin, the Balkan vourdalak . In an atmosphere that is both gloomy and burlesque, we follow a Vourdalak in puppet form. Originally written by Aleksey Tolstoy, a distant relative of the author of War and Peace, the story of Vourdalak leaves us equally unsettled by the singular presence of this figure who transforms an already strange family into something even more sinister. Travelling down less explored paths in fiction, this tale introduces us to a family waiting for their patriarch. However, what they receive is not the father they knew, but a vampire-like figure, rooted in a myth that few still believe in. The impasse deepens when the victims of this unusual being tend to be those closest to him. Now adapted for the cinema by Adrien Beau, this story plunges viewers into a suspense between horror and tragicomedy, questioning the nature of family ties and the limits of what is real. (Jéssica Pestana)

This is Justine Lemahieu’s encounter over several years with Lila and João, the two artists and activists from Fado Bicha band, whose songs embody and give voice to LGBTQIA+ stories and struggles. Backstage, words and glances intersect, questioning our relationship with appearances, gender norms, language, and sexuality. Fado Bicha’s ethos doesn’t just involve revolutionising and experimenting with the traditional fado genre, there’s also a strong activist streak, making the songs especially poignant and urgent, and their role in the world of Portuguese music fearless and fundamental. Throughout the documentary, we discover more about what is important to the two people who make up the duo, but we also discover their sense of humour, the beauty of their relationship with music and all the other ways they find to express themselves — through, literally and otherwise, fashioning a role that could be considered subversive in the world of fado. Which makes their vision of music that much juicier and delicious. (Ana Cabral Martins)

Two friends, school mates, try to break the rules, just like any other teenager in the world. These are rites of passage that countless generations have lived through. But in this case, the two friends are Iranian and society’s rules will make the consequences more painful. At an Iranian school for girls, two friends try to get around the strict rules of customs and teaching and take a bottle of whiskey to have fun together. Much of the teenagers’ enthusiasm comes from the act of transgression and not so much from the contents of the bottle, but when they are caught by the school management, the justification of the events will test the friendship between the two, caught in a web of emotional manipulations in which different family backgrounds determine different forms of treatment. Power relations, authoritarianism and fear are manifested throughout Iranian society, and not even in an exclusively female school are women safe from male domination. (Margarida Moz)

C. Tangana is a global phenomenon. He’s also an artist who values his ability to write lyrics, who doesn’t feel totally part of hip hop culture, who likes Tolstoy and who thinks he can’t sing — but does it anyway. C. Tangana is a Spanish rapper that has conquered the world and now presents his vulnerability as an artist in a documentary about the production of a concert, in a struggle between artistic vision and logistical limitations. A globally successful album – El Madrileño – and an ambitious, explosive and sold-out tour, supported by an imposing live show that brought together around 50 people on stage, around a table worthy of a real banquet, are the basic ingredients of this film. From the debut of the album to the stage, behind the scenes of the tour, the negotiations, the anguish, the rehearsals, the complicity, the difficulties, the spirit of unity and even the despair that happens away from the public eye, during a whirlwind of concerts that C. Tangana gave in Spain and Latin America. (Helena César)

A boy from Peru, herding alpacas, dreams of the national football team going to the World Cup in Russia, in 2018. His two friends are an alpaca called Ronaldo and a dog called Rambo. In the midst of the child’s utopian dreams, something darker is happening in the village where he lives, because the lake is being polluted. When Ronaldo disappears, everything begins to take on a more serious shape.

This tiger lives in a ceramic dish, in which he is its decoration. And he loves living in the dish, because food is always close at hand. But when it’s not, the adventure begins and the search for something to snack on is the master idea.

Iben tries to attract Jonas’ attention and Oscar tries not to attract attention to himself. A late afternoon trip to the beach ends with a bittersweet taste when a cruel prank turns into an opportunity for generosity.

Annabelle Amoros delves into the world of tornadoes at the heart of the United States, within communities affected by these meteorological phenomena and the ways in which capitalism has to respond to the fears of those who want to protect themselves. Annabelle Amoros is a regular at IndieLisboa, and Tornadoes marks her sixth short film appearance at the festival. Her films explore peculiar spaces, their inhabitants and the nature around them. Tornadoes is the result of an exquisite exploration of these spaces and the people who inhabit them. We travel to Tornado Alley, an area shared between several states in the United States where tornadoes most easily appear. We follow a group of people whose routine is completely dominated by looking for and chasing tornadoes. Annabelle Amoros offers us a window into a fascinating community with a filmmaking rigor that is equally noteworthy. (Rui Mendes)

Bram Stoker’s Dracula set in a French neighborhood with a pre-adolescent girl is, perhaps, a simple idea, but the atmosphere created by Rodrigue Huart and the final crescendo gives the film a touch that is as surprising as it is shocking, and a little naughty. Young French director Rodrigue Huart makes his fiction debut with this interesting short film, winner of the 2024 Grand Jury Award at the SXSW Festival. The setting is a French suburb, an urban space where several teenage neighbours spend their time when they are not at school. Ewa, 10 years old, needs someone to accompany her to reign over her province. So, will Transylvanie be a film about bullying a young girl who thinks she’s a vampire?; a work about pre-teen love?; or will it simply be bloodlust and eternity? There are multiple references, from Buffy the Vampire Slayer, Twilight , Dracula, Carrie or Fright Night . However, between the horror, the social drama and the comedy, the doubt remains until the last image. (Carlos Natálio)

Tulips to be tended break into operatic and epic lyrical song to welcome spring and perhaps play with a gardener with a rip in his trousers. Marie-Sarah Piron weaves an absolutely charming, poetic and entertaining short film. The colours are vibrant, and you can feel the texture of the 16mm film it’s shot on, but above all, what animates this film and elevates it to the pinnacle is the use of humour and operatic lyricism to tell a story that, if not mundane, is at least quite simple. The gardener is the conductor, but it’s the flowers as the choir that have to look after his interests and it’s within this game that the director creates 4 minutes of pure delight. (Ana Cabral Martins)

The film focuses on the Uruguayan urban left-wing guerrillas, the so-called Tupamaros, and was filmed at the height of their operation and within their members — the filming was clandestine and carried out by various people who didn’t know the real purpose of the film, which shows the history of the struggle and the desperation that led to the guerrillas’ operationalisation.

The animation is made of clay and glass, in a delicate exploration of maternal love and what it can be like to be the parent of a child on the autism spectrum. There are monsters everywhere, but also shelters from the dangers of the world.

Jan Ijäs is a director who uses narration to transcendent effect. Here, he plays with two Italian settings of importance in the two Great Wars of the 20th century: the monastery of Monte Cassino and the connection with Ludwig Wittgenstein; the village of San Pietro and the connection with John Huston. Jan Ijäs is a director who’s been to IndieLisboa before, always bringing films that play with the relationship between what we see and what is narrated in ways that are always mesmerising. Ijäs’ trump card is the way he not only chooses topics but then develops and weaves them together, uncovering connections, creating tension and anticipation, always with a sense of humour that doesn’t go unnoticed. In this film, he takes two wars and two characters that he follows because of their connection to them. World War I and Ludwig Wittgenstein and World War II and John Huston, who was part of the American war effort, along with other renowned American directors — such as John Ford, William Wyler, Frank Capra and George Stevens. (Ana Cabral Martins)

aw: Silvestre Prize for Best Short Film (Escola das Artes)

films.syn: Archive images that fly over what is archaeological, natural, ancient and desert, contrasting with what is human, destructive, cultivating or just playful. The face of a changing geography, seen through the eye of aerial surveillance.

When you’re a bat, you sleep upside down and everything is seen upside down. But imagine that instead of sleeping during the day, you take the opportunity to wake up and feel the sun on your wings? And maybe meet a new friend? He’s a little mouse and he doesn’t walk upside down.

A couple try something that, instead of opening up their relationship to new possibilities, ends up creating a distance between them, becoming hard to think won’t become permanent. When they return from a trip out of New York, they drift apart and one of them tries to unravel their feelings. A trip to Vermont haunts a couple. Everyone keeps asking how it went, if the scenery was beautiful, if the atmosphere was romantic, if it was fun and relaxing. The two boys give short answers. Clearly something happened in Vermont, but it hardly matters. Joseph Barglowski, the director, is more interested in the emotional consequences of that supposedly idyllic weekend and how, from then on, a friction is generated in that relationship that throws each of the boys in different directions (and into different bodies). The sudden instability of that moment, which is not one of rupture but of torsion, allows Barglowski to build a portrait of a city (New York), a community (queer) and an environment (tense and cold). Vermont is therefore a gloomy urban symphony, in which 16mm photography (and reminiscent Super-8 sequences) merges with anti-psychological acting direction (there’s something of Robert Bresson’s “models” here) to produce a melancholic portrait of a generation. (Ricardo Vieira Lisboa)

The offices of the Iraqi Airways in Geneva have been abandoned due to the embargo on the country in the 1990s. But the place remains, like a haunting ghost, with all the elements of the time. Neighbours are interviewed and fears and fantasies are revealed.

A freak accident causes Satake’s death. Asagi, her friend, is distraught by the incident, but the rest of the friend group seems significantly less affected by the loss. The friction that is created calls for a change, a cut, a break. Asagi finds herself on the roof of her school with her classmates. One of them mentions Satake, a close friend of the group who died unexpectedly. Asagi feels uncomfortable at the brief, casual mention of Satake. The group seems to have moved on, but Asagi is not in the same place emotionally. Her grief takes the form of a haunting that gradually deteriorates her mental sanity and, subsequently, that of the rest of the group. This is Iwasaki Yusuke’s first film and he already has an extremely confident grip on how to create tension without losing his emotional anchor. (Rui Mendes)

A pre-adolescent kid spends a family summer holiday at a golf village. A newly built lake on a golf course becomes the backdrop to a mysterious encounter. And the discovery of an unknown other becomes the discovery of the unknown self. A pre-adolescent kid is on holidays with the family. What better time to relax and let yourself feel? The sounds of the construction of a pond near the country house where they are staying will push the kid to delve into something that does not know but senses, something that lies diffuse in the subconscious but begins to take a shape that becomes more and more clear. Will them be able to recognize the new skin? What will the new face be like? The one that still exists only in tomorrow. – Miquel Escudero Diéguez
A couple’s relationship is seen in a decontextualised way, through slides that were found at a flea market in Vienna. These pieces of personal history intersect with the historical context.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: European Short Film Network)

films.t: We are Fugazi from Washington, DC
films.ot: We Are Fugazi From Washington, DC
films.syn: Fugazi are a post-hardcore band from the United States, with a particular political and social conscience — and an influence that reverberated in the future of punk and alternative music. Always with a “do it yourself” ethic, they never wanted to leave the independent music industry for the big labels. This documentary is a testament to that ethos , comprising rare archive footage captured by fans at the band’s numerous gigs. In the history of music, there is a monument of ethics called Fugazi, a band founded in 1986 and co-led by the charismatic Ian MacKaye, who had previously made his mark with the Dischord label and the no less influential Minor Threat. MacKaye and Fugazi became the beacon of a generation for their DIY aesthetic and attitude. On top of this, there was their concern for the community and the most marginalised people and an anti-capitalist and anti-consumerist code of ethics, which didn’t see profit as the main incentive and through which they defended, for example, the non-existence of official merchandising and the control of concert ticket prices to a maximum of 5 dollars, even in more recent times. But this film is above all about another of the things that made Fugazi great and mythical. Their concerts. Every concert was an earthquake. A raw and brutal energy on stage, which spread in waves to the audience and often forced them to stop the concerts when they detected outbreaks of violent attitudes among the audience. To see a Fugazi concert is to feel like you’re close to something that is extinct. A time that no longer exists. Luckily for us, there are several concerts in this film, all filmed by fans and concert-goers. Unlike today, when it is often forbidden for the public to capture images and record the sound, Fugazi allowed and encouraged everyone to record their concerts with images and sound. In the history of music there is the before and after of seeing Fugazi live. For those who weren’t able to, we’re left with the images of the concerts. (Carlos Ramos)

Maria Inês experiences the first breezes of love during a summer vacation. Accompanied by her friends, she strolls through the neighborhood where she lives, spending her time between beads and a movie shoot. Maria Inês, a young girl full of energy and curiosity, dives into the effervescent emotions of her first love experiences during her summer holidays in a social neighborhood in Lisbon. Accompanied by her inseparable friends, she explores the streets of the neighborhood where the heat of the sun mixes with the ebullition resulting from the diversity of people who live there. Between laughter and secrets, the group of friends has fun playing games and improvised choreographies. This collaborative process between the director and the neighborhood children allows them to make a film where there is no shortage of improvisations and spontaneous dialogues, which reflect not only the experiences of Maria Inês and her friends, but above all the importance of belonging to a community. (Margarida Moz)

Fátima says she doesn’t have any feelings but finds herself dreaming about her new policeman neighbor. Her son Vítor secretly wears that policeman’s uniform, hoping it might bring pleasure to a boy he met online. Grandma Júlia wants to escape her retirement home and run away from her husband, but she doesn’t know where to go. A spiral of insomnia and nocturnal illusions leads to misunderstandings and impossible relationships, all seeking a little air. We’re on Air, the title of Diogo Costa Amarante’s debut feature film, presents us with a duality of understanding. On the one hand, the expression indicates the act following take-off on an aeroplane journey: and this is where the characters, Fátima (the mother), Vítor (the son) and Júlia (the grandmother), find themselves, that moment following the change. Each of them is trying to live with that shiver we feel after boarding the plane and each of them, in their own way, is trying to find their own space of comfort on this journey. But ‘We’re on air’ also means that the television programme is live, being broadcast. And in this sense, each of the characters is also watching the lives of the others from the audience point of view (this is literally Vítor’s job), without this interfering with their choices. This almost mathematical narrative duplicity, interspersed with confident and fearless editing and stunning photography by Sabine Lancelin (who was the DOP of Manoel de Oliveira’s last films), makes for an unexpected film. We’re on Air is inviting to the viewer, films a Porto without time, and leaves you complete at the end. Warning: if you’re not in the mood, stay at home! We’re on Air is for those who like cinema without prejudice. – Miguel Valverde

Preview of Pedro Lino’s series À Boleia da Ciência , showing three episodes: “Tornado is coming”, “Let’s help the dolphins” and “Mother Lynx”. We’ll follow a family of scientists who, using their van with its unique properties, will explore the mysteries of science.

The family circumstances are tragic: Leni is battling an illness that is breaking her down, and her mother is working day and night (as a lady of the night) to take care of her daughter and her health. There is little imagination in their lives. Until the day Marcel comes along, a playwright marked by aloofness who will find his convictions challenged by Leni’s desire to make the most of life.
A day to explore every child’s favourite toy in the classroom, and Teddycat has brought out her superhero. But before she presents him, she’ll have to deal with Little Dog.

A feline and a bird meet, get together and develop a codependent relationship, until it becomes toxic. Liberation comes, but not before a transformation that upsets their dynamic. In a charming animation, Conte Sauvage transports us to the story of an unlikely friendship between a feline and a little bird. At first glance, the film seems to be aimed solely at children, conveying an easily decipherable message: that, despite our differences, there are always possible paths to acceptance and affection. However, as the narrative progresses, we discover that the true essence of friendship lies not in physical differences, but in character traits. Can manipulative individuals – birds or people – really build genuine bonds of friendship? (Jéssica Pestana)
A bark beetle girl, who should be spending her days relaxing in a forest, sees her world upended when a fire separates her from her family and traps her in a city where all the dangers are gigantic.

It’s an adaptation of a chapter from the book Dialogues with Leuco (1947) by Cesare Pavese, which delves into the myth of Sappho (a poetess of Ancient Greece) and the nymph Britomartis, in connection with the foam of the ocean and the idea of heartbreak-induced death. Avoiding a linear narrative, components such as footnotes or extratextual information are also adapted, giving the film a poetic dimension that transcends the boundaries of the text. Tú me abrasas, Matias Pineiro’s new film, moves away from his previous style: first of all, because it is the first of his films that is not based on the works of Shakespeare. It is an adaptation of Sea Foam, one of the chapters of Dialogues with Leucò by Cesare Pavese. But also a mixture of fragmentary works by Sappho, which were recommended to him by one of the film’s secondary actresses, Agustina Muñoz (herself a regular in his work). And finally, he inserts the diary he kept during the making of the film. It is a film shot on 16 mm film, bathed in warm colors and lots of sunlight, which speaks of desire and nostalgia. Matias Piñeiro discovers that he feels a connection, a closeness to the discussion between Sappho and Britomartis. One was real, the other was a nymph, a creation, a mythological figure. This mixture gives us an idea of desire, death, will, accident, problem. A cycle of recurring shots tries to answer the question of what an adaptation of a poem could be. The discussions between the poet Sappho (Saidón) and the nymph Britomartis (Villar) reject the logic of the reverse shot and focus on various other types of images, or on silent portraits of the actresses. The film is an invitation to reproduce the fragmentary experience of reading in a cinematographic context.

In a world where we’re more apart from each other than ever, we meet a band that pulls the rug out and teaches us empathy. 5ª Punkada embark on a European tour and give us the chance to know them intimately while opening a window into the world of artists with disabilities. Com amor, Medo follows the European tour of 5ª Punkada through four countries – the Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovenia and Luxembourg. The punk energy, the music, the emotions of a band born in the Associação de Paralisia Cerebral de Coimbra. Fausto Sousa, one of the founding members, is the purest definition of punk, and his band is a life plan, which also includes Fátima Pinto, Jorge Maleiro and Miguel Duarte. A journey through joy, work, obstacles, resistance, difficulties and what it means to be an artist with disability. Preparing their second album and with an album released in 2021 by Omnichord – Somos Punks ou Não? – and performances at various festivals, 5ª Punkada’s career has been going for 30 years and has no signs of stopping. (Helena César)

aw: IndieMusic Prize

films.syn: Set in a fishing village, this delicate animation is about the weight of loneliness in a community, where humans and animals face the hardships of winter. We witness the birth of baby kittens to the sound of Godflesh’s industrial rock and are immediately placed in the universe of violence and fragility that constitutes this winter tale set in an isolated, snow-covered fishing community. This inhospitable, icy setting, painted in an imprecise, nervous outline, will be the backdrop for the relationships of interdependence and cruelty being established (between humans, between animals, and between humans and animals). Until, one Christmas Eve, when a heating failure brings the community closer together, the collective memory of unspoken violence comes to haunt and irreparably break this place. Something strange seems to be in the air. (Cláudia Marques)

aw: Silvestre Prize for Best Short Film (Escola das Artes)

films.syn: In this film, the director brings the Japanese technique of kintsugi (using gold tracing to recover fragmented, broken pieces) to the cinema, “piecing together” — with the parsimonious help of sound and a transhuman walk through the Basque landscape — some disparate but very personal elements: Oskar Alegría’s father’s Super-8 camera, two unused film reels and two pieces of footage stored, all intact after 41 years. “This film is about a path. But above all about a way of walking.” The director rescued his father’s Super-8 and travelled through what was familiar to him: the remains of home and an old shepherd’s trail. Forty years ago, the film camera went silent just as Oskar Alegria’s grandfather’s voice was about to be recorded for later remembrance. From this premise, Zinzindurru n karratz takes us to listen for the first time, weaving the principles of cinema that we always take for granted: the synchronism of sound and image. In this inventory of small gestures of nostalgia, we realise how impossible it is to hold on to the thread of the present moment, since the imprint of the past and ancestral knowledge on the ground is so tangible. (Bianca Dias)

The Popular Unity Table was part of the furniture that, in the post-Independence period, the Mozambican State intended to attribute to all families and brought together the socialist idea of equality and social justice with the concept of National Unity, Frelimo’s basic assumption for the harmonious development of the country. Today, we sit down at that table again, to revisit the process of building a Nation and the utopia of a more just society.
Markus Maicher compresses a decade of home movies to give us this digital autobiography that overwhelms and disturbs our senses. There’s nothing quite like nostalgia at the speed of light.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: European Short Film Network)

films.syn: There are ordinary situations that sometimes lead to dramatic consequences. That’s what happens in this story, in which a disagreement between two children on a sports day leads their parents to take extreme measures. Families gather in the school’s gymnasium to watch a children’s championship — so what could go wrong? In Sinan Taner’s fun debut, apparently, everything. An elderly man refuses to give up his seat in the stands, a lady ignores the long line at the snack bar while tasting every wine available, and a simple misunderstanding between two boys sparks a violent escalation between their parents. With its delightful zooms (especially the hilarious shot of a pigeon), expressive plongées, and meticulous sound design, the mise-en-scène keeps the tension palpable, revealing, with every gesture and confrontation, the worst side of human nature. (Pedro Gonçalves Ribeiro)

A performance involving three artists (Bartlett, Klinkowstein, Tanbellini) who have never met, are in three different parts of the world (Holland, Canada, United States) and will try to work at the speed of a freeze frame.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: European Short Film Network)

films.syn: António wakes up to find an exact replica of himself floating inanimate in the pool. Without explanation, he and his family try to deal with the confusion, mistrust and a sense of mourning that settles in between them. Between absurdity and conflict, life goes on, undisturbed, as if not much had changed. What if one day you find your double dead in your swimming pool and the whole family is planning to mourn him? Starting from this absurd situation, filmmaker Tiago Rosa-Rosso, who has already accustomed us to ambiguous, ambivalent and strange situations in his films, once again takes the water to his mill, proposing a comedy of surprises, in an obvious theatrical game, in which a holiday home becomes a real stage. Little by little, the film turns into a kind of comic tragedy in which the protagonist seems to be living a reality that is beyond him. And the more the protagonist tries to understand the situation, the more he seems to bury himself in an idea of Kafkaesque absurdity, from which there is no possible way out in which everyone will emerge unscathed. But Rosa-Rosso masters this theatre game and its actors, making us believe in the impossible. (Miguel Valverde)

At the producer’s request, the screening on May 7 – C.118, will not have descriptive subtitles in Portuguese. It’s springtime in Lisbon and Nicolau turns 24, but he’s not celebrating. Living in his parents’ house, hostage to a dream of being a musician that never comes true and plagued by the ideal image of an ex-girlfriend who left him a year ago and never came back, Nicolau feels incapable of moving forward and inventing a life of his own. He takes odd jobs until the day he discovers that his mother is just as dissatisfied with life as he is. Nicolau is shaken, but he doesn’t stumble. ‘Of all the things that are certain, the most certain and known is doubt’, is sung at the start of the film, which takes us through Nicolau’s uncertainties in current Lisbon. The young man’s footsteps guide us through bars and meetings, nights and walks, the city welcomes us bright and nocturnal. A long-distance love, friendships and Nicolau moves between rehearsals, bookshops, cafés, the cinematheque, random encounters. He gravitates towards the desire to be a musician, not knowing and letting go in the lightness of spring. (Carlota Gonçalves)

The weight of religion is felt in Elahe’s life when she returns to Mashhad, Iran, the city where she grew up. Her parents are moving house and she’s going to help them move — but the address isn’t the only thing she wants to help change. Elahe returns to the city where she grew up – Mashhad, Iran – to help her parents with a move. Returning to her hometown brings her face-to-face with a past in which the director no longer recognizes herself. A Move is, in every sense, a film about courage, rupture, and new beginnings. But above all, it is a film about confrontation: with tradition, with family, with culture. The use of the hijab is approached as a key element in the struggle for personal autonomy of Iranian women, who live in a fragile balance between conformity and possible resistance. Sometimes, the solitary act of a woman can be the starting point for a deep transformation, inspiring others to challenge conventions and seek collective change. (Jéssica Pestana)

films.t: A Round of Applause for Death
films.syn: This atmospheric short takes us through dreams with different abstract scenarios of murder and manslaughter, all ending with a round of applause for Death, the conclusion of all (these) dreams. A secondary character in many films and works of art over the centuries, Death takes center stage here for a change. In this short film by Stephen Irwin – not to be confused with the ill-fated Australian naturalist of the same name – the tone is sometimes serious, sometimes ironic and even funny, but the aesthetic is always sombre. Is this an exploration of the end-of-the-world mood we’re all feeling? An existential vent about the only certainty we have in this life? A morbid observation on the spectacularization of pain and tragedy? We don’t know. But we are well entertained as we watch this series of short sketches in which Death is always the protagonist. So we applaud it. (Bruno Pereira)

films.t: Antígona ou a História de Sara Benoliel
films.syn: Sara loses her brother due to complications from the Covid-19 virus, starting a journey where she looks for a traditional burial that respects the memory of her brother and the Cape Verdean culture. In a world silenced by the pandemic, Sara will find her mourning in forgotten communities. An ode to life. A woman in a mask looks at us, the spectators, in a sweet and sad lament, as she hears the news of the death of her brother, Ulisses Benoliel, in the covid-19 pandemic. This Antigone/Sara, synonymous with strength and perseverance, wants to be absolutely sure that the man she is burying is her brother and that the funeral takes place according to the tradition of Cape Verdean culture. All things that were impossible at the time. But the heart and determination of Sara, whose camera stubbornly watches and exacerbates (and appeases) every emotion, drives her to move mountains. This first film by Mira Godinho, whom we know from other projects by Leonor Teles, Miguel Nunes and Bernardo Lopes, demonstrates the strength of his gaze, his ability to synthesise and a delicate work with non-actors, which stems from a communal desire to celebrate cinema, made with people and their emotions. That’s why we feel that this directorial debut is something precious and unique. It’s a film that will stay with us, that we will like more and more and that the future will show its place. (Miguel Valverde)

aw: Prize for Best Portuguese Short Film

films.syn: A delicate subject, filmed in a raw and lucid way. Nina is an obstetrician who is being accused of negligence. Nina is also the only possible help patients have in this rural community in Georgia where abortion is illegal. A cry for women’s bodily autonomy and the weight of fighting against institutions that don’t grant this freedom. The film won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival. After Beginning , the first film by Georgian filmmaker Dea Kulumbegashvili, which won a historic victory at San Sebastián (Best Film, Best Director, Best Screenplay, and Best Actress), expectations were high, and Kulumbegashvili amazes again: with her second feature, April , she won the Special Jury Prize at Venice. The film’s title anticipates its inexorable symbolism: April is the month of renewal, but also the cruellest month. Through a unique and meticulous cinematic language, Kulumbegashvili captures the rural beauty of Georgia, the blossoming of trees, and the changing of the seasons, all indices of a OB-GYN’s, Nina, journey of self-discovery. The director immerses the audience in the emotional state of her protagonist, creating a claustrophobic and immersive atmosphere where the constant tension in the life of a woman who refuses to be silenced by a patriarchal society is palpable. Dea Kulumbegashvili’s latest cinematic work challenges conventions and offers a profound reflection on abortion and the ramifications of that decision, putting the self-determination of women’s bodies at the forefront—an ongoing and urgent struggle. Produced by Luca Guadagnino, April is a truly captivating film that leaves an indelible mark and invites the viewer to rethink women’s autonomy and their right to control their own bodies and destinies. This film features scenes that could shock the sensitivity of some viewers. (Alexandra Ferraz)
A pattern of pixels evolved into a continuous loop. An experience inspired by the first video arcade games, with a soundtrack produced by converting images into audio.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: European Short Film Network)

films.syn: Léonor Serraille brings us a delicate, warm and suis generis character study, which unfolds its meanings as it goes along. The titular Ari wants to be a primary school teacher but collapses during an episode in class that becomes the catalyst for a journey alone in the city, in search of a friend who might be a safe haven, and in which he revisits his choices and his future.

A boat on which everyone is asleep. An actress who arrives in the Azores to join a theatrical tour of The Tempest , but finds something unexpected and magical instead. The whole island is a stage and all of Shakespeare’s plays are performed throughout the day. The world of the movie merges with the world of the play and with the real world and we immerse ourselves in this poetic and metatextual game. How many adaptations — modern, post-modern, contemporary — are there of Shakespeare? One of the most adapted authors, known by those who have never seen his work, his name is an adjective and, at the same time, a trigger for a list of plays whose titles we know by heart: The Tempest, Romeo and Juliet, Hamlet, and many others. Lois Patiño, who brought us Samsara in 2023, once again brings us a bucolic film, with a cadence that is not far from the languid waves of a tide at sunset. The film plays with ideas of performance, of who is the actor and who is the character, and what exists in the real world and in the world of the narrative, whether they touch and merge or are totally watertight. Here the narrative leaps into life and reality is fiction. In this movie Agustina Muñoz is Agustina Muñoz and Irene Escolar is Ariel, a character from The Tempest, but she is also Irene Escolar and she is also the character Ariel from Lois Patño’s Ariel. Don’t worry, it will all make sense when you see the movie. Ana Cabral Martins

aw: Honda Silvestre Prize for Best Feature Film (ex aequo)

films.syn: A Norwegian thriller starring the incredible Renate Reinsve from The Worst Person in the World (2021), which begins as a not entirely unlikely day for the parents of two students: the two six-year-olds have seemingly had a fight at school and the families are called in to try to clear up the incident. The film won the Caméra d’Or at Cannes for best first feature. What if one day they accuse your child of such a horrible thing and force you to sit in front of an improvised ‘tribunal’ made up of family members, friends and teachers? You could just shake your head, submerge yourself, get angry or listen, which is what Armand ‘s protagonist (Renate Reinsve from The Worst Person in the World (2021)) does. The film takes place almost entirely inside a school building where the facts and procedures to (possibly) take in cases like those described in the film are spelled out. An apparent aggression is the motto for a disagreement between two boys who are classmates, but also the unfolding of a family story with peculiar and unpleasant contours. The classroom, transformed into a theatre stage, allows the actors/ jouers to unleash their anger, passion, drama, comedy (the blood dripping from the teacher’s nose is anti-climactic for the whole scene), energy. The result is an astonishing and virtuoso camera work that enabled its director to win the Caméra D’or Award at the last Cannes Film Festival. As the grandson of Ingmar Bergman and Liv Ullmann, you could say that an apple doesn’t fall far from the tree. (Miguel Valverde)

As seasons change over the course of a year, a square in the center of Lisbon shifts. Repetition is observed through the four windows of a street kiosk. Madalena Fragoso worked at the Praça das Flores kiosk for a year and, during her shift, she used her smartphone to film the day-to-day life of the neighbourhood. As Flores looks at the kiosk space as a filmic dispositif: anchored in space, facing outwards, central and panoramic. Thus, from static shots (almost entirely shot from the inside) that circulate around the circumference of the pavilion, the director stages a kind of inverted panopticon, a watchtower for everyday events. Figures reappear, gestures are repeated, routines are established, as well as their disruption – the tarmacking of the street, the painting of a letterbox, the pruning of trees, a police raid, tourism. This is a choral portrait (as centrifugal as it is centripetal) of a place, understood as a microcosm of (co)existence. But there’s also a spectre that haunts this square: cinephilia. João César Monteiro lived there and Fernando Matos Silva is still around. In As Flores we spy on banality and let ourselves be haunted by absence. (Ricardo Vieira Lisboa At the director’s request, the screening on May 7 • C.406, will not have descriptive subtitles in Portuguese.

The prodigal son returns. Antonio has built a life for himself outside the rural Andalusia of his origins and where his family still resides. When they meet again, tensions are exacerbated by an acute need: Antonio’s twin brother, Javier, has a physical disability that requires care. And everyone needs Antonio’s help. But will he come back to stay?

An animation that proposes something radical: announcing the ecological apocalypse and delivering it by hand. The announcement coming true. In a desolate and decaying desert setting, two perfectly incompatible teenagers face boredom under a scorching sun. Locked in an empty motel, the tension between them grows as they disagree on nearly everything—whether to lie stretched out in the sun or to go down to the sea. News of an imminent apocalypse blares from the radio, but the terrifying warnings are met with calm indifference, as if the end of the world were merely a distant detail. Yet, there are no safe places: the impending danger of catastrophe ultimately leads them to a distressing, and possibly futile, escape in an attempt to save their lives. Apathy and inaction in the face of the announced environmental disaster: here is a portrait we all know too well, and yet we continue to ignore. (Jéssica Pestana)

films.t: Até o Céu Leva Mais ou Menos 15 Minutos
films.syn: The difference between turmoil and harmony can be as little as 15 minutes, which is the time it takes for three children and two mothers to get home on a car journey. A sigh at the end.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Cinema at the Pool)

films.syn: A movie that turns the reality of migration into a fantastical experience. It’s the 1990s and we follow Agata, a girl who leaves her home country alone to live in another one. Her father is left behind and she uses the trip to write to him. Until her pencil falls out and she is forced to talk to the other passengers.

Sara Cwynar returns to IndieLisboa with another film that works according to the logic of the Internet: ideas interconnect like hyperlinks and associations of terms and searches, going, like Alice, down the rabbit hole. From a Mercedes Benz car, we move on to Benzo(diazepine) and the world is our oyster. ‘It started because I couldn’t sleep.’ From this sleep deprivation comes the delirious ‘Baby Blue Benzo’, which starts with the baby blue Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR – a legendary icon from the 1950s that combines racing performance and elegant design – to delve into insomnia, which ‘corresponds to the necessity of vigilance, to a refusal to overlook the horror and injustice that pervade the world.’ The exclusivity of this car gives it an almost mythical status among enthusiasts and collectors, endlessly fuelling desire and anxiety, while insomnia ‘can cause visual distortion, perceptual alterations and hallucinations’. In 1955, at the same time as the 300 SLR was launched, benzodiazepines (Benzo) appeared, drugs that were recognised for treating anxiety and insomnia. Coincidence or not, the sequence of images in the film establishes a relationship between luxury, desire and beauty – evoked in the figure of Pamela Anderson – and proposes a critical reflection on how visual culture shapes reality and influences human experience. (Margarida Moz)

When her boyfriend’s constant complaints (tinged with narcissism that makes her feel invisible) leave her bursting with anger, Laura has to dosomething to get out of this situation where even the landscape is bleak. As I watch and re-watch this new work by the French director Tohé Commaret, a strange anguish overtakes me as I enter Laura’s fragile world. Everything seems adrift: the protagonist herself, the gazes – and the absence of them – the tracking shots, the unanswered calls, and even the faded shades of blue. The buildings around her seem to crumble, while her nails, perfectly made, appear ready to break. A strange coming-of-age, this disturbing work invites us to witness a rupture that resembles the end of the world, only to later reveal a sigh in its stunning microscopic shots of an ant in a garden. (Pedro Gonçalves Ribeiro)
Lines of text that describe what we see flickering on the screen. Pure image, pure sound, and words that enter our subconscious. And maybe stay there.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: European Short Film Network)

films.syn: A film made up of collages that reimagines Cerro Blanco-Guayaquil, in Ecuador, a territory under Swiss rule, its destruction in foreign hands. The voices of rebellion from Latin America and Caribbean radios are highlighted, in a film that makes us want to change the world. The times we live in need films like this. The urgency of responding to what’s happening in the world with an engaged, pamphleteering, outspoken film. We unfold the world map on the table, with the European continent in the centre. The answer and solution are in the title. Below and to the left. The hypothesis of Latin America as resistance, through the voice of guerrilla radio. History is known and repeats itself. The rich will do anything for the poor, except get off their backsides. A performance film with grace and rhythm that puts us in front of the possibility of action. And something has to be done. (Carlos Ramos)

films.t: Between the Sea and the Island
films.ot: Entre o Mar e a Ilha
films.syn: Between the Sea and the Island is a search, an autobiographical archaeology, an essay on the relationship between an island son and his father and the sea. And there are endless layers, thoughts and memories in this space-time “between” this sea and this island. Between the Sea and the Island, by José Rodrigo Freitas, is an intimate and poetic short film that explores the relationship between a son and his father, shaped by distance, the sea, and memory. Blending past and present, the film follows the director’s search for traces of his father a fisherman often absent from the island but deeply connected to the sea. The boat built by the father, once their meeting point at sea, becomes a symbol of connection and absence, now sailing through an almost imaginary space between land and water. A visual essay about what remains unsaid, and the space that exists between people, places, and memories. (Liedson Carvalho)

aw: Novissimos Prize - Honourable Mention

films.syn: A film with DIY origins that premiered at the SXSW festival in 2014, featuring a collection of scenes from teen movies, particularly from 1995 and 2004 — the title is a reference to Clueless , the successful 1990s teen movie with Alicia Silverstone that adapts Jane Austen to the American high school. The narration is by Fairuza Balk, the protagonist of The Craft , and includes an original soundtrack by the British duo Summer Camp.

You are about to die. Your death rite of choice is Celestial Bridging. In Black Hole Descending the boundaries between life and death blur as this obscure ritual unfolds. Using the particular lingo of educational science or sci-fi films, Rita Macedo proposes a mental experiment in which the perceptual contradictions of quantum and relativity theories are playfully highlighted near the edge of a black hole – and she does this for the second time, remember This particular nowhere (2015), where physicist Eugene Wigner’s proposal about the influence of the observer (of the observer) was taken literally in an infinite succession of linked gazes. The director presents a situation of ‘celestial bridging’ where a death gasp occurs near the event horizon, where the fabric of space-time is highly distorted. What results is a paradox between the experience of death (fleeting) and the vision of mourning (immensely distended). Black Hole Descending orchestrates this solemn event to – in the most literal way and as an expression of queer desire – turn it into a slow-motion slapstick gag. ‘In space, no one can hear you laugh.’ (Ricardo Vieira Lisboa)

Kahlil Joseph is best known for his work on Beyoncé’s music film Lemonade . Now he’s making his feature debut with BLKNWS: Terms & Conditions , a film that draws inspiration from everywhere: it’s Afro-futuristic fiction, an archival investigation, a multimedia work, an intimate and personal story and an exploration of the collective memory of the Black diaspora. It’s an ambitious and audacious project, which maintains its connection with music and video installation.

Sometimes being in your twenties means not having a clear direction in your life and that’s what happens to Errol and Sasha. We see their day-to-day lives unfold in fragments, we see who they are with, what they do, and how they intertwine. But bluish is about this condition of ambiguity in which everything is still possible, not all the choices have been made yet. Errol and Sasha don’t know each other. Despite both being women of a similar age who live in Vienna, a lot seems to separate the two, and their paths never directly cross. Directors Milena Czernovsky and Lilith Kraxner don’t establish a traditional narrative progression, preferring instead to show us fragments of the protagonists’ quotidian existence: we observe their routines, the spaces they inhabit, the silences that surround them and the desires that traverse them. Czernovsky and Kraxner film with care and attention the passage of time in these characters’ lives, and show us with subtle poetry a profoundly contemporary youth, caught between solitude and yearning. Nabil Aouad
Bobel is a mushroom, and a poisonous one at that. But that doesn’t stop him from dreaming of becoming a cook in his village — not that the locals are as keen.

Christopher Andrews writes and directs a film about generational trauma, the baggage of toxic masculinity, what we do when we feel the weight of responsibility, or when we just make the wrong choices at every turn. Two shepherd families with petty rivalries find themselves on a collision course where every gesture escalates the situation. With Barry Keoghan and Christopher Abbott. Christopher Abbott is Michael O’Shea, a young man who is introduced to us as having a violent streak and a difficult relationship with his father, Ray (Colm Meaney), and the family legacy, which involves an ancestral vocation for pastoralism. Barry Keoghan is Jack, the son of Gary (Paul Ready) and Caroline (Nora-Jane Noone), Michael’s ex-girlfriend. These two families see their paths intertwined by petty choices that will dictate everyone’s future. This is a generational portrait that struggles with the weight of tradition and the fragility of life in rural Ireland. Christopher Andrews doesn’t give us a black and white world, there are no good guys or bad guys, there are people broken by life and the choices they make to survive. The beauty of the landscape is the metaphorical ray of sunshine in the narrative and Abbott and Keoghan are masterful in the way they capture the violence and vulnerability, with a soupçon of tragicness, of their characters. (Ana Cabral Martins)

A film about surviving something that didn’t go as expected. Manuel is going through a break-up with Camila, and, at the same time, he has to rethink the whole artistic project that has been his focus for the last few years. To give Camila space to pack, he leaves for a seaside location, where he continues his preoccupation with recording sounds of all kinds. His inertia about the future will be challenged by something extraordinary that happens to him on the beach.

Adilkhan Yerzhanov had his brilliant Steppenwolf at last year’s IndieLisboa and now returns with Cadet , with this film being a gesture that changes the pace from the dystopian westerns of the director’s past. Also returning is Anna Starchenko, who plays Alina, the mother of Serik, a shy boy who is bullied by his classmates and teachers in a military school where violence haunts every corridor. Serik is the new student at the most prestigious military school in Kazakhstan, where his mother,Alina, works as a teacher. From the very beginning, it’s clear that his adjustment will be difficult: he is a shy boy, slight in build and vaguely androgynous—traits that draw mocking stares and harsh criticism in an environment defined by rigidity and discipline. The school, however, is shaken by a series of mysterious deaths, which the authorities handle with inexplicable indifference. Alina finds herself lost in the confusion stirred by these events. Suicides or homicides? Through the dark paths of masculinity construction, bullying, physical violence, and psychological terror, Adilkhan Yerzhanov also reveals other ghosts: the repressed echoes of the Soviet past. (Jéssica Pestana)

Restoration of a cult movie set in a post-apocalyptic world, embracing science-fiction ideas, where pornography springs from sexual frustration. This is Café Flesh , where in the aftermath of a nuclear event, 99% of the survivors can’t stand human touch and can’t have sex (the sex negatives). The minority, the sex positives, are placed in a position of entertainment for the rest, an erotic-musical theater. The imminent arrival of sex legend Johnny Rico tests a breaking couple. Imagine the iconic Cabaret reset in a Reagan-era post-apocalyptic nightmare, trading the glamour of Weimar Germany for heroin chic and with a stage filled with pornographic performances instead of musical numbers. In this surreal setting, sex-negative customers flock to Café Flesh to watch sex-positive actors forcibly engage in explicit acts, and the premise is as straightforward as that. Yet the director Stephen Sayadian aka Rinse Dream, who has made himself a name as a creative director at Hustler Magazine, hijacks the world of adult film, venturing into freakish and/or subversive territories. Picture a man dressed as pencil mounting a woman on a desk, who monotonously asks, “Should I take a memo?”, or a giant rat man engaging in a 69 with a girl in front of a crowd of screaming man-babies. The camera uncomfortably turns its eye to the voyeuristic audience, and their dead eyes and gaping mouths get at least as much screen time as the folds of flesh and the mechanical thrusts of the bodies on stage. As Sayadian’s co-writer puts it, it’s a “fuck you” to pornography. It’s not a surprise then that the film flopped in the traditional porn market, before it gained cult status as a midnight movie.
