Presented in a newly restored digital print. (Anastasia Lukovnikova)
The director just wanted to test a new camera and use an expired 16mm film stock. Seeing his crew out of ideas, Charlie Shackleton tells an amusing family story involving a 1963 Cadbury ad.

A serene but complex film that begins with an investigation into the craftsmanship of the zampogna, a kind of bagpipe from Calabria, to expand into a more general overview of a series of local traditions, seven to be precise, from various regions of Italy — Calabria, Marche, Liguria and Sicily. A film that speaks of traditions that cross generations, with a delicate and contemporary gaze, so that certain musical expressions of the oral tradition survive. Starting with the construction of a zampogna, a traditional Italian wind instrument, the De Serio twin brothers guide us through various regions of a deep Italy in a remarkable journey of musical collections and oral traditions. The pleasure of discovery and slowing down, in stark contrast to contemporary life in big cities, leads to encounters with music, stories, landscapes, and people who are guardians of memory and identity. A work close in spirit to the gestures of Michel Giacometti in his series Povo que Canta, with his musical and oral recordings throughout rural Portugal in the early 1970s, yet the De Serio brothers move away from a direct documentation style, opting instead for a poetic and cinematically fascinating approach. (Carlos Ramos)

Based on true events, we follow Vera, Madalena, Conceição and Gabriela, victims of domestic violence in a shelter. Together, they rediscover their place as they try to gain the independence and security to start their lives anew. Each episode is dedicated to one of the women and also to Joana, the psychologist who works with them. These are personal and unique testimonies of women who are not limited to the dramatic situation in which they find themselves, without ever being able to forget it. Almost a home-grown filmmaker, Laranjeira premiered his first film (a school film) at IndieLisboa in 2008. After some shorts, we then saw it grow into a feature film, and now he’s taking a new step towards television series, in a very special project called Casa-Abrigo . As the name might suggest, this mini-series will talk about domestic violence, about women (especially women) who have to find the courage to report the crime and, at the same time, run away from the aggressor, because in this period, violence always escalates, hence the number of fatalities among married women due to crimes perpetrated by their partners. The series follows a group of women who meet in the house, featuring actresses such as Maria João Pinho, Leonor Silveira and Rita Cabaço who play different women, all with a history of violence. Unlike most films and series that may want to exercise pity, this one exercises strength, courage and the assumption of fear. All because you feel that this story is so real that it hits you head on. (Miguel Valverde)

Chinese director Jia Zhang-ke tells the story of a failed romance that unfolds over 20 years, with an evolving China in the background. But the focus is on Qiao, a singer and dancer who gets involved with a dubious music producer, Bin, who leaves her to try his luck in another city, promising to send for her when he has money. Qiao, waiting, writes to him and, receiving no reply, decides to go searching for Bin. The adventure is not without its perils.

A short film that takes us back to the nostalgic 1990s and the TV guide that accompanied the day’s broadcasts. Here, we follow a very bad day in the life of the CEO of a cable channel who sees her programming attacked by mischievous hackers. Edible Arraignments. Gladiator Moms. Diagnosis: Death. Go Attack! Okay? Farts: Reloaded. Trolley Problem: Live! Dog Court. These are just some of the programs that flash across the screen as we spend time on this channel dedicated to guiding the viewer through the day’s broadcasts. What may start as normal American television names quickly becomes a succession of increasingly absurd examples, with constant references to series or films. This is one of the funniest aspects of Channelvue , in a short film that shows a wildly entertaining descent into madness — and (almost?) makes us feel sorry for this CEO so focused on maintaining order — that aims to satirize the violence imbued in American consumer culture. To transport us to the 1990s, a vintage Betacam, reprogrammed original Prevue Channel software and a Commodore Amiga emulator were used to create the visuals. (Ana Cabral Martins)

An innocuous beginning: Yoshii has a job that doesn’t satisfy him. What does satisfy him is the adrenaline rush of reselling products online in order to exceed his initial investment. The adrenaline becomes addictive and so does the money. But the film develops into something much more intriguing when his behavior in the digital world begins to have very real consequences in real life and the hostility that would remain in a comment section is taken to its ultimate consequences.

Charlie Shackleton explores a possible vein of inspiration for one of the most successful horror films in American cinema, Wes Craven’s iconic Scream (1996): an obscure film by Rolfe Kanefsky, There’s Nothing Out There , which works in the same metatextual universe that winks at the horror genre.

A cult movie from 1971 that plays with the erotic and the terrifying and is now available in a restored format. Based on the legend of Elizabeth Bathory, a Hungarian countess who killed young women in the 16th and 17th centuries, Hary Kümel co-wrote and directed this film, which is set in a Belgian hotel by the sea, empty because it’s winter. A young newlywed couple (who should have chosen another location) meet a lesbian countess (played by Delphine Seyrig) and her apparent secretary, both shrouded in an air of mystery. With Les Lèvres rouges, aka The Daughters of Darkness, Delphine Seyrig takes a daring leap into a role that’s as magnetic as it is eccentric. What could possibly draw her to the démodé character of Countess Báthory who’s playing a game of seduction with a seemingly innocent couple of newlyweds against the Ostend’s stormy landscapes? Is it the sheer delight of camp, champagne, and glitter? A myriad of stunning gowns? Perhaps it’s the quirky blend of genres where vampire lore collides with arthouse flair? Or maybe it’s a playful nod to the legendary Marlene Dietrich? Could it be a rare opportunity to embody female homosexual desire? Whatever the reason, it all comes together beautifully, resulting in a bit of a trashy tale of a woman’s emancipation, where danger leads to liberation, and seduction is salvation. 4K restoration of a 70’s kind of cult classic. (Anastasia Lukovnikova)
A translation game that takes Edwin Abbott Abbott’s novel Flatland into the world of digital image compression algorithms.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: European Short Film Network)

films.syn: When we move house we want to make it our home. We bring our things, organize everything and the space becomes ours. But as the months go by in her new apartment, Daniela notices that her clothes are beginning to show strange shapes and holes. What could be causing this?

Presentation of the restored version of this cult but little-seen Spanish film which, despite its homoerotic disruption, slipped through the cracks of Franco’s censorship. Over the years, the film’s rediscovery has affirmed its importance for its contribution to the history of Spanish musicals and its representation of a non-normative sexuality. In Different , we follow Alfredo, a bon vivant who rejects the precepts of his wealthy family at the same time as they reject him. A eulogy to the pleasures of queer extravagance. Alfredo (Alfredo Alaría – the name coincidence demonstrates the self-reflexive dimension of the film, since as well as playing the lead role, Alaría was also the co-writer and responsible for the film’s choreography) is the ‘hedonistic’ and ‘eccentric’ son of a wealthy and conservative family. His love of theatre and dance leads him to hang out with ‘bad company’. Diferente is an extravagant queer musical set in Francoist Spain. Littered with homoerotic innuendo (sometimes not very subtle), the film stars an ostentatiously gay character whose desire is represented with no moralistic overtones, and yet it still managed to escape censorship (“not a single frame was taken away, not one. The first person to come out of the screening was Father Benito, who exclaimed: ‘It’s the first artistic film I’ve ever seen in my life!'” recalled director Luis María Delgado years later). Critic and film programmer Olaf Möller described it in Sight and Sound magazine as “a camp film avant la lettre made on a generous budget. It’s eye-popping. It’s mind-blowing. It’s unique. It’s a true pioneer.” (Ricardo Vieira Lisboa)

For Júlia, life in Glasgow is a way of starting fresh, of creating something that is hers alone, without interference from her family, from those she knows, from her history so far. But her brother, in Barcelona, wants to maintain the bridge that unites them. And bridges are Julia’s favorite thing to photograph, until her eyesight begins to fail.

Two sisters, Ernesta and Justė, go with their husbands and children to a lake house for a weekend away. The differences between their marriages, and their relationships with their children, are highlighted over the course of the days. Until a traumatic event occurs and it’s the beginning of something that will mark the family forever. This Lithuanian drama is told in a series of flashbacks, revealing its layers.

In the path between the house and the church, doubt has settled. Clinging to the faint memory of the faith that once was certain, a nun repeats barren and mechanical rituals, hoping for different outcomes. In her involuntary penitence, risking the profane, she seems to fear both the abyss of mourning and the luminous power of ecstasy. On this day of celebration for Pope Francisco, the idea that the church is made up of ‘mechanical and sterile rituals’, repetitive and always waiting for something to change or for a miracle to happen, continues to be perpetuated. In a highly contrasted black and white, which lights up every shot, every moment, this first film by Pedro Baptista brings us a nun who, following her vocation and the movement expected of her, begins to have doubts. She begins to question herself, to look around, to become aware of her own repetitive movements. And so the profane interferes, darkness and light fight, and the outcome is uncertain. In a complex game with a choreography of a body, a church, a countryside landscape and a sound silence, a moment of cinema is fused. Oh God, and now, which way should I go? (Miguel Valverde)

Ana, Malú and Martina already have a strategy in place: find some rich guys, seduce them, put them to sleep and steal their money. And as in other stories like this, they only have one last job to do. The target is an eccentric millionaire who manages cryptocurrencies. The plan goes wrong, the dosages are miscalculated and they discover that being alive is not necessarily the opposite of being dead. But being dead is perhaps the best time to discover love. El tema del verano could’ve been just a movie about zombies, just be a romantic comedy with zombies involved, or even be an allegory of the pandemic with zombies on the margins. But it’s much more than that. This film is a satire on a certain kind of lover of capitalism made up of cryptocurrencies, of a certain kind of dilettante or derivative artist, of a certain kind of arts patron. Uruguayan director Pablo Stoll risk a little juggling act of various ideas that results in something amusing and unexpected. The actresses, Azul Fernández, Débora Nishimoto and Malena Villa (El llanto), are a charming and intriguing trio and the key to the film’s charm. (Ana Cabral Martins)

A movie that thinks of death, or rather life, as having an epilogue. Imagine that if using the ashes of someone who died and was dear to us, we could talk to them again, relive the moments we spent together and have a new perspective on the life we shared. That’s what happens to this husband, devastated by his wife’s death.

Signing briefly as Charlie Lyne, Shackleton travels through a plethora of horror films (apart from the opening and closing sequences). It comprises material from other films (classic, cult, etc.) to explore the viewer’s relationship with fear and cinema.

films.t: Filhos do Meio – South Side Hip Hop Stories
films.ot: Filhos do Meio - Hip Hop à Margem
films.syn: This film tells the story of rap music in Almada and Miratejo, one of the first major spots of this musical genre in Portugal. Guided by the protagonists who built and lived the movement intensively, we travel through their memories, stories, and inspirations to discover the great landmarks of this culture on the south banks of the Tagus River — built in a territory of demanding and politized working classes, with great cultural diversity in the post-Carnation Revolution. Without being a history of Portuguese hip hop, “Filhos do Meio – Hip Hop à Margem” drives us straight to its epicenter, by which we mean the south bank of the Tejo river, Almada, Miratejo and the neighborhoods where hip hop first fermented and came to fruition in Portugal. It is a movie of memories, told by those who were there in the founding years of the 1990s, a movie that, through period photos and raw, evocative archive footage, takes us into the heart of the action, rhymes breaking out in defiance in the streets, the concerts, the recordings. “Filhos do Meio – Hip Hop à Margem” is an important document: It offers us a story yet to be told, that of Portuguese hip hop, with its center in Almada, narrated through those who were there and stood out, such as Black Company, Líderes da Nova Mensagem or Chullage, but also by fundamental names that, without published music to ensure the generational passage, could fall into oblivion – it is important, then, to know about a group like Nexo. “Filhos do Meio – Hip Hop à Margem” doesn’t stop there, though. This is a documentary about hip hop, but it’s also about the land and the cultural context that led to its emergence. It’s the past rediscovered, but it doesn’t stop at nostalgia, it moves forward till the present. (Mário Lopes)

Emily Wilson returns after her previous short, Danny’s Girl . This time, the protagonists are two sisters, Dinky and Flossy, who couldn’t be worse off. They need money and they need it now . And that means a visit to their father, who is suddenly looking very wealthy.

Mateus Lagoa and his wife Irene will celebrate their 20th anniversary at a luxurious resort on a tropical island, leaving their teenage son dangerously adrift. There is a characteristic in Sandro Aguilar’s cinema that sets him apart from all other Portuguese filmmakers. His ability to tell elliptical narratives, at the same time accompanied by timelessness, by an intextuality between text and image, which he always embodies in unique artistic objects. First Person Plural adds humour, sensuality and more elegance to his previous works. This is a piece of cinema that doesn’t respond (as current cinema tends to do) to the issues on the agenda of the day. Aguilar’s cinema is part of a deeper line of cinema, which is the reflection of image and sound, for a time of its own that is conditioned by the experience of cinema itself. The trio of actors, Isabel Abreu, Albano Jerónimo and Eduardo Aguilar, play multiple characters, creating forms that go beyond the normal composition of a character, because they speak with their bodies, their expressions and their presence. This is a film that, being outside of a present time, brings us back to our present. A couple celebrates 20 years of marriage and goes travelling, their son stays at home amidst the doubts of his adolescence/youth. From here, the possibilities are endless, because it’s Aguilar’s gesture, controlled improvisation and sense of narrative that command, like a conductor, an orchestra of elements that lead us to a Portuguese Marienbad. (Miguel Valverde)

A film that threads the blurred line between documentary and fiction to explore a story that seems to be more myth than reality: Caspar Salmon tells us how, in 1980, he attended a meeting on an island in Wales where only people with surnames related to fish were present.

Carolina, Carlota, Clara and Constança are four sisters whose parents have insisted, every year, on taking the same picture. In Porto Santo beach, from 2003 to 2024, Clara Figueiredo narrates her childhood memories, which she associates to each of the pictures, reflecting upon the sisters. ‘Between the first and the last photograph, they changed, the world changed, but neither the beach nor the family has. Since 2003, Carolina, Carlota, Clara and Constança have been ritually photographed by their parents every year. Clara, the third of the sisters – and the film’s director – reflects on these images that awaken happy memories, reflect on the process of growing up and talk about the bonds of sorority. (Catherine Boutaud)

A stop-motion animation about a creature that has become too afraid to leave its cage, even when that’s already possible. What brings it out of its shyness cocoon is something that needs to be taken care of.

A short film that lets itself be carried away in a carefree and abstract dance focused on freedom of movement. We’re on a snow-white summit and the immaculate scenery is interrupted by the excitement of skiing down the mountain.

In one of the last rural schools on the border between Galicia and Portugal, Mariana, a four-year-old girl, discovers the world through the stories and legends told by her teacher. As Mariana grows, these tales and the passage of time shape her view of the world, until at eighteen, she faces a crucial decision: to leave her village or remain in this borderland by her mother’s side. Looking at a place again so that it remains new. Is it possible to understand the immutability of a time that never stops moving forward? Gods of Stone is undoubtedly a cinematic gem in which the time and space of the frontier are challenged through the tireless metamorphosis of images that never stop searching. Legends, myths and memories intertwine in the echoes of ancient voices. And yet it’s all a story. A reflection of the passage of existence. (Miquel Escudero Diéguez)

aw: Prize for Best Direction for a Portuguese Feature Film - Special Mention

films.syn: Yuyan Wang, a Chinese director and artist now based in Paris, imagines a world where oil, or an oil-like substance, is the glue that holds everything together, an allegory that messes with global notions of capitalism and extraction and questions the future — of this world and ours. Yuyan Wang once again demonstrates exceptional mastery in exploring the plastic and rhythmic possibilities of editing, manipulating images sourced from the internet to build a critical reflection on technology. Here, it is the gory logics of petro-capitalism that is exposed and orchestrated to the rhythm of the machine — and of the black ooze that drips like a living organism — the hidden side of the technological promise of a bright future. One might say Wang manipulates even sound: a hit from the 1980s appears here distorted, dragged out like the oil flowing through the images. The result is a truly hypnotic visual and sonic trip, in which we find ourselves watching with melancholy the imagery of the most concrete apocalypse. (Cláudia Marques)

On a remote volcanic island, where everyone wants to leave, little Nana learns, between tides, to want to stay. “Mother, within us, broken pieces are glued together with gold,” says the protagonist Nana, anchored in the future, to her mother in the time just before her birth and before departing the island, leaving her in the care of her grandmother. Denise Fernandes’ debut feature film impresses with the serenity and empathy with which it weaves a visual poem in the form of a film, both through its dramaturgy and the sequence of imagery it creates. It’s an evocative journey, with elements of magical realism, exploring notions of identity and belonging as it follows the protagonist’s path from childhood to young adolescence on the island of Fogo, in Cape Verde. She faces her mother’s abandonment, supported by a community, with melancholy but without falling into any trauma moralism. The tone is always affectionate, focused on giving new meaning to the broken pieces. Several family members or acquaintances leave that place, while she, in contrast to the dominant narrative, achieves full emancipation—by choosing to stay. (Susana Santos Rodrigues)

aw: MAX Prize for Best Portuguese Feature Film

films.syn: An allegorical movie about the power of trying to fight what threatens those we love. Fien enlists the help of their parents to help her sister Hannah get rid of a malicious crocodile that alarms her.

Jay Rosenblatt is a softy. In this moving film, the protagonists are the filmmakers, couple Jay Rosenblatt and Stephanie Rapp, who set out on a journey 25 years ago in order to have their own offspring. 25 years later, the movie is in dialogue with the contemporary erosion of reproductive rights. In an intimate documentary, ‘Heartbeat’ questions the limits of privacy. Jay Rosenblatt, who has already been honoured at IndieLisboa in 2006, teams up with Stephanie Rapp, his wife, to direct this visual diary filmed 25 years ago when they decided to become parents. The agreement was to film each other without restrictions, allowing them to capture moments of the couple’s daily life, avoiding censorship and prejudice. The result is a work of editing that, so many years after the images were taken, reveals significant choices, where what you see ends the very second you don’t want to see any more. What could be embarrassing becomes an affirmation of their personal freedom, suggesting that the discomfort we feel reflects our own circumstances. The film exists and makes sense because so much time has passed between what we see and where we are now, and this striking temporal distance, which echoes the spirit of the previous film, ‘How do you measure a year?’, is both terrifying and fascinating. (Margarida Moz)

Spring is a time of renewal. Nature comes out of a period of hibernation to strut its stuff in all its splendor. In the south of Italy, in Basilicata, this moment is celebrated with an arboreal wedding rite in the form of a dance, in which human beings join hands with the natural world to achieve something sublime together. Every spring, a pagan rite takes place in the Italian region of Basilicata, consisting of a marriage of two trees. Angelo Toscano not only has the merit of preserving this rite with his film, which is in danger of disappearing like many other regional customs throughout Italy and Europe, but he does so with a mysterious contemplation and respect for the passage of time. It’s a courageous film by someone thinking about an idea for cinema while observing the union between human beings and nature. (Carlos Ramos)

Hemel is Hemel Hempstead, the director’s hometown, which was a planned community. Danielle Dean places the history of Hemel Hempstead in dialogue with a horror and science fiction film shot on location and explores the relationship between the two. Hemel is a personal essay that combines science fiction and documentary to explore Hemel Hempstead, the director’s hometown and a symbol of British modernist urbanism – a post-war attempt to rethink the city and the community. This may also be why the B-movie The Strange World of Planet X was filmed there in 1957, about an alien entity that infiltrates human minds with sinister thoughts, echoing the anxieties of a space moulded by social engineering. Between the planned utopia and the disenchantment of an unforeseen socio-cultural complexity, Danielle Dean plays a character composed between herself and the film’s detective, linking real and fiction, past and present. With archive footage, 16mm filming and extraordinary sound work, the film constructs an anachronistic universe that both elucidates and deepens the mystery and ghosts of a small town with modernist promises. (Margarida Moz)

At just 15 years old, Lois embarks on an investigation to discover the fate of her sister’s soul, who died tragically and too soon. In the middle of Arkansas, to dare to ask is to dare to hope. The storytelling prowess of Holy Water is absolutely disarming. It is the product of an acute examination of the director’s memories of growing up in an ultra-religious environment (Claire Barnett was raised in a Baptist community). In fact, it’s a period film and dates back to the time when a wave of teenage suicides began in that same community. As a period piece, the film takes on an ambiguous status: it is set in a specific time, the late 2000s (at one point we see a CD of Radiohead’s In Rainbows ), but it also feels like a revision of the teens films of the 1990s (with an explicit reference to The Craft ) – a revision fraught with the trauma of loss and the contradictory feelings of guilt. The impact of Holy Water lies in the restrained nature of the filmmaking, in the succinct and unflustered way in which the scenes are constructed and the action organised and, of course, in the way in which the actress Abby Miner transcends the pain of loss through the confrontation between the elements: ‘circle of fire’/ ‘holy water’. (Ricardo Vieira Lisboa)
Wouldn’t it be magical to cure loneliness by creating an extraordinary friend? That’s exactly what happens here and one’ll need to be very careful to look after this companion.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Cinema at the Pool)

films.syn: The possibility of having a safe environment in which to have honest conversations about difficult or even taboo topics is essential. Here, Peter is a teacher who gives workshops dealing with sexual and religious issues and he allows his students the space they need to think, feel and talk.

French duo Caroline Poggi and Jonathan Vinel ( Jessica Forever , Eat the Night ) return with an animated short in which a cow, an elephant, a penguin, a lion, a pig, a wolf, a monkey and a rabbit try to change the world by curing the ills that afflict it. In a natural and organic world devoid of human intervention, live-action footage of the real world is overlaid with its inhabitants, a diverse little group of CGI animals, with an aesthetic reminiscent of mass-produced cartoons, Instagram reels for fetuses, and the lights and colors of Cocomelon . On an isolated holiday away from the rest of the world, we witness the everyday clashes of these little digital animals with foul mouths and minds colonized by contemporary smog (and completely sick of this oppression). One of them is an elephant. The elephant hosts a podcast. The animals exchange ideas. They swap catchphrases. Fed up with the world. The podcast transmits ideas and catchphrases. For the island to listen, even if it is inhabited only by those who already speak. Either very funny or very sad. Both, inseparable. (Vasco Muralha)

films.t: How the Bear Composed a Song
films.syn: A bear can be a very multifaceted and talented animal. In this movie, our bear is going to compose a song, but he won’t be alone: he has the help of many baby animals who are experts at making noise and creating sounds.

Hurikán has a mission: to find a keg of beer that can impress the girl he has a crush on, the waitress at his favorite bar. The mission isn’t easy, but he has to be up to the task. Hurikán , by Jan Saska, is a charming and melancholic animated short with a touch of subtle humor. The story follows a pig who calmly goes to a beer stand, only to fall in love with the human vendor. When the beer keg runs out, she asks him to fetch more from the other side of the city. The pig then embarks on a serene journey, moving through the city in a nostalgic atmosphere, where small details make his mission almost hypnotic. With a stylized animation and a slow-paced rhythm, Hurikán is a simple yet captivating story about longing, persistence, and the unexpected encounters of life. (Liedson Carvalho)
Guy comes across something unexpected while flying through the forest: a discarded box. But a dropped box can be used in many ways. Guy just has to choose one.

films.t: I Want to Know What Love Is
films.syn: Hanna missed her train. Her destination was the event of a DJ in Berlin with whom she’s flirting. Now she has to go on a car ride that raises a lot of questions, including whether all middle-aged men are a bit perverted. Oh, to be young and do the craziest things for love… Who hasn’t? In this unique Swedish production, where the title is taken from the anthem sung by Foreigner and Mariah Carey, our animated heroine misses her train and rushes to hitch a ride to Berlin. She is determined to see her boyfriend, DJ ___snorksenzation__000, play at one of the coolest techno clubs in the city. But love is blind, and not everything is as it seems in this authentic road movie, which started as an art installation and thankfully turned into a film. A work that reminds us that getting disillusioned and having our hearts broken can be painful, but in the end, it’s truly a delight. (Pedro Gonçalves Ribeiro)

A film with a very precise objective: to start from the visual noise of pixels and then find the beauty that lies within them. Made using an Atari Mega 2 ST and software created using Forth and Assembler.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: European Short Film Network)

films.syn: André lives in constant apathy. He sleeps during the day and works in a warehouse at night. Armando rejects all of his son’s attempts to approach him. André mimics his father in the relationship with Júlia.

films.t: In and Out of the Hornbeam Maze
films.syn: A sung and rhymed story that delights us with the more sinister aspects of nursery rhymes. One by one, four children enter a bucolic labyrinth and come face to face with their fears. Based on a horror ballad by Scottish poet Helen Adam. In 1980, Kubrick immortalized the maze as the perfect setting for horror. In 2025, Tomas Stark once again plunges us into that endless, claustrophobic space. Guiding us through its paths are, once more, children—playing, running, or fleeing, descending into the abyss of our personal fears. Inspired by the haunting poem of the same name by Scottish writer Helen Adam, In and Out of the Hornbeam Maze wraps around us like an old lullaby, growing darker with every step, slowly unveiling a disturbing truth: there is no way out. (Jéssica Pestana)

Being in your 30s means having bills to pay and trying to climb the career ladder. But it’s also trying to be an exemplary child to the single parent who raised her. And for Cristine, it’s also about becoming a character who first belonged to a book and will now belongs to a movie. Reality and fiction and meta-fiction merge in this adaptation of Lavinia Braniște’s novel Interior Zero .

A digitally restored version of a fundamental title in the history of Brazilian cinema that mixes fiction and non-fiction in a road movie — starring a young girl from Iracema and an unruly truck driver — that travels through the destruction caused by a specific type of post-colonial capitalism: the construction of the Transamazon Highway. The film explores an area of the Amazon that was under the control of the armed forces at the time of the military dictatorship in Brazil. Iracema, Uma Transa Amazônica is a fundamental work of Brazilian cinema. Firstly, because it calls on cinema to — in parallel with the greedy exploitation of capitalization in the Amazon region carried out by the government at the time — enter this space, documenting the process of land purchase and disfigurement of the terrain with the construction of roads, deceiving and putting at risk many of its population. Instead of a paradisiacal Brazil, the film, banned during the dictatorship, openly brought the environmental issue into play. Secondly, Bodanzky and Senna’s film is an important film for understanding how the tension between fiction and reality, in a method close to Jean Rouch’s shared anthropology, allows us to reach a sense of intense truth. Iracema is constructed without a script, based on the improvisation of the central actors in the “plot” (Paulo César Pereio and Edna de Cássia), and their spontaneous interaction with many of the people, loggers, farmers, prostitutes, who tried to surve in that place. (Carlos Natálio)

Feeling that her mother may no longer be able to live on her own, a woman moves back to her childhood home. As she tries to adapt to the new situation, her mother continues to drift away. It Shouldn’t Rain Tomorrow, by Maria Trigo Teixeira, is a delicate and emotional short film about returning home and facing a parent’s ageing. A woman moves back to her childhood house, feeling her mother can no longer live alone. As she tries to adjust to this new reality and reconnect with her mother, an invisible distance grows between them. While the daughter tries to get closer, the mother slowly drifts away into her own world. A sensitive reflection on fragility, time, and the challenge of dealing with change within the family. (Liedson Carvalho)

dream hampton (who spells her name in lower case, like bell hooks), has made documentaries such as Surviving R. Kelly and Ladies First: A Story of Women in Hip-Hop , but has roots in music journalism, having written influential articles, including on the beginnings of feminist hip-hop theory. hampton shows us the beginnings of the golden age of American hip hop through archive footage from her time interviewing big names like Dr. Dre, Notorious B.I.G., Snoop Dogg and Method Man, between 1993 and 1995. Directed by dream hampton, It Was A Dream is a visual memoir from the director’s personal archive about the beginning of the golden age of rap and hip-hop, in 1993, when she was a journalist, music critic and film student at New York University. At the time, she filmed moments with various superstars, such as her neighbour The Notorious BIG, or names like Snoop Dog, Mobb Dee and Wu-Tang’s Method Man, and many more, taking us inside the studio during the recording of landmark albums in hip-hop history. A time so fruitful that Enter The Wu-Tang (36 Chambers) , Wu-Tang’s debut album, and Midnight Marauders , A Tribe Called Quest’s third full-length, are released on the same day, Salt-N-Pepa’s fourth album, Very Necessary , takes the band into the mainstream, and Doggystyle , Snoop Dog’s debut album, enters at number one on the Billboard 200 , with 800,000 copies sold in its first week, and we were only at the beginning. It’s a film in which we watch mostly unseen archive footage from the early days of this musical genre right through to its global conquest. (Helena César)

A film about distance, loss and the fragility of life symbolized through a garden that fell and a sea that swallowed it up. It went with the sea, her grandparents’ garden. It took with it so many moments of sharing, of family togetherness. It was there that everyone gathered and experienced family life outdoors, in that garden facing the sea. But nature is given to its whims and life has a fragility with which the strength of the sea is not always sympathetic. Gone was the garden with the sea and the photographs and memories of the moments remained. The collapse of the garden opened the way to thinking about loss and with it the time that is thought to last forever: on an island it is the sea that takes those who are no longer there, either because they have ceased to exist or because they have chosen to exist elsewhere. ‘It Went with the Sea’ is, after all, a poem dedicated to the director’s grandparents, her childhood, nature and the island of Madeira where all this intersects. (Margarida Moz)

Anyone who has never strolled along the paths and graves of the Père-Lachaise cemetery while dreaming of Gothic novels and masochistically listening to “Tous les garçons et les filles” until discovering a drawing of a particularly intriguing couple can cast the first stone. There are filmmakers who, due to their continuous practice, figure on the cinema scene as metronomes. Friedl vom Gröller is one such figure. Every year she produces between two and six films on film, almost always in black and white, using only a single 16mm reel, so the films usually last no more than three minutes. Each new film marks a change of season or the start of a new year. They are fleeting, lyrical records of everyday life: portraits of friends (or for friends), records of trips or meetings, ironic or parabolic comments on current affairs. Jelena is based on a song, sung a capella by Jelena Arrouas, ‘Tous les garçons et les filles’. Vom Gröller punctuates the film with bare images that are beyond mere illustration: a hand at the window, a stony staircase, an empty boulevard, two faces in a tomb, piercing eyes, a panning shot facing the winter sun. A harbinger of death bursts from the song’s romantic melancholy. (Ricardo Vieira Lisboa)

Have you ever imagined Jesus returning as an interstellar traveler who didn’t allow anyone to die, everyone hated him and two siblings made secret plans to destroy him? This movie did. In the 1983 banger ‘All Night Long (All Night)’, Lionel Richie sang it like this – “We’re going to Party, Karamu, Fiesta, Forever”. So let’s focus on the possibilities of ‘fiesta,forever’. Jesus 2 uses – inadvertently, almost certainly – the premise of a ‘fiesta, forever’, in a libidinal-surreal and psychedelic adventure set in a futuristic dimension where you can’t die, which is to say, in a futuristic dimension where nobody wants to live anymore. Two space pirates are determined to restore some meaning to their existence and end the curse of immortality. To do this, they will have to eliminate Jesus 2, the evil messiah responsible for these existential anxieties. All this with Midnight Gospel and Adventure Time vibes. Although we live in an age of sequels, prequels, reboots, remasters, shared universes and all that, the Mouth of Madness committee is confident that it’s possible to watch and appreciate Jesus 2 without having seen Jesus 1. (Bruno Pereira)

This captain wanders the sea in search of a particular orange lighthouse with a beautiful light. His search seems to come to nothing until the day he is surprised and something finally comes ashore. Now it’s up to him to decide whether he’s going to fulfill his dreams or not.

A documentary not about the former president of Yugoslavia, Josip Broz Tito, but about his parrot, Koki, very talkative at the age of 67. The film brings together fragments of moments and images in which Koki appears and speaks, including state visits with figures such as Khrushchev or Indira Gandhi. In the beautiful essay Why Look at Animals? , John Berger argues that animals have been expelled from their mythical and symbolic universe over time, becoming mere marginal presences in our lives. Koki, the speaking cockatoo of Josip Broz Tito, leader of Yugoslavia, may be proof that animals still have, and should have, a central role in human history, more than just being their “pets.” Brilliant in introducing the narration of the bird itself, Quenton Miller’s short film also becomes highly political by giving a voice to those other beings who, just like us, also shape the most significant moments of the world, even if they seem to only be in the background. (Pedro Gonçalves Ribeiro)
Nugget is a rooster without a voice and, therefore, unable to sing. When he discovers a squeaky toy, he thinks he’s found the solution — but will it be forever?

La Durmiente explores the story of the medieval Infanta Beatriz of Portugal through fabulation and children’s imagination. Shot at the Monastery of Sancti Spiritus in Toro, Spain, where her tomb lies, these children stage and interpret fragments of the life of this character erased by history. La Durmiente is based on a re-enactment of the figure of Infanta Beatriz of Portugal, proclaimed queen at just 10 years old during the Portuguese dynastic crisis in 1383. A group of children take on the roles, bringing to life situations at court between dinners and meetings, moments of leisure and exploration of space. The film fictionalises and documents, plays with genres, refines details, gestures and looks. The subtilty of the characters and their gracefulness rhythms the beauty of the images. (Carlota Gonçalves)

aw: New Talent Prize McFly

films.syn: A look at Operation Scanner, during Margaret Thatcher’s final days in power, a case where the police arrested 16 men convicted of the crime of filming consensual behavior linked to sadomasochism. Their story has been told by everyone but themselves.

Found footage is a cherished subgenre of horror cinema. Here, it’s a documentation of when a birthday party suddenly found itself without salt. “Gonna party like it’s 1991”. A punk film about a birthday party in 1991 with friends, music, drink, police, but no salt. (Carlos Ramos)

This first feature film by Binka Jeliaskova was made alongside her husband, the screenwriter of many of her works, and focuses on a group of young revolutionaries who witness the death of a comrade at the hands of the Nazi army. Years later, in a country now devastated by unemployment and poverty, one of the survivors, a member of Parliament, decides to erect a statue of his fallen friend. When he finds himself surrounded by critics, he begins a purge. A film, banned for 33 years by the Bulgarian Communist Party, that anticipated Polish protest films, the Czech New Wave and inaugurated the exposure of state totalitarianism that marked the bankruptcy of communism in the Eastern Bloc.

It’s Autumn. A young woman and an older man travel by train to Douro, looking for a light phenomenon. They wait during the day but it’s in the silence of the night that things starts to appear. The invisible becomes visible, but is it still possible to believe? We hear the train, the wind blowing, and suddenly, the Douro Valley pours in through the window. The starting point for this journey: a rare light phenomenon that occurs in that region every 20 years. For many, it’s a myth they’ve never witnessed. Others might say that those who look to the sky are searching for something within themselves or hoping to touch the unattainable. The hunt for the ephemeral sublime in Mariana Santana’s first fiction short film presents us with a naturalistic and incantatory dance between light and shadow, day and night, leading us to reflect on the possible relationship between this girl and this man. A relationship that remains mysterious, where the outer world leaves clues about the inner one. (Susana Santos Rodrigues)
Every creature on this planet must move through life at the pace that is most convenient and pleasurable for them. This can be slow, like our snail, or faster, like a hare, a leopard or an ostrich.

Urzelina is a half-hearted level crossing keeper. In the middle of the day, she drinks a cup with half milk, half coffee and eats half a toast. It is also in the middle, between the past and the present, that her days are spent in service of the railway line. One day, something different happens in her routine. Urzelina, Lina, Line. Through her minimalist style and the repetition of her movements — at times circular, at times linear — Margarida Madeira retrieves from collective memory a profession on the verge of extinction: that of the level crossing guard. A job mostly carried out by women, solitary, repetitive, strictly punctual, and the lowest position in the railway hierarchy. But this is also a film made of halves, Lina from Urzelina, about unfinished things and the suspension of time. (Carlos Ramos)

James Benning has been making experimental films since the 1970s, including projections and computer installations. He is also a professor at the California Institute of the Arts, and there’s something of his pedagogical side that is imbued in this film. In little boy we see both the painting that precedes the meticulous construction of a scale model of several buildings and its final form. The painting is done to the sound of music, the final presentation to the sound of historical speeches. A movie that uses the past as a herald for the future. little boy is the name of the first atomic bomb used in warfare, dropped on Hiroshima in 1945. In the hands of James Benning, however, the term becomes a delicate yet incisive essay on historical violence. Through simple tableaux documenting the construction of miniature American scenes—interwoven with popular songs and political speeches—Benning returns to his landscapes to reshape the foundations of U.S. history with his signature formal precision. Between a million-year-old dinosaur fossil and the looming repetition of past mistakes—marked by the rise of the far-right—little boy reconfigures the Yankee lexicon, proposing a play of affects between political and poetic discourses and their many forms of power. Here, the landscape is not merely backdrop, but language itself. Lucas Camargo de Barros

aw: Honda Silvestre Prize for Best Feature Film (ex aequo)

films.syn: Jem Cohen raises his meditative gaze to the heavens and tries to show us people who are concerned about things beyond the Earth, in the cosmos, whether little or big, but always far away. We mainly follow an Austrian astronomer named Karl, the missives he shares with a colleague from the academic world, his connections with his wife and grandson, who are in the United States, and his own desire to continue worrying about looking at the stars, finding the darkest possible sky on this planet.

An animation that brings together carefully hand-crafted stop-motion sets and characters as well as hand-drawn elements for a story about Ben, a boy who, despite being judged for his weight by a trio of spiteful classmates, is characterized by how cool he really is, primarily through his sense of humour and love of music and cooking elaborate meals. But insecurities, his parents’ and Ben’s, can lead to an adventure of self-acceptance.

films.ot: Lola et le piano à bruits
films.syn: Lola is the older sister of Simon, aged 5, who lives in a world of his own. By observing him, she notices how sensitive he is to small, hidden sounds. With her friend Rolih, she decides to build a noise machine to communicate with him.

Sometimes we are afraid of things that seem worse than they really are. That’s what Lulina discovers when she turns the moon into her canvas, drawing problems that, when they come to life and she gets to know them, aren’t as terrible as she imagined.

A film that returns to the universe of The Last Word ( Poslednata Duma ), where Binka Jeliaskova explored the circumstances of a group of women sentenced to death for their anti-fascist political struggle during World War II. In Lullaby ( Nani-Na ), we meet children who, because their mothers are imprisoned, are born and raised in the penitentiary. Their lives and destinies are forever marked by the dreaded figure of prison.

An airport is not an easy place to navigate when the aim is not just to get on a plane. There are security systems in place to make sure everything runs smoothly. He watches, she engages with the game. Meanwhile, a group of activists continues with the plan. The Moon is their witness. A game of glances, a plan set in motion, a dance between control and chaos. In a setting where surveillance is total and bodies move under the constant gaze of cameras, a man silently follows a woman’s steps through security screens. But she knows — has always known — that she is being watched. And she plays with it. The surveillance cameras, as ubiquitous as the particles in the air, do not merely provide us with the point of view of God — here, God is in the most unexpected details. The spectator is also drawn into this game of observation and deception, with their expectations continuously challenged until the final outcome. To give shape to this universe, animation veterans Olga and Priit Pärn employed motion capture technology, combining real actors, 3D puppets, digital drawing, and collage. The result is a hybrid and highly expressive aesthetic: the bodies move peculiarly, their faces are living masks. Between contemporary themes and plenty of surrealist imagination, Luna Rossa ’s atmosphere evokes De Chirico, Italian popular culture, and the codes of film noir — the man embodies the detective archetype, the woman that of the femme fatale, and in this hunting game, there is something of eroticism, mystery, and moral decay that make up the genre’s codes. Strange and fun until the end, Luna Rossa raises questions about power and resistance in a world where everything can be seen — but not everything can be avoided. (Cláudia Marques)

Karima Ashadu brings us a film that is part of her post-colonial research work. We’re in Lagos, where the government has banned the use of motorcycle taxis, but these “machine boys” continue their work, facing the consequences of this ban, in search of financial independence. Machine Boys , by Karimah Ashadu, explores the informal economy of motorcycle taxis ( Okada ) in Lagos, Nigeria. Despite the government ban, many riders persist in their work, striving for financial independence. The film captures their daily struggles while examining the masculinity they project and their inherent vulnerability as part of a precarious working class. With an innovative visual style, Machine Boys reflects on informal economic structures and the influence of patriarchal norms in Nigerian society. (Liedson Carvalho)

Romain is a young adult who goes to his usual friend to try something new. On a drive home laced with cocaine and something else, the music blares and the euphoric feeling is interrupted when someone who shouldn’t be on the road gets in the car. What follows is a descent into a, shall we say, zombie apocalypse in a movie that employs the one-shot with a sure and fearless hand. MadS has an uncanny aesthetic sense that harmonizes with the exquisite tension it builds. It makes sense that the last night is the maddest. A young party boy tries a new drug, recommended by his dealer. ‘Caution!’ he says, but now it’s too late… On his way back, he comes across a babbling wounded woman, but in trying to help her, he finds himself caught up in a series of surreal events. Constructed in one glorious shot, MadS is a small technical marvel, crossing the tension of horror cinema with the narcotic euphoria of the horny house party movie, an unofficial genre that we all know perfectly well. Imagine Dawn of the Dead without the political context and subtext, mixed with Project X, a small masterpiece of recent American cinema. The night progresses but our questions remain – are we facing a virus or the worst collective bad trip in history? Is this all a prank? It doesn’t really matter. What matters is the way in which MadS sustains the single-shot gimmick for 90 minutes, almost never slowing down or losing its footing, in an impressive control of tension, maintaining anxiety and realism. (Bruno Pereira)

A film that’s a hallucinated (and hallucinating) journey through the literary world of José Rizal (a Filipino nationalist writer and revolutionary during the Spanish colonial period), which reconfigures and plays with the colonial history of his country. The gesture is surreal and based on allegorical characters: the poet, the priest and the madwoman. The film is silent, using the out-of-date 35mm reels as a canvas that was painted on. A suis generis movie and a delicious delirium. Khavn, a subversive filmmaker, writer, and composer from the Philippines, reimagines the legacy of the revolutionary writer José Rizal as an acid-infused avant-garde silent film that could never have existed. The film is crafted from hand-painted, expired 35mm footage, scarred, it seems, by the brutal violence of Spanish colonial rule. At its heart is Madwoman, a tormented figure symbolising a raped nation searching for her lost children. Her lovers — a rebellious sad poet and a lustful evil priest — circle her in a frenzied dance of destruction. In his quest for identity, Khavn steps into the role of the priest, while fellow cult filmmaker Lav Diaz, enters the scene as Castrated Christ. “The world is sick. But the band plays on,” the opening intertitles scream. It’s not about finding a cure; it’s about shaking the world up with color, rhythm, and pure anarchy. Anastasia Lukovnikova

It’s the classic porn trope: the pizza boy brings a pizza, the woman has no money to pay for it and, together, they come to an agreement. But this movie imagines the situation through the prism of Marxism and takes this to its ultimate consequences. Notions of currency or market value have never been so sexy. A woman orders a pizza but, when it’s time to pay, she cheerfully announces that she doesn’t have enough money, and proposes an unusual solution to the delivery guy—one straight out of an adult film. The red-dot aesthetic of Make Me a Pizza is, from the outset, an entire statement. But when the offer seems too good to be true, suspicion kicks in, and the delivery man thoughtfully reflects on the production cost of a large meat lover’s pie—a meal, and a value chain, after all. Can the exchange value be measured by anything other than cold hard cash? Blending parody with workers’ rights, Make Me a Pizza shows how everything boils down to a commercial transaction, if even an innocent pizza can become an eloquent allegory for the increasingly impersonal exchanges of consumer society. In a joint effort, the unlikely couple tries to break away from that logic and, in a symbolic twist, decides to become the pizza themselves (you have to see it to believe it), turning into objects of desire for one another. Junk food served on a motorbike, all to the taste of macho porn: the lust we’re entitled to in the “late stage.” We already are eating from the trash can all the time , says the philosopher. (Jéssica Pestana)

Portugal, 1872. The Emperor of Brazil, Pedro II, travels to the city of Porto, and stays at the Grand Hotel du Louvre, property of Maria Henriqueta de Mello Lemos e Alvelos. In the present day, the attempt to make a film about this episode becomes an invocation. A good haunting. A curiously banal episode takes us to the middle of the 19th century, during a visit to Porto by the Emperor of Brazil, D. Pedro II. Letters exchanged with the owner of the Grande Hotel do Louvre, Maria Henriqueta de Mello Lemos e Alvelos, are introduced into this story to refine the details of the stay. The hotel is the centrepiece and the sound takes us inside, intensifying in a dramatic line that accompanies the unusual outcome of the situation. (Carlota Gonçalves)

Michel Gondry (known for films such as Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind ) directed this movie that combines paper cut-out animation and stop-motion, mixing a bit of live-action sequences in the non-animated world. Gondry likes creative ideas and that’s exactly what happens here: to maintain communication with his daughter, Maya, who lives on another continent, he makes films from ideas she suggests, in an incredibly inventive process.
A poetic combination of audio and animation that come together in a vindicatory gesture in the face of an anti-consumerist struggle, where food is the tool of protest.

A Greek film that draws on the great tragedies becomes a crime thriller that is also a commentary on migration and masculinity, particularly its aggressiveness. In a small town, a moral dilemma arises that stems from a decades-old dispute. Takis has a neighbor who believes that part of his land is his own, and when Takis prepares to open his new butcher’s shop, the conflict escalates enormously, involving his son, Pavlos, and an Albanian employee, Christos.

NOTE: For technical reasons beyond the control of the festival, this film cannot be screened. A renowned emblem of Portuguese interventionist theater, the Cornucópia tear appeared in fascist obscurity to combat the dictatorship on stage. Among the classics, a project is born and dies, but one face remains iconic: Luís Miguel Cintra, who shared his art with the permanent complicity of a filmmaker, Solveig Nordlund. Together, they organize their drawers, guided by images, traces and testimonies of the protagonists who survived this History. There are theatres in Lisbon that bring back many memories, which is why the title chosen for this film seems entirely justified, given that the Teatro da Cornucópia will always be one of them. With Luís Miguel Cintra and Jorge Silva Melo, in 1973, at its inception in an attempt to professionalise their experiments in university theatre, a meteorite falls in Lisbon. A revolutionary bomb avant son temps . And it was always in a theatre that questioned, thought about, debated, as a group, as a team, but with the personality of its founders that this project was shaped. Silva Melo’s departure at a certain point forced the project to be restructured, but it continued under the baton of Cintra and set designer Cristina Reis, a key member of the team. The film continues with archive footage of various shows from their inception to their closure, including emblematic pieces, the company’s actors and actresses, the texts and the sets. This is a film by Nordlund, who has accompanied this company and its protagonists over the years, making this collective memory his own through the medium of cinema. A film for everyone who loves theatre and has memory. (Miguel Valverde)

Through a commission for the centenary of the aluminium manufacturer Gruppo Laminazione Sottile, the artist Adrian Paci thinks about the factory, the workers and the labor, transforming the factory into a collective body in which the workers and the material share and reflect a common destiny. An organic and performative dialogue. Paci’s gaze is not just that of a mere observer. Through the exquisite work of sound, editing and choreographed gestures, the factory becomes a space for creation. (Carlos Ramos)

Milton Nascimento is a singer, a songwriter and a connoisseur of multiple instruments. Music is at the core of his being. He is also considered one of the most important Brazilian artists in its history, with musical partnerships (and friendships) with all of Brazil’s greats, and several Grammys to his name. The artist’s history and legacy are explored in this film, whose starting point is Nascimento’s farewell tour. Accompanying Milton Nascimento’s farewell tour – A Última Sessão de Músic a – which also stopped in Portugal in 2022, this film shows us one of the greatest living legends of Brazilian music. Filmed over two years and narrated by acclaimed actress Fernanda Montenegro, Milton Bituca Nascimento takes us to his last concerts, but also behind the scenes, sharing more than 40 testimonies from Brazilian and international artists and personalities, such as Caetano Veloso, Quincy Jones, Simone, Spike Lee, Chico Buarque, Gilberto Gil, Djavan, Maria Gadú, Tim Bernardes or Maria Rita, who says that when Bituca – as he is affectionately known – ‘sings, he opens a window for people’s souls to breathe’. A portrait of both personal and professional sides of this iconic artist and a tribute to a man who says that ‘music came before speech’ and that he has never felt alone, because music has always been with him. (Helena César)

One of the most renowned contemporary experimental animators, Tedd Wiggin allows us less than 4 minutes to give an orange to a snake. MIMT focuses on three main visual themes: a cat, a snake, and a butterfly. In less than five minutes, the film follows a path of constant metamorphosis where these three icons are distorted, repositioned, rotated, and fused. Without a direct narrative, it exists in a constant symbolism of associations, without ever falling into an overexposure of meaning. In a stroke that embraces the very specific granularity of digital line pixelation and the approach to a 3D rotation of flattened objects that refuse to adopt contour shadows, MIMT is a beautiful film on the limits of what exists in the possibly symbolic. (Vasco Muralha)

Doubt creeps in as Cosmo, a space traveller, addresses his gender identity. In need of clarity and change, he wants to risk crossing the Butterfly Nebula. His spaceship, on the other hand, has a personality of her own. Cosmo will need to negotiate change with a certain loss of control. ‘Fly with me, Past Jupiter and Mars… come and see… fields dappled bright with stars… galaxies in astral seas above… on cosmic paths we’ll trace Cosmo’s journey into space’, wise phrases taken from the 80s children’s series “Once upon a time… space” that could be adapted to this low sci-fi film by Caio Soares. Our Cosmo is a space traveller who begins to question his gender identity. The spaceship, like a giant dinosaur egg, is heading, at Cosmo’s will, for the butterfly nebula that is said to have a transformative power. But the spaceship has ideas about it and seems to be afraid of change. And because our perception is constantly questioning itself, we take a turn and contradict ourselves. Confused? After Club Splendida, this is Caio Soares’ new adventure. (Miguel Valverde)

Poet and artist Ross Sutherland and his parents were watching an episode of the British soap opera EastEnders when they were interrupted, and they never finished it. This film revisits that episode twenty years later.

A variety of animals make up a lovely mobile. However, one cow is alone, for the sake of the balance of the whole. From her solitude, she sees that the other animals have company. When she manages to catch the attention of a mouse, she tries a weight redistribution maneuver — so that she has more friends.

films.ot: モジャッピ 〜いただき！ホットケーキ〜
films.syn: Who wouldn’t want a tower of pancakes to devour? That’s what this mischievous trio thinks when trying to steal this delicacy from their friends. But things don’t work out the way they want!
A short film about people who have to make extraordinary efforts against the difficulties that life has thrown at them, however unusual they may be.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Cinema at the Pool)

films.syn: Meredith Monk is an exceptional figure as a composer, singer, performer and multidisciplinary artist who has influenced artists such as Björk and David Byrne. Monk faced a sexist and often dismissive world to become a recognized pioneering and unique voice. A film that looks into her past, but also onto the future, an anticipation of how her work will survive in her absence. After giving two sold-out and unforgettable concerts in Portugal at the beginning of the year, Meredith Monk returns, this time in film format. Composer, interpreter, performer and interdisciplinary artist, Monk is a visionary, recognised and awarded as one of the most peculiar and influential artists of our time. As her contemporary Philip Glass says: “She, among all of us, was – and still is – the uniquely gifted one”. However, the first reviews of her work in the 1960s and 1970s were far from such recognition. Early reviews in The New York Times were vicious and sexist, with Clive Barnes calling her ‘a disgrace to the name of dancing’. Monk in Pieces is a mosaic or set of pieces that reflects the original structure and diversity of this artist’s work, never accommodated in her 60-year career and 82 years of age, crossing singing, musical composition, theatre and opera. Here, we enter her daily life in her loft in Tribeca, where she has lived and worked since 1972, learn about the creation of her most recent work, Indra’s Net , delve into a rich archive of films and photographs and hear testimonies from artists who recognise a profound influence from Meredith Monk, such as David Byrne or Björk. (Helena César)

films.t: Move Ya Body: The Birth of House
films.syn: Director Elegance Bratton places Vince Lawrence, a DJ and pioneering producer, as the anchor figure in this film that examines the birth and evolution of house music, which emerged on the heels of disco in South Side Chicago. The film focuses on Lawrence’s origins and the impact of the “Disco Demolition Night” (an event promoted by broadcaster Steve Dahl against disco music, repudiated by rock fans), a riot that exposed the racist and homophobic veins that inspired the initial rejection of disco, as well as its successor, house music. The story of the birth of house music in the late 1970s, clandestinely, in Chicago clubs and at the birthplace The Warehouse. A film that gives credit and recognition to those who created this genre of music and how it evolved from disco to house music. The beat could be heard blocks away and was a challenge between locals, police and those who danced the night away. Vince Lawrence is one of Chicago’s sons, one of the pioneers and catalysts of the house movement and one of the main figures in the film – “It wasn’t about what you wore, or how much money you had. It was about the feeling.”. Marshall Jefferson, another of the pioneers and author of one of the genre’s biggest hits – Move Your Body , which gives the film its title, says in the documentary: “House music is freedom. House music is joy. House music is life.” In the same vein, Frankie Knuckles – who began mixing elements of disco music with electronic elements – said that “clubs were a sanctuary. People left their worries at the door”. A natural sentiment that has lost its edge in a good way, as Jesse Sauders (“When we started, house music was just about having a good time. Nothing more, nothing less.”) or Chip E. (’We weren’t trying to make a movement, we were just trying to make people dance”). And so, out of the underground dance clubs on South Side of Chicago, a group of friends turn a new sound into a global movement. As someone once said, “no party, no revolution”. (Helena César)

Mr. Fragile is made up of a set of blocks and is perhaps more fragile than the rest of us. But he likes to do the same things as any other creature: like sleep, drink or go for a walk. But what if he’s missing a tooth, can the dentist help?
A film in three acts in which figures, ranging from eight to 14 elements, change color, direction and location.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: European Short Film Network)

films.syn: A childhood memory — a family vacation in the 1970s — is revisited when Moonjoo sees a version of herself meeting a younger version of her parents.

films.t: Nina in a Series of Encounters
films.syn: A comic look at someone who no longer feels like they belong to the same things they used to, whether it’s a house or a group of friends. What remains between doubt and longing? Hope. Nina is a disenfranchised and alienated young twenty-something living aimlessly in Berlin. As the title suggests, the film takes place in a day of her life, characterized by this “series of encounters.” This indecisive girl, unsure of where to turn, either meets or seeks out various people during her day. Aside from a bit of connective tissue (brief moments before/after an encounter, short individual reflections, and in less common cases, a quick shot-reverse shot at the moment of the initial clash), the film devotes one shot to each of these encounters. In this succession of elongated confinements of characters within cinematic cages, there is a dramatic extension of a downward failure. Balancing between a dry, distressing, and nervous humor, and a real, spine-tingling distress and nervousness, the film manages to map, in a surgical way, the life of a girl, or rather, that of a very specific demographic and generational intersection, in an equally acerbic and, in the end, warm manner. (Vasco Muralha)
What if we could see what the naked eye can’t? This short film sets out to do just that, taking us on a journey beyond the machine, nature and humanity.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: European Short Film Network)

films.syn: The American collective Omnes Films ( Christmas Eve in Miller’s Point , Eephus ) explores stories in a hypnotic way, without slipping into classic Hollywood tropes. It’s independent cinema looking for a way to make movies in which the present moment is all that exists. Here, several characters anticipate a hurricane, in a suspended state in which the worst can happen — or not.

When the noise of a lively party fades, Booker feels a sense of emptiness, invited on by the darkness of the night. The morning light could be the balm he needs. The second film in a trilogy in the making that follows the musician Booker. A film in two parts that complement each other. A party with friends, the buzz of conversation. The emptiness that follows and an intimate morning of personal reconciliation. Spirituality and melancholy, like Alice Coltrane’s music, like Booker’s music. A rehearsal of the return to creativity through silence. A self-proposed exile. A serene, mysterious and very seductive film. (Carlos Ramos)

Nuno, a young man who tries to understand how his destiny is connected with his long-dead uncle’s story, Nuno, who he never met. Nuno, by Nuno Taborda, follows the story of a young man trying to understand how his life is connected to that of his long-dead uncle, also named Nuno, whom he never met. Through family stories, silences, and small traces left behind, the protagonist embarks on a personal journey of identity, belonging, and discovering the invisible marks left by previous generations. A film about emotional inheritance, memory, and the weight of the name we carry. (Liedson Carvalho)

A couple, Maurilio and Fidela, found love in a funeral home. We, the director and the audience, find reflections on our own mortality. Maurílio and Fidelia live in Cuba, where they have worked together at a funeral home for 17 years. United by love and work, the couple has built a shared life, constantly surrounded by death and its rituals. Through relaxed conversations about decomposing bodies, explanations of the process of preparing the deceased, and a visit to the unusual spaces of the establishment, Maria Salafranca offers a genuine view of this couple’s daily life. With humor and lightness, the film reveals how, for them, death loses the symbolic weight that most people attribute to it, becoming just a natural phase of existence – the final one. So, fear not: when the time comes, Bauta Funeral Home will always be ready to welcome you. (Jéssica Pestana)

aw: Special Jury Prize (International Short Film Competition)

films.syn: Fragmented and animated, this film explores the relationships, loves and heartbreaks of four characters who can’t understand each other. We are offered the different perspectives on how Olivia, Ramón, Bárbara and Mauricio interconnect and how they deal with their ghosts, secrets and disappointments, in a film whose delicate animation unfolds in symbologies of unusual beauty. The first feature film by Dominican Tomás Pichardo-Espaillat is a visual and aural gem. In his first feature, Dominican director and animator Tomás Pichardo-Espaillat takes a seed from Bergman’s “Scenes from a Marriage” and plants it in his native soil, cultivating a tender and surreal story of mismatched affections. Olivia’s past love lurks beneath her bed, trading tearful clouds for flowers, while Ramon’s feelings blossom in a potted plant. Barbara pours her unreciprocated tenderness into the fictional characters of her own animation, and Mauricio, who rejects her… Well, I won’t reveal all the secrets! This film, a decade in the making, is a collaborative effort by a team of local animators brought together by Pichardo-Espaillat who embraced their diverse styles within the discontinuous storyline. As a result, the disjointed world that celebrates subjective viewpoints grew into a community where shared imagination and knowledge flourished. Pichardo-Espaillat works as a sculptor, blending elements of 2D, stop-motion, clay, and rotoscope animation with Super 8 footage and a rich soundscape, crafting a tapestry of human connections in all its imperfect beauty. Anastasia Lukovnikova

This film written and directed by Rungano Nyoni puts its finger in the wound while hugging us. It all begins when Shula finds her uncle’s dead body in the middle of the road. The absurd drollery with which the moment is staged is transformed, throughout the film, into a meditation on how far a family will go to deny secrets that, deep down, everyone knows. And as much as this Zambian family wants things to remain unsaid, some things are hard to keep quiet. At dawn and on their way back from a party, two women find their uncle Fred dead by the side of the road and the mourning rituals begin in an almost dreamlike shared setting. Rungano Nyoni’s second feature portrays a middle-class family in Zambia with a majority female presence. During the gatherings and cultural performances of grief, family secrets emerge among the younger women, in which the older ones have been complicit. In an interview, Nyoni says that ‘you can have agency in some aspects of your life, but in others you become a little girl’. The film reveals this hypocrisy, as well as the difficulty of changing the patterns of violence and repression that have been collectively perpetuated. Bianca Dias

aw: Grand Prize for Feature Film City of Lisbon

films.syn: The final chapter of Binka Jeliaskova’s Silence Trilogy is also her last film, which was also her only foray into television and was originally divided into two episodes. The plot revolves around two very different girls, united by having the same name: Nadezhda (in English, Hope). But despite their different temperaments and goals, little by little, their dissimilarities fade and their roles reverse. This film will be screened exclusively with Portuguese subtitles.

Camille Anker takes us on a road movie where we, like the protagonist, sit in the passenger seat. But instead of looking out of the window and enjoying the journey, she just wants to get to her destination. The driver endeavors to stretch out the time in the car. This road movie takes us through the anguish of abusive relationships for which there is not always a way out, a destination. Like passengers, we travel along endless roads that seem to lead nowhere. Behind the wheel is a man whose connection to the protagonist, sitting in the passenger’s seat, is not entirely clear. That relationship is gradually revealed, at the same time as a somewhat imprecise unease sets in, where the feeling of imprisonment deepens with every kilometer traveled. The road becomes a reflection of conflicting emotions, a space where fear and uncertainty accompany the monotony of continuous movement, and where a silent threat lurks around every bend. Who are those people? Do they want to be there? Do we want to be there, like passengers hitching a ride in a relationship full of unspeakable tensions? After all, how can we escape from a journey for which we don’t have a map, nor do we know for sure if there is a point of arrival? (Margarida Moz)

films.t: Once Upon a Time in Dragonville
films.ot: Il était une fois en Dragonville
films.syn: It’s not easy being a dragon in Dragonville, especially when that dragon is Samson, who is so bullied by his companions that he is forced to go to the land of humans. But it’s there that he meets Simon, whose friendship will give him the strength to change his life.

One day, then another, a worker in an automated factory does his job and forgets his past. The factory fails. Accuses. He runs away. One day, but then another, the man sees through his memory to a disconcerting reality. “The People United Will Never Be Defeated”. That’s how Catarina Romano’s new film begins — with a poster on the wall that carries the historical memory of a revolution and is placed in dialogue with recent times: automation, artificial intelligence, alienation, the climate emergency, and other announced ends of the world. A political, enigmatic, and intriguing film. A film that asks us questions and becomes even more relevant as we witness a process of reverse revolution unfolding across the world, with a car as the symbolic figure of retrogression, just like in this film. And all of it brought to life through an animation of incredible plasticity. (Carlos Ramos)

Organza is an artist, but even in space, it’s hard to live off one’s art. The difficulties compound and the solution seems to be only one: revenge. But revenge can be a journey along which one meets creatures that point to another possible destination. Harsh, resentful, and a terrible shipmate, Organza is a failed artist in a galaxy not so far away. According to her naturopath, there’s only one cure for her nervous colitis: to find and kill her ex-lover. With a deliberately handmade, nostalgic, and punk aesthetic, Organza’s Revenge dresses up as a sci-fi adventure to satirize — with biting humor — the anxieties, egos, and vampiric figures of the art world, turning that critique into a mirror for a range of serious (both timeless and timely) concerns: the role of gatekeepers, the crushing machine of artistic aspiration, the handling of identity politics, and more. In the end, Organza’s intergalactic crusade will lead her to discover that there may be more value in embracing her vulnerability than in pursuing revenge. (Cláudia Marques)

Orlando Pantera (1967-2001) was a gifted Cape Verdean musician who died at 33 before releasing his solo album. This film revives his legacy through innovative sound and archival material from his daughter. It features contemporary interpretations by artists like Mayra Andrade and Princezito, highlighting his lasting influence on musicians today. The return of Catarina Alves Costa to IndieLisboa ( Um Ramadão em Lisboa , 2019) takes us to Cape Verde and offers a deeper portrait of the innovative musician Orlando Pantera (1967–2001), who had already featured in her 2001 film Mais Alma . This return stems from an idea by Pantera’s daughter, Darlene, in a heartfelt and well-deserved tribute to a key figure in Cape Verdean music and to the legacy he left behind. Catarina Alves Costa films with sensitivity and avoids the trap of hagiography, giving texture to a life as complex and contradictory as any human’s. Orlando Pantera died at 33, on the eve of entering the studio to record his first solo album, becoming a comet whose passage left behind not debris, but seeds — now germinated in the music of artists such as Os Tubarões, Tcheka, Mayra Andrade, Lura, and Princezito. (Carlos Ramos)

aw: IndieMusic Prize

films.t: Our Father – The Last Days of a Dictator
films.ot: Pai Nosso - Os Últimos Dias de Salazar
films.syn: Portugal, 1968. Salazar, the longest-serving fascist dictator, falls from his chair and suffers a stroke. Returning to his Palace to recover from illness, he is no longer President. No one reveals this him: neither his loyal housekeeper, nor his hard-working maids, nor his doctor. In the final years of the fascist regime in Portugal, isolated in the Palácio de São Bento, Salazar lives in a bubble carefully constructed by a strict housekeeper and three submissive maids. A make-believe world where power is an illusion maintained at all costs. The palace, like the country at the time, is marked by the violence of small things and by relationships where lies and obedience blur together.
