Through hallucinations and nightmares, the film dives into the mind of a dictator in decline, revealing through his animal side a possibility of dehumanization wrought by fascism, as well as the nostalgia for an idealized rural life. The figure of the housekeeper Maria, hauntingly portrayed by Catarina Avelar, stands as a symbol of control and obedience. José Filipe Costa’s first fiction feature rescues a little-known episode, absent from school textbooks, which ends up reflecting—perhaps unintentionally—the frightening echoes of that past in the present: the illusion of order, the cult of the traditional family, fear, and authoritarianism that, then as now, insinuate themselves into everyday discourse and gestures. (Carlos Ramos)

Jaume Claret Muxart is a director with the eye of an aesthete and a delicate hand. Here, Gal-la works in a radio station and the sound of music, her voice, and life is the thread that unites her with her son and a stranger who comes to bring ideas of shared melodies from the room they inhabit. In a sound recording studio, an on-air announcer falls asleep to the sound of a Chopin symphony. From then on, the boundaries between dream and reality begin to blur. The eight-year-old son has to be put to sleep, but how can he if his mother falls asleep before him? A bedtime story is read and both colours and places fluctuate: spatial continuity is broken (the radio waves pass through the walls), languages are mixed (Catalan, French), musical genres change (electronic, classical, contemporary), false raccords impose a dreamlike uncertainty (the blues and reds of the jumpers) and figures are distorted into reflections. Sleep dominates (in)consciousness and it is the very instability of the image that contaminates the senses. Jaume Claret Muxart’s second film (IndieLisboa screened Ella i jo in 2021) emerges as a somewhat feverish delirium that ends up in the domestic space, and finally imposes itself as a solar commentary on the reconciliation of work and family. (Ricardo Vieira Lisboa)

*Screened as an installation in the Rank Room, with free admission and the director’s occasional presence Paint Drying (an expression that refers to the most boring activity imaginable) is a cheeky protest against the British Board of Film Classification (BBFC), a board that assigns a compulsory classification to all films that want to be exhibited in the UK, charging an excessive fee that weighs mainly heavily on independent filmmakers. Shackleton made the film (with the help of a crowdfunding campaign) specifically to force the BBFC to sit for 607 minutes, without audio, looking at a static shot of paint drying on a brick wall.

Following the Q&A of The Afterlight at the Cinemateca Portuguesa, the audience is invited to join the filmmaker on a walking tour towards the Rank Room at Cinema São Jorge for an intimate happening marking the conclusion of the epic installation Paint Drying.

In the early 90s, Portugal experienced its own dance music explosion. Raves of epic proportions and a new sound shaped what was then called: “Underground house music from a paradise called Portugal”. Featuring exclusive footage and interviews with DJs, producers, dancers, and promoters, the story unfolds to reveal the birth and evolution of Portuguese rave culture and its lasting influence on electronic music worldwide. Sometimes you might think that there aren’t little pieces of paradise in Portugal. But they do exist and this was one of them. Come for the archival footage of José Rodrigues dos Santos introducing the rave phenomenon to the general public in Portuguese prime time, and stay for a host of big names who lived through the explosion of dance music in Portugal in the 1990s and who tell, in person, what it was like to live through such a revolutionary moment in Portuguese music: the adventures, the stories and the sleepless, but thoroughly danced-through, nights. A film made with those who know the subject, by those who know the subject, in this case producers João Ervedosa (aka Shcuro) and Maria Guedes (Maria Amor) and director Daniel Mota. (Ana Cabral Martins)

An immersive sensory journey through the bustling streets of Barcelona’s old town, where time, space, and human presence intertwine in unexpected ways. The film captures the tension between the sensory overload of the modern world and the slow, deliberate pace of analog filmic expression. Barcelona has experienced many influxes that have questioned mass tourism, the lack of housing for its residents, price inflation and gentrification. Even with public policies to combat this exaggeration, the city continues to experience a vortex day and night. This Perpetual Disorder forces us to stop, to reduce the voracity of time, to create silences and slower rhythms, to make us look again. Filmed in 16mm with multiple camera exposures, we are increasingly fascinated to look, as if through a game of mirrors, or just through impressions. The architectural landscape, the streets and the people blur together. There are shadows, there are ghosts, there are magical figures who, in the end, populate the city but are hidden from our gaze as angry tourists. In this perpetual disorder, the traveler reappears, the one who looks, the one who spends time, the one who pays attention to detail. Traveler João Carlos Pinto has seen it all and is trying to show us, in his own time, at his own pace. Barcelona’s old town has never been as beautiful as it is here. (Miguel Valverde)

A film that was inspired by Pizzagate, one of the most absurd conspiracy theories that came out of the 2016 US elections between Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump, and which leads Charlie Shackleton to take a theory from his youth in order to explore notions of scepticism.

films.t: Pompon Ours – The Dream of the Totem Tree
films.syn: Pompon dreams of the Totem Tree and when he wakes up he doesn’t want to waste any time, he wants to go on an adventure!

This Progress Mining Company is hanging by a thread and may need some construction work done, but in the meantime, a new staff member arrives to be introduced and start his job. One of his duties is to feed the monster. The Progress Mining Company is on the verge of collapse and important decisions have to be made. Mary believes that the mine should be closed for repairs but the suggestion is not well received: ‘Do you want to be right or do you want to do the right thing?’. It’s up to Nick, the veteran worker who has already assimilated the absurdity of the system, to stick to the routine, not to ask questions and, above all, to ignore Sector 3. It is he who guides If, the newly arrived worker, to the door of the enigmatic sector and gets him in. The essential map of the sector is forgotten, but the recommendation is assertive: ‘Don’t pay attention to anything unusual.’ In a surreal visual and sound style, this animation invites the viewer to enter a more interpretive and sensitive state. To do this, Gabriel Bohmer opts for a kind of homemade cubism, in stop motion through an assembly of cut-outs and small objects. In an aesthetic that adopts imperfections as an essential part of its language, the style works as a tool to deconstruct the normative logics of labour, production and progress. (Margarida Moz)

A French queer musical that puts two aspiring pop (and punk) stars on a collision course. What results is a first love in all its fullness: filled with intensity, anguish, sweetness and volatility. Mimi Madamour (Louiza Aura) and Billie Kohler (Gio Ventura) are stars who have fallen by the charts’ wayside and are now remembered only by their most devoted (if not obsessed) fans. The rest is herstory. After the success of the short film Les Démons de Dorothy , which garnered the Silver Leopard at Locarno in 2021 and was featured in over a hundred festivals worldwide, Alexis Langlois ventures for the first time into feature films with Queens of Drama , which had its world premiere at Critics’ Week at Cannes. The film was inspired by a past romantic relationship of Alexis. Like the two protagonists, the queer diva who is also a YouTuber, Mimi Madamour, and a lesbian punk star at the peak of her career, Billie Kohler, Alexis reveals: our relationship was a blend of admiration, rivalry, and class warfare intertwined. We loved each other like crazy, but we couldn’t be together. From chart-topping hits to emotional meltdowns, Mimi and Billie’s tumultuous relationship shatters dreams of stardom and leads them down a path of self-destruction. Superfans like Steevyshady will immortalize their story and turn them into symbols of a generation. The film’s songs features artists such as Rebeka Warrior, Yelle, Pierre Desprats, Mona Soyoc (KaS Product), and Louise Bsx. Queens of Drama is a French queer musical — camp, hilarious, chaotic, frenetic, bursting with pop culture references in a celebration of queer culture. Infinite adjectives for a film that simply won’t leave our minds! Warning: the songs will very likely get the audience up from their seats and turn the cinema into a dance floor. Les Reines du Drame is screened together with the short film The Exploding Girl by Caroline Poggi and Jonathan Vinel. Alexis Langlois will be present for a Q&A with the audience. (Alexandra Ferraz)

films.t: Quisiera no sentir todo este ruido
films.syn: A fiction that imagines anxiety as literal explosions of light, surging out of one’s body. Tonight’s anxiety, this girl’s, is linked to her interrupted pregnancy. On a hot night in an anonymous town, a woman wakes up. The sound of a rubbish lorry can be heard. There’s also a neighbour who records TikTok dances in the middle of the night and another neighbour who decides to move an armchair late at night. These are all elements of the sound ‘ecology’ of large metropolitan areas and poorly constructed buildings. And all this would be banal if the protagonist wasn’t having a medical abortion that night. Lucila Mariani films this event – which involves a certain amount of anxiety – between banality and surrealism. The power of everyday life and the ‘indifference’ of the world imposes itself on the procedure, and yet reality seems to infuse things with a dreamlike strangeness: a bottle of water glowing in the kitchen counter, a dog licking the trickle of blood running down a leg, a slug crawling unperturbed across the tiles in the living room. The ordinary becomes extraordinary and the atypical customary. Here is a fable about the enigmas of everyday life. (Ricardo Vieira Lisboa)

A small bird tries to hunt down a small stone, causing a landslide, but also igniting an adventure. What begins simply enough, a bird drawn with simplicity in search of a stone, becomes something more complex that is transformed by new experiences.

Evoking the human, the organic and the extraordinary, Raw+Porous is a story of obsessive love and a surreal entropy of surroundings between two people who give themselves over to absolute desire. ‘Beauty will be compulsive or it won’t be’, said Breton, and this is echoed in raw+porous , which feels like a film-material, full of skin and desire. Inside the house, two women and a closeness that is explored at the table, on the sofa, in bed, sharing the pleasure that drips from the mouth, runs out and drips from the juice of the fruit that is tasted. Image frames that are paintings, dreamlike flashes and sounds that stick to the skin, and an ultra-sensorial vertigo runs through the body of the film. (Carlota Gonçalves) The second instalment of a complex story, this raw + porous film begins where Blue (the filmmaker’s first film) left off. From the change of colour – from blue to orange, from rationality to emotion, from the absence of touch to the intense necklace of desire, from rationality to, finally, emotion. It is in this new terrain of exploration that we accompany the character played by the author. And it’s feeling every bud, every pore, every vibration, every vertigo, every touch, every sound, every shot, every image, every photograph, every perspiration, every EVERYTHING. Infinite vertigo in a film of pleasure, flavour, colour, viscosity and sensuality. Ágata Pinho has a lot to give us, but what we feel in this film is already a beautiful version of what is to come. (Miguel Valverde)

In 1998, two schoolgirls sent a letter to Iran’s first-ever women’s newspaper. While they waited to be published, they considered making an impossible film. After Irani Bag (2020), director Maryam Tafakory began to focus on the cinema of appropriation in a systematic way, making iconoclastic collage-films based on images from Iranian cinema that she superimposes, solarises or mirrors. If in that film the object of study was the representation of relations between men and women in the post-revolutionary period, from then on the director has developed a series dedicated to non-representation, to what Iranian cinema has left unseen: free, emancipated and desiring women. Along with Mast-del (2023), Razeh-del deals with the love between two women. However, it is also a film about the first women’s newspaper in Iran ( Zan – which means ‘woman’) and how during its short run in the 1990s it became a powerful source of inspiration. The saturation of signs, layers, excerpts, newspaper pages, intertitles, subtitles, text and photographs serve a phantasmatic purpose, summoning – as in a séance – the absent women to the screen. (Ricardo Vieira Lisboa)

aw: Silvestre Escola das Artes Prize for Best Short Film

films.syn: What I saw when the ultrasound was shown to me, I couldn’t believe. Inside my uterus there were hundreds of tiny creatures, shaped like spiders, but of flexible and tender body. A young woman goes from gynaecologist to gynaecologist searching for a diagnosis for her unexplained pain. Mysterious spider-like beings seem to inhabit her uterus. ‘Mum, what’s wrong with me?’ In a unique and unsettling atmosphere, the young woman confronts the unknown illness that inhabits her. (Catherine Boutaud)

A satire and pastiche of spy movies, including but not limited to James Bond’s. The movie follows John D, who returns to a luxury hotel on the French Riviera where he relives memories of his golden days in the 1960s, but where he also senses the paranoid idea of the return of his enemies coming to the fore. We jump between the past and the present, in an exquisite work of editing that swirls with homages to martial arts, slashers and giallos . A gripping movie that leaves you with a touch of fever.

“Together Forever”. Refuse Room is a film by Simon Liu, who returns with an exploration of what it means to live in the city of Hong Kong, in a struggle between the vertical and the horizontal, from the endless buildings to the detritus of the population. Hong Kong revealed in the details of everyday objects, present and forgotten, vibrant lights, colours and fragments of graffiti messages on the walls. The film’s breakneck pace mirrors the dynamics of a metropolis in constant acceleration. Simon Liu returns to IndieLisboa to honour his territory with intimate precision, revealing a city that pulses beyond its skyline of skyscrapers. In every almost abstract detail, subliminal inscriptions emerge, criticising and applauding that place which is so special, so penetrating. We can almost feel the heat, the humidity in the distorted vocalisations of a resistant Cantonese language. The frenetic editing alternates short shots and contemplative moments that invite the viewer to unveil the chaotic and poetic soul of the city in the shallow flight of a butterfly and the steady gaze of a cat. This is no ordinary place, this is no ordinary waste, this is Hong Kong and you can feel the film on your skin. (Margarida Moz)

An intimate view of the director’s relationship with the knowledge of why his father died, a truth that was hidden from him and then altered over the years, until it was revealed during a family member’s drunken moment. Like the numerous AIDS memorials, physical or digital, RICHARD carries the simple beauty of giving voice, body, and justice to those who died from the disease without the truth being said, processed, and respected in life — as was the case with the filmmaker’s father, who passed away in 1993. With The Sweetest Taboo playing, Manuel Wetscher honors him and allows Richard to exist, even belatedly, without secrets as an HIV carrier, even if only through archival footage. A sweet historical reparation that starts from the intimate to dialogue with a world where, 32 years later, the cure still doesn’t exist, and the fight strongly continues. (Pedro Gonçalves Ribeiro)

Cate Blanchett, Roy Dupuis, Nikki Amuka-Bird, Charles Dance, Takehiro Hira, Denis Ménochet, Rolando Ravello, Zlatko Burić and Alicia Vikander. But if one had to say more, one could add that it’s a comedy that imagines a meeting of the G7 leaders, who have to deal with an unspecified global crisis (left to our imagination), and find themselves surrounded by figures straight out of a horror movie. A satire with brain — in more ways than one.

The drawings are minimal, the story is hairy. Hair is also important in this construction of masculinity: from the first trip to the barber to the initial hair loss, and much more. We follow the life of a character as they journey from childhood to adulthood, with particular attention given to their hair and eyebrows. It may seem like a trivial theme. However, a closer look reveals how S The Wolf explores issues of identity construction and masculinity. From childhood trauma at the barber to first love, and, of course, hair loss and eventually the greatest loss, the death of the father, this narrative illustrates how physical appearance becomes a reflection of the internal transformations of the human being. Between self-love and the incessant need to please others, the character faces these challenges armed with a sense of humor that, even in the toughest moments, offers a light and ironic perspective on the process of growing up. With a playful tone, the animation addresses complex issues about image, acceptance, and societal expectations – which are also impossible to satisfy – without ever losing its charm and grace. (Jéssica Pestana)

In this love story, a young couple faces an uncertain future between Africa and Europe. When they reunite in Lisbon, sharing a house with other immigrants, farness and closeness will test their relationship. When newcomers are overlooked and never fully seen, the cinema can be a place to celebrate their existence. And so it is in Sabura, a film that is beautiful and relevant in everything it represents. It’s not about writing declarations of intent, but about filming these gazes. Let them exist inside their homes, with all their stories and misfortunes. In short, a home. Your home. (Miquel Escudero Diéguez)

Roadways and expressways. The train tracks. What remains of the factories, the wastelands. The clouds, the rain, and the wind. The river. A film about a suburb of Lisbon. The suburb where I was born and raised. The streets and interiors: houses, businesses, and associations. A film of pathways and details. A few work notes suggest that the film is looking for its own structure. The music? A suburban symphony. Somewhere between the praise of banality and an elegy of time.

An isolated island of rocks and deserted landscapes, abandoned by humans due to the overexploitation of its resources. Yet, the island is not as desolate as it appears. Traces of human presence linger, their shadows and souls imprinted on the terrain. Memory records to give new meaning to existence. Explosions of light, shadows and sounds in a suspended time that floats between reality and fiction. It’s winter on the island of Porto Santo, but the space remains mysterious. Marked by the rhythms of Adolfo Bioy Casares’ The Invention of Morel, the story becomes a celebration of detachment. Everything moves and everything returns, like the Atlantic Ocean that bathes the images of Saint Bartholomew with stardust. (Miquel Escudero Diéguez)

Kiyoshi Kurosawa revisits and remakes his original 1998 Serpenth’s Path , now in cooperation with Cinefrance Studios. Made with a sure and clinical hand — Alfred Hitchcock would approve —, there’s something dense, thematically speaking, and raw in this movie that asks us if revenge has ever an end. United by the need for retribution, a man whose daughter was killed and a woman full of mysteries go in search of those responsible. And will they ever stop? Remakes are in fashion, more so in Hollywood, of course, but they are still in fashion. 26 years after the original Serpent’s Path (1998) Kiyoshi Kurosawa joins a very small circle of directors who have made a remake of an older film of theirs, a circle that includes Alfred Hitchcock ( The Man Who Knew Too Much , 1934 and 1956) but also Michael Haneke ( Funny Games , 1997 and 2007). The remake is a strange beast, often the reason they exist is strictly monetary. It’s easy for a cinephile to hate remakes, the original movie already exists, why make it again???? Among other pleonasms. I understand this point of view and sometimes you can find me actively participating with a response like that. But sometimes, the reason for remaking a movie isn’t completely monetary, sometimes it’s a “flea behind the ear” that stays and stays and stays… (this is an expression in Portuguese, literal translation but please bear with me) A director remaking his own film will always be an inherently interesting proposition, whether for formal, narrative or academic reasons. 2024 was a year blessed with three films by Kiyoshi Kurosawa, in addition to Serpent’s Path you can also see the excellent Cloud in the Silvestre section. Personally, I’m very happy that Kiyoshi Kurosawa decided to take care of his “flea” 26 years later. (Rui Mendes)

When the stranger becomes the source of our fear, our unease about our surroundings turns us into shadows of ourselves. The feeling of being persecuted. If history reminds us at every turn of women and men of different religions, creeds and beliefs who have been questioned, arrested, imprisoned and sentenced to death, it is impossible not to look at this animation in the light of current days. This distressing, demonstrative, uncomfortable feeling is conveyed to us in this film through a play of shadows created using the sand animation technique. If we think about the technique itself, the use of this mineral, sand, as a set of degraded rock particles formed by the erosion of time, we can see a metaphor for what is hidden under that sand, what is concealed or what doesn’t want to appear. It can be a shadow, a hiding place or a prison, it always depends on the perspective of the one looking and the one being looked at. That’s why Serrazina built this work, which is both abstract and concrete, with light and shadows, to the sound of a lament that comes from far away, from time immemorial, and which tinges, breaks, ignites and causes disturbance. Serrazina once again surprises us with an arresting cinematographic gesture. (Miguel Valverde)

A film set in different moments: in the 16th century, in a forest, fighting for communal land; then, in a forest being monitored and the confrontation between notions of public and private, with the figure of the wild boar as an agent of chaos. The French visual artist Elsa Brès returns to IndieLisboa with her first feature, which can be read as a manifesto that continues the poetic struggles of Monique Wittig and Donna Haraway and calls for disobedience. The film invites us into a tactile journey through the landscape and past of the artist’s home region in an open-ended structure where documentary and fiction blend, and meaning is conveyed through gestures rather than words. Brès superimposes the uprising of peasant women against the enclosure of common lands in the 16th century with the modern-day intrusion of wild boars into the privatized and monitored territories of the Cévennes. Night, silence, and the forest emerge as marginal spaces of resilience, where the wild and domestic forge an unlikely alliance against the grip of capital and men, proposing cohabitation as a new form of living. Anastasia Lukovnikova

A little girl in Tehran, Rose, decides to rebel against a tradition that no longer makes sense to her in the modern world: the sacrifice of little lambs and the distribution of their meat among the community. Rose will try to save as many lambs as she can.
Wandering through disillusioned Portuguese landscapes, a man reflects on the ruins of his love. Multiple voices, reading fragments of his diary, share his restlessness and vulnerability.

Three people who use the train in San Francisco to commute to work and back, each tell us what it was like to get stuck on the train and the experiences (or fantasies) they had. Every day we descend the subway stairs into our everyday underground. In the pulsing atomization, do we ever consider the hundreds of parallel inner worlds, equally hypnotized in their self-absorption? And what if there were a system failure that called everything into question? In this film, a momentary halt in the vehicle becomes the starting point for a choral orchestration: a free and collective conjugation of all the thoughts imprisoned in the tunnel. Through a free and dynamic association of images of an anodyne and apocalyptic contemporary setting of industrial society and a soundtrack composed of a complex tapestry of voices, this film launches us into a game between those most intimate inner worlds, never before shared, now together in the carriage in a flaming heat. (Vasco Muralha)

It all starts with a bullet, then you have to trace its path. An exploration of French police brutality, using both modern and archaic cinematographic techniques. In their previous film, Contraindre, the duo Fleuryfontaine (Galdric Fleury and Antoine Fontaine) had already tackled the issue of police violence through 3D animation, giving a digital body to events of abuse and mistreatment. In that film, the motion capture technique was used to develop a conceptual reflection that opposed the accentuation of physical characteristics (skin colour, body shape) to the ‘disembodiment’ before the authorities: a film made in the interval between coercion and constraints. Five years later (now outside the framework of Le Fresnoy), the duo continues their hybrid research, where animation now serves as a tool for analysing video surveillance footage that captured an act of ‘non-lethal’ violence. Soixante-sept miliseconds is a film about trajectories, about bodies and projectiles in motion; it’s a film-denouncement, but it’s also a short treatise on the documental validity of cinema – somewhere between Marey’s chronophotography and the Forensic Architecture’s investigations. (Ricardo Vieira Lisboa)

In this village, at night when they go to sleep, the children carelessly throw their slippers aside. In the morning, they disappear. The children’s parents explain that the Slipper Keeper Kitty has taken them. The children search for her in the forest, the Kitty returns the mended slippers — and they promise to be more careful.

films.t: Sly Lives! (aka The Burden of Black Genius)
films.syn: Ahmir “Questlove” Thompson and producer Joseph Patel had already teamed up for the documentary Summer of Soul — a film that played at IndieLisboa and ended up winning the Oscar for Best Documentary in 2022 — and now they’re back with another story rooted in African-American culture. This time, the subject of their gaze is the blazing star that was Sly Stone in the 1960s and 1970s, who later saw his career fall into obscurity. The film goes beyond this musical legend to explore the particular difficulties faced by black artists. His musical genius is recognised and undeniable, preserved on albums like ‘Stand’ or ‘There’s a Riot Goin’ On’. Even so, given what Sly Stone built, a new and unheard of music that suggested the possibility of another America, a new America, no less, and given what his Sly & The Family Stone represented during the turbulent transition from the 1960s to the following decade, when they were the most important band in the country, undisputed kings of the stage, authors of the best concert at Woodstock, it can be fair to say the portrait that posterity has kept of them seems too blurred. Enter Questlove, the Roots’ extraordinary drummer turned director with “Summer of Soul” (2021), who pursues an extraordinary story, that of a multiracial band, made up of men and women, led by a visionary musician who collapsed under the weight of his ambition, the temptations brought on by success and the pressure of being a black voice and body bursting unbridled into the heart of an America that had only recently emerged from the ignominy of segregation. (Mário Lopes)

A story in which the Stone of Destiny is not just a plot device or MacGuffin, but the main character. In this case, the Stone of Destiny wants to discover its own, well, destiny. A musical about finding one’s way. Stone of Destiny is a musical animated short that follows the restless journey of a stone in search of its place in the world. Motionless by nature, the Stone longs for movement; solid, it feels fragile. It leaves its ancestral home — where it no longer fits — in search of solace, meaning, and inner peace. Along the way, it encounters mysterious symbols, dreamlike visions, and a pet demon it carries as a living memory of the past. With a distinctive visual style and original music by Johana Novotná (Johuš Matuš), which greatly contributes to the film’s strange, poetic, and playful atmosphere, Julie Černá’s film turns mineral stillness into animated poetry, revealing that even stones — firm, silent, seemingly whole — can yearn for change and embrace the uncertainty of the journey. (Cláudia Marques)

One of the Coen brothers’ classics, a movie about a “Dude” (Jeff Bridges) who just wants to relax and bowl. However, he is mistaken for a millionaire with the same surname and begins an adventure that will take him too far — not least because, in all honesty, he just wanted his rug back. It really tied the room together. With Sam Elliott, Julianne Moore, Steve Buscemi, John Turturro, Philip Seymour Hoffman, David Thewlis, Peter Stormare and Ben Gazzara, among others.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Cinema at the Pool)

films.syn: The titular bath takes place on the Bulgarian Black Sea coast and is taken by an idiosyncratic group of friends who get together during the summer holidays for a celebration that has become a tradition. But like all traditions, its constant observance has turned it into a boring obligation. To deal with the discontent, there’s nothing better than testing the line between life and death. A recipe for the tragic and the oneiric. The second chapter of the Silence Trilogy.

A Brazil where old people are treated as a nuisance to be exiled far away from those who are old enough to contribute to society, labor-wise. Tereza may be 77, but she’s not going to give up her unfulfilled dreams or her freedom that easily. She embarks on a journey through the waters of the Amazon to accomplish one last dream.

films.t: The Bright and Dark Side of Things
films.syn: In this film, Binka Jeliaskova returns to the universe of The Last Word ( Poslednata Duma ) for an incisive look at the prison system, now in a period far removed from the Second World War, in the middle of the Cold War, filmed before the fall of the Soviet regime. In The Bright and Dark Side of Things ( Lice I Opuko ), poverty is the motto for stories where you have to steal to survive, where violence is domestic and where children can be a saleable commodity.

films.t: The Building and Burning of a Refugee Camp
films.syn: Seeking asylum in Ireland is difficult in the face of various hostile forces: from the very policy that provides (or prevents) asylum, to the xenophobic mentality that is proliferating. “Resist against racism harassment,” we read at the entrance of a refugee camp in Ireland. Hatred and violence stay outside. The Building and Burning of a Refugee Camp examines the heartbreaking – yet, for us, so difficult to conceive – reality of refugees, in confrontation with the all-too-familiar evidence of the alarming rise of far-right movements around the world. In doing so, we are confronted with our collective failure to defend human rights and build a just and inclusive society. In a raw and relentless manner, Dennis Harvey forces us to face a daily reality we prefer to close our eyes to: a world where fundamental values of humanity, solidarity, and decency are daily denied to the most vulnerable. (Jéssica Pestana)

aw: Special Jury Prize (International Short Film Competition)

films.syn: The child just wanted to fish, but he didn’t count on any possible interruptions. First the dog, then the frog, then the duck… where’s his carp after all?
The cow was sitting quietly in her meadow, but not so that she didn’t want some company and a drink of water. Tiny Toot may be camping with her family, but that doesn’t stop her from helping out!

Candice is a girl who explodes. She has been exploding several times a day for three months and doesn’t seem to stop. Candice is reborn from her explosions like a phoenix and wants less to prepare for the end and more to be present in the moment before she explodes — a metaphor for many things. My name is Candice. For 3months, I’ve been exploding daily. Even public holidays. Even strike days. Sometimes even 2 or 3 times a day. Caroline Poggi and Jonathan Vinel return to IndieLisboa with The Exploding Girl . The filmography of this extraordinary French duo is filled with works marked by a strong hyper-realistic aesthetic influenced by video games. With The Exploding Girl , they once again delve into the margins of French society, using this aesthetic and 3D computer graphics techniques to construct the film’s images. Through the language of artificial worlds, the film addresses the real issues of modern life, focusing on younger groups in an uncertain future, yet holding on to hope for a better world. The music is by Malibu. Through the voiceover of Candice, who accompanies us throughout the film, we enter her world. The perspective of what is shown on screen is often her gaze. We step into an environment that reveals the turmoil of a French suburb and even Candice’s bedroom. Alone, she fragments. But she feels desire. She seeks to seize the days of an apocalyptic existence marked by a thirst for all sensations. A film about many things, where many other things also fit: a reflection on the precarious condition of being human, social unrest, or the nature of being a woman. In just 19 minutes, wonderfull cinema unfolds. This film features scenes that could shock the sensitivity of some viewers. The Exploding Girl is screened together with the film Queens of Drama by Alexis Langlois. Alexis Langlois will be present for a Q&A with the audience. (Alexandra Ferraz)

films.t: The Flamenco Guitar of Yerai Cortés
films.ot: La guitarra flamenca de Yerai Cortés
films.syn: Antón Álvarez is C. Tangana, a Spanish musician and rapper who has become a global phenomenon (the film Esta ambición desmedida , about his latest album, was shown at IndieLisboa last year). With this film, he makes his directorial debut and brings us an intimate and family portrait of the talented flamenco guitar player Yerai Cortés. A documentary that serves as a cathartic revisitation through music. Antón Álvarez, known by his nom de plume C. Tangana, manages with a fearless and sure hand, especially given the fact that this is his first feature film, to tell us not only this intriguing story, which brings together family sorrows, stormy loves and gypsy culture, but also to infect us with his enthusiasm and fascination with the palpable talent of Yerai Cortés, but also with her incredible life story. Álvarez underlines notions of fate and destiny, building a moving story within the genre of the music documentary. The film is populated, inevitably and fortunately, by performances that flow along the spectrum from the most classical to the most contemporary. La Guitarra Flamenca by Yerai Cortés won a Goya 2025 Award for Best Documentary. (Ana Cabral Martins)

The first crush is the deepest. The girls in this movie are growing up and discovering their power, and nothing could be more in keeping with the codes of the horror genre as female rebellion and sisterhood. Laura Obradors makes a movie with a classic cinematic trope: the coming of age story. In this short film, Obradors takes a trio of girls who are having their first confrontations with the difficulties of adolescence: their relationships with the boys they like, the relationships with each other and the ones they have with themselves. The director wants to mix these moments of initiation into adult life with the clichés (in a good way) of fantasy or horror cinema and include notions of female essence and liberation that are in dialogue with elements such as magic and sisterhood. Bonds are tested until the final catharsis. (Ana Cabral Martins)

This handyman’s work is not recommended for children under 18. A simple proposition: a fictionalized version of the director confuses an innocent phrase from a hired handyman with a sexual advance. Once the mix-up is cleared up, the tension still remains. Faced with this, the Handyman proposes a mutually beneficial solution: he agrees to show his naked body to the filmmaker if, in return, the filmmaker records him in a music video for his favorite song. The bulk of the film ends up being this video. In a state that Leal briefly describes as “narrative (?)”, through this metatextual and self-fictional framework, the film appropriates the language of the music video to delve into a delirious and humorous exploration of desire. The desire of the individual, of the camera, and the reconciliation of both. Amidst overblown neon lights and increasingly gratuitous ways of framing genitals, the film becomes a filtration of fantasy and desire through an already existing language, creating a suspended dream capable of acknowledging its own absurdity. (Vasco Muralha)

Janica is a young woman who arrives in a small town and gets a job in a restaurant owned by the welcoming Miočić family. However, the feeling of welcome soon turns into a feeling of paranoia. A young woman starts working as a waitress at a family-owned restaurant located in a remote town in Croatia. Despite some initial awkwardness with the dynamics of the restaurant and the family she also shares a roof with, Janica immediately feels integrated and welcome. However, an unexpected event interrupts the state of harmony and immerses the family environment in growing tension. With a bold approach and the use of unconventional techniques, Martina Marasović’s camera captures the sensitive nuances of human interactions and their moments of discomfort, deepening an overall sense of uncertainty and unease. The question lingers: do they know what happened? (Jéssica Pestana)
A community garden brought moments of happiness to an entire community. For Henry, it was a safe haven. If only they could decide on how to save the garden before it’s demolished.

Living in a small village or town has its drawbacks. One of them is seeing things not go as expected, when little changes, or those you know leaving for new adventures. In the end, what’s left? The Last People plunges us into a sleepy village where time feels suspended and every gesture carries weight. In elegant black and white, the film captures with precision the closed, familiar atmosphere of a small town — both stifling and strangely comforting. The characters’ almost motionless routines are contrasted by bursts of energy that light up the screen: cars doing donuts in an open field, fluorescent sneakers dancing to techno at dusk, nights at the same old bar to the sound of ’90s eurotrance. It’s a film that lives in the tension between the desire to leave and the inertia of staying — and leaves us pondering what happens when a once-assumed presence disappears, and the world’s quiet balance begins to tremble. (Cláudia Marques)

Gia Coppola orchestrates the career revival of Pamela Anderson, who received nominations for Best Actress at the Golden Globes and the Screen Actors Guild awards, and the cast received the Special Jury Prize at the San Sebastián Film Festival. The film centers on Shelley Gardner, a Las Vegas showgirl in her mid-teens, facing an uncertain future. Also starring Jamie Lee Curtis, Billie Lourd, Dave Bautista and Kiernan Shipka.

The Last Word ( Poslednata Duma ) is a non-linear film that blends the past and present of a group of six women who are sentenced to death for their anti-fascist political struggle. One of the only films by Binka Jeliaskova to premiere in Portugal, in the summer of 1975 after a run in the Cannes Official Competition, it was also her most internationally recognized.

Yoni is his own worst enemy. Wandering around the merchant district of Buenos Aires with his mentor, Leon, trying to get by with a bit of smuggling, he’ll realize that blind loyalty can be the element that clips his wings. What at first glance appears to be an electrifying film about petty crime between friends is transformed by Tomas Murphy into a vibrant portrait of the complex power relations between Yoni and León on the streets of Buenos Aires. Yoni aspires to more than a secondary role in their little scams. Her loyalty is about to be broken. A claustrophobic film, continuously accelerating until the final adrenaline rush. (Carlos Ramos)

Family vacations can go one of two ways: very well and be cherished memories for the rest of one’s life; or very badly and serve to erupt the tensions that have built up. When this family of four and their dog arrive at a Thai hotel, perhaps the outcome is the second option. A family of four and their dog arrive at a seaside hotel in Thailand. A cut in the family portrait soon begins to emerge — it is through the father’s emotional detachment that the behaviour of the mother and children comes into focus. At the centre of this fragile structure is a small dog, carried like a baby, serving as an innocent mirror of the emotional disarray of its owners. When the family leaves the hotel to visit a Buddhist cave, the film takes an unexpected turn. The change in setting transforms both the narrative’s tempo and tone, inviting the viewer to immerse themselves in the characters’ silent crisis of faith. From dusk into darkness, time slows, silence thickens, and the camera lingers on the texture of the rocks as if digging into them for echoes of human suffering. A mysterious, meditative experience of almost liturgical beauty. (Cláudia Marques)

A Spanish-French television miniseries — created by Rodrigo Sorogoyen, Sara Cano and Paula Fabra — The New Years corresponds to the New Year but also to the birthdays of Óscar and Ana, who turn 30 on the 31st and 1st respectively. They meet, fall in love and their very different lives become intertwined. The series follows their lives for 10 years. *TVCine series preview. First three episodes will be screened The series is trying to uncover the subtleties and invisible gestures that occur within a couple. The attempt itself is already powerful. Sorogoyen was able to search for a form that had not yet found a place in his cinema. The actors, Francesco Carril (you may have seen him in Jonás Trueba’s films) and Iria del Río (an actress with wonderful talent), are given space to shine. That’s where the best of the series takes place. When we’re in their private space, a true intimacy emerges. (Miquel Escudero Diéguez)

The boots lead our little boy to explore the surroundings of his house at night. He takes advantage of his parents’ distraction and goes on an adventure. But he encounters a lonely creature who may not let him return.

What would happen if we were on the beach digging a tunnel and didn’t stop? Would we meet someone in the middle? Two kids from opposite sides of the world do just that. Together, they decide their next destination: the North Pole!

A beautifully colored animation that explores a mother’s absolute and total need to get rid of her husband and children to have a playful afternoon to herself, in pursuit of a roe deer. From the beginning, there is something deeply unsettling in this film. Perhaps it is the postures, the stiff/frontal characters. The very erect limbs, rigid and bending only at the joints. Frontal in their two-dimensionality, they seem to pose for us in challenging and complex ways and then stare at us once they have struck the pose. The turning of two-dimensionality in the film always carries something directly presentational. All of this makes perfect sense in the film’s narrative. A nuclear family—a mother/father/son/daughter—lives in a house beside a forest. After two intense clashes with an unexpected hunt, the shock of hearing gunshots, and a face-to-face meeting with a deer, the tense—and not entirely happy—mother of the family enters a pulsating vertigo. In the next 24 hours, the line between inner fantasy/time/identity crumbles, and we enter a completely subjective version of this animalistic crisis of social pressures, where symbols and reality act in equal validity. (Vasco Muralha)
Tidying up toys isn’t the most fun part of the day, but with two little imaginary friends, Mathilde manages to turn this task into a real race to see who can tidy up the fastest. Ready, set, go!

Simultaneously the first film by Marva Nabili, in a stunning directorial debut, and the oldest surviving (in its entirety) Iranian film directed by a woman. In this 4K restoration, a young woman in pre-revolutionary Iran finds herself at a crossroads between tradition and the desire for freedom, where her refusal of marriage offers is equated by her family with possession by malevolent spirits. Digitally restored by the UCLA Film & Television Archive with funding provided by the Golden Globe Foundation, Century Arts Foundation, Farhang Foundation and Mark Amin. Restored from the 16mm original A/B negatives, color reversal internegative, magnetic track and optical track negative. Laboratory services by illuminate Hollywood, Corpus Fluxus, Endpoint Audio Labs, Audio Mechanics, Simon Daniel Sound. Special thanks to Thomas Fucci, Marva Nabili and Garineh Nazarian. Shot in just six days in the year before the Iranian revolution, Khake Sar Beh Mohr ( The Sealed Soil , 1977) is the first film — at least of with a copy that has survived — directed by a woman in Iran. Marva Nabili’s film, inspired by real events, is set in a village in the south of the country, where a young girl is pressured into marriage. Nabili worked meticulously with the protagonist, the non-professional actress Flora Shabaviz, building a space of authenticity that the influence of Robert Bresson and the presence of all the other characters, real inhabitants of the village, helped to compose. With a background in painting, and using long takes, Nabili shows us a beautiful but oppressing space of the house where, in a patriarchal and conservative society, the female condition is thought of from the perspective of imprisonment and repetition of domestic tasks, as opposed to an urban outside, and, above all, to a solitary unveiling of poetic moments of escape. (Carlos Natálio)

Returning from a vacation, a girl notices a boy and her world opens up a little more. Maybe this is what it means to grow up. The director Terence Davies, the ‘singer of memory’, understood the English pub as a place of communal cohesion, where it was the music – the songs, chanted in chorus by everyone! – which sought to strengthen the bonds between neighbours and different generations. In his films, the pub is a place of aggregation where, between beers and singing, a process of class identification and union takes place. Die Sänger shares this same collective (and collectivising) spirit, locating it in the Austrian countryside. However, it does so from a distanced perspective, taking the point of view of a city family that accidentally enters a mystical territory where everything is foreign to them: the landscape, the rites, the customs. This exteriority allows us to glimpse the fissures of that town (thus circumventing any possible essentialist exoticism): alongside the community spirit is provincialism, alongside the pubescent boy is drunkenness. ‘Because beauty needs to have a reminder in it, for the salvation of men’. (Ricardo Vieira Lisboa)

Two sisters — with very different experiences and memories — come together for a celebration in their parents’ immaculate old house, now occupied by the eldest, Karen (Maren Eggert). Impenetrable to her children and husband, she is contrasted with the jovial Julie (Britta Hammelstein), enamored with her partner and their baby. The family reunion is punctuated by the thorniest barbs imaginable, thrown by everyone at everyone. But everything that’s tense will have to be let go. The warm colors of the kitchen, the food preparation, the view of the garden. Everything seems idyllic in Karen’s home, and that’s what fascinates us at first. The mastery of the decoration, the delicacy of the gestures. Yes, everything seems idyllic until the sentences the characters exchange become increasingly cutting. This is not the bucolic place we imagined or anticipated. Ramon and Silvan Zürcher (the film is presented as being by the two brothers, with Ramon having duties as director, screenwriter and editor, while Silvan is in charge of production) once again take on something characteristic of their filmography: a certain distance from the lives of their characters. But underneath this observant camera that hovers over everything, emotion and perturbation are ready to burst forth. And perhaps some catharsis. Ana Cabral Martins

Binka Jeliaskova directs the film that marks the beginning of her Silence Trilogy: The Swimming Pool ( Baseynat ), The Big Night Bath ( Golyamoto Noshtno Kapane ) and On the Roofs at Night ( Noshtem Po Pokrivite ). The Swimming Pool portrays a triangle, one that plays with notions of love, desire, friendship and performance. The protagonists are a lonely widower, Apostol, who discovers Bella, a teenager disillusioned with her first love, on the night of her graduation. The harmonious balance is broken by the actor, Boyan.

A political allegory with unique imagery: a barrage balloon floats through the Bulgarian countryside, flying over village after village. The peasants who watch it or chase it make comments about the origin of such a powerful object, untethered from the surface. But the barrage balloon also comments from its point of view, seeing humanity as small and ignorant. The Bulgarian Communist Party saw the allegory as an attack on the state and banned the film.

A film in three parts, each focusing on a different woman, but all haunted by the same unknown and invisible figure, only perceptible if seen through the camera’s gaze. Pedro Martín-Calero’s first work is methodical, atmospheric and visually captivating, creating an anxious tension delicately and elegantly. And perhaps the best use of text-on-screen in recent times. With Ester Expósito (from the Elite television series) and singer and actress Malena Villa ( El tema del verano ). The gallery of horror cinema’s greatest demons is vast – Freddy, Jason, Leatherface, Xenomorphs, Pazuzu, Cenobites, etc., but there’s always room for one more. El llanto presents an evil that we all know but which is more insidious than those listed above: an old white man who silences and takes away the place of speech from young women, until he murders them. This metaphysical patriarchal specter haunts and makes everyone doubt their reality, sowing fear until it becomes a shadow for the three protagonists, three young women separated by thousands of kilometers and decades of distance. The film, Pedro Martín-Calero’s debut feature, skillfully and sensitively explores gender violence and the nature of trauma, and how certain hauntings have become universal, inescapable phenomena. An essential feminist thriller, timely in times of machismo and misogyny, latent and otherwise. Sound familiar? Yes, indeed… (Bruno Pereira)

David is a shy sculptor who accepts a friend’s invitation. Her summer house might be the ideal place to read. But David discovers more than he bargained for, including that the world exists when you step out of your bubble. David agrees to spend a weekend in the countryside with a friend. As a true introvert, he brings along a book and the hope of some peace and quiet. But upon arrival, he is faced with the presence of strangers — confident, warm men, unlike himself. From this unexpected gathering emerges an intimate confession that pushes him out of his inner refuge and confronts him with the possibility of opening up to the world and to others. With a self-reflective voice-over and a chaptered structure, the film takes on a literary tone that will appeal to fans of Rohmer — and that won’t be the only evocation of the director’s universe, even if the naturalistic framing is subtly subverted. El mundo es afuera is a reminder for those who live turned inward: a film about friendship, generosity, listening, and what can be gained when we allow ourselves to be seen. (Cláudia Marques)

A visual experience about a geographically disconnected experience. The focus of this short film is workers in the global south who have to teach the Artificial Intelligence that drives cars how to navigate streets they have never seen, streets that are in the opposite hemisphere to where they are. Nicolas Gourault takes up the theme of autonomous vehicles to give voice to the workers of the Global South who, in the isolation of their homes and countries, cut out, identify and catalogue each image: ‘person’, ‘object’, ‘animal’. Everything is entered into a database that aims to build the ‘eyes’ of these robotic vehicles that will circulate on the streets of the First World where these people can hardly walk. Despite being essential, these workers are paid significantly less than those in the North, reflecting a logic of global labour exploitation and inequality in the distribution of global wealth. The invisibility of this work and the lack of awareness of the value it generates make labour demands difficult and accentuate the perversion of the system. However, hope is emerging: through widespread access to geolocation tools, these workers are beginning to organise themselves, challenging the attempts of large companies to reduce costs by exploiting the labour of the specific few. (Margarida Moz)

aw: Grand Prize for Short Film EMEL

films.syn: Over the course of one night, René, a Brazilian immigrant in Lisbon, grapples with the choice between staying illegally in an increasingly alien city or returning to the home she once fled. Her external struggles and internal conflicts intertwine, exposing the complexities of life between two worlds. Wandering, a way of life. As the Polish author Olga Tokarczuk wrote, “change will always be a nobler thing than permanence; that that which is static will degenerate and decay, turn to ash, while that which is in motion is able to last for all eternity”. In Those Who Move, the first short film by Stephanie Ricci, this wandering is permeated by a melancholy: in René’s gaze, facing the port of Lisbon; in the jokes exchanged between friends that exorcise the hardships of the migrant condition; or in the most beautiful stairway encounter of recent times. The stairways, also symbols of movement and transition, embrace this moment of disarming intimacy. Each fragment of René’s night is revealing, formally chameleonic, and yet subtle and organic – possibly even slipping past the gaze of passersby. Those Who Move reveals the sincere and relentless search for a connection, for a sense of belonging that can calm the wandering soul. (Susana Santos Rodrigues)

The kiosk window doesn’t just sell news (or cigarettes), it also receives news, or small talk, or unending complaints. Life can be seen through this window, in all its glory and avarice. Through the Window , by Daniel Stopa, is a short film that observes everyday life through the window of a kiosk. Throughout the day, various customers stop by to buy newspapers and cigarettes, but they also bring small stories, ranging from the mundane to the meaningful. With moments of humor and melancholy, Through the Window turns seemingly simple conversations into a genuine human portrait that leaves no viewer indifferent. (Liedson Carvalho)

Speaking your mother tongue is a good way to maintain a connection with your culture. But, if that fails, perhaps other means can be used, such as learning more about a fish and its history. A boy of dual nationality tries to learn about his birthplace and its culture, while not knowing how to speak the language. This is achieved through a fish, a creature that normally does not speak, but here does in the narration – and is of dual nationality like the boy. Crispin Yanisi weaves a poetic narrative of discovery and belonging through two parallel threads: the young man’s journey of discovery and the account of the fish’s life, from sea to table. Between the visual portrayal of the animal world and the auditory context of the young man’s world, the void is filled in the fish’s voice. Although it is clearly a narrative film, with a “beginning, middle, and end,” this story is pared down to its essential elements, leaving open space for a poetic reverie. Between the film photography of a beautifully pale, multicolored palette and an intricate orchestration of sounds and voices in all their panoramic potency, Tila•pia is a long pilgrimage from the lands to seas and back again. (Vasco Muralha)

This film sets out to break with the sensation or experience of time in a linear way. Here, we see the future, the present and the past at the same time, in order to build patterns and rhythms that go beyond everyday human experience.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: European Short Film Network)

films.syn: *This screening has the support of APAV (Portuguese Association for Victim Support). After the film there will be a Talk: Educate to Exist, and Resist A film that aims to remind the world that the war continues in Ukraine and that it’s the most vulnerable who are suffering the most. The film avoids any use of interviews, voice-over, or other documentary techniques, to simply show the impact of the war on this country, offering the day-to-day life of schools in the Kiev region, with all the difficulties and small victories that this entails. TIMESTAMP, a film by Kateryna Gornostai, offers an unvarnished look at how education serves as a cornerstone of resistance in Ukraine during wartime. In this documentary, which had its world premiere in the Official Competition at the latest Berlin Film Festival, interviews and reenactments are deliberately avoided. Gornostai films the everyday life of schools with a discreet and natural approach. Through intimate yet powerful scenes, such as graduation ceremonies or classes held in shelters during bomb alerts, TIMESTAMP further explores the power of education as an anchor of the kind of normalcy that the population seeks, even if fleeting and under the constant threat that has loomed since the Russian invasion on February 24th 2022. Despite the devastating effects of the war, school life continues, with teachers and students preserving hope and dignity amidst the physical and emotional destruction surrounding them. Without explicitly showing the bloodshell, TIMESTAMP offers a profund reflection on the courage of a people fighting to preserve their culture and identity, and the role of education in wartime as a symbol of hope for the future. Also, this work invites us to reflect on the reality of children in war zones and the universality of the desire to continue learning to (re)build a world that will never be the same. (Alexandra Ferraz)

Opposites sometimes attract and that’s what happens when an indolent beetle meets a hyperactive ladybug. Together they form a parent/child relationship not unlike that of their fellow travelers, the humans Pauline and her parents. Let’s see who gets into more trouble.

Ada has moved with her husband to Hamburg and is well into her pregnancy. The American war correspondent of Polish descent finds herself a little adrift in her new country, until she receives a package that brings with it childhood memories and a mystery. Roksana is an old friend and has dedicated her now-published memoirs to Ada, in which she exposes the sexual abuse she suffered at the hands of her father. Roksana and Ada join forces on a painful adventure in search of answers to these deep wounds.

João stars in a biopic about Liberada, a gender-nonconforming figure persecuted by the Inquisition. After the director is mysteriously paralyzed, João faces haunting dreams and struggles to honor Liberada’s story. Signifier and signified, representation and presentation, character and actress, fact and fiction, figure and legend, flesh and spirit, description and re-enactment, objectivity and subjectivity, history and spectrality, research and invention, film and video… The list of epistemological polarities could go on for a long time and would still fail to guide us through the maze of mirrors that Paula Tomás Marques has set up in Two Times João Liberada . Based on an investigation into the Portuguese Inquisition’s trials of people who, in retrospect, would be understood as ‘gender dissidents’, the director proposes a kaleidoscopic self-reflection on the past, its contemporary revisitation and the limits of its (cinematographic) portrayal. Actress, character and ghost coexist and clash in a post-modernist exercise where the ‘film within the film’ satirises and questions the problems of mythification and historical speculation. This is a playful and iconoclastic meta-film about the ephemerality of the past and the impossibility of its representation. (Ricardo Vieira Lisboa)

aw: Prize for Best Direction for a Portuguese Feature Film

films.syn: Inside several narrow and crowded stores with different crafts, we follow the gestures of care, the relationship between material and hand, and the trained technique of renovation. The documentary ‘Under Repair’ leads us to discover the different crafts that keep alive the objects that time deteriorates. In a rhythmic choreography, each gesture of shoemakers, stitchers and mobile phone repairers reveals the delicacy of those who prolong the life cycle of these objects that we connect with out of necessity or affection. At the same time, the camera captures the atmosphere of these small shops with their workbenches, tools and materials, but also their place in the city. Lisbon has changed: heir to traditions, it now welcomes new artisans; migrants from faraway origins who are challenging the disappearance of the old professions that gave their names to the streets in the city center. These are the new Lisboetas who have recovered the slow rhythms and given back to the city a patience that accelerated tourism has consumed. (Margarida Moz)

aw: Novissimos Prize

films.syn: It wasn’t with that intention that Kaori Oda started this film, but it ended up becoming the final chapter in a trilogy that explores underground spaces and includes Aragane (2015) and Cenote (2019). It all started from a desire to film various locations, underground or in caves, that would allow for a historical exploration of what happened there, how it affected the people who lived there, or nearby, and the trauma associated with these spaces. The actress Nao Yoshigai plays a human presence in the film who interacts with what is external to her, from which viewers can feel things and touch them. Director Kaori Oda proposes herself as an intermediary for recording human and non-human lives and relationships, the affective memory of the spaces and objects that surround them. Storyteller Mitsuo Matsunaga collects bones in his spare time and introduces the filmmaking team to memories in Okinawa’s underground caves. Underground is the result of intensive research and is the final part of a trilogy about the collective consciousness of ‘various underground spaces in Japan and how they impact the people who live in and around them’, from the most obvious repercussions to ghostly forms. Bianca Dias

A comedy by Matthew Rankin ( The 20th Century , 2019) that imagines a Canada (minus Quebec) that is culturally intertwined with Iran. The film follows, with an aesthetic that delights, disparate stories with seemingly no points of contact: two girls trying to withdraw money that has frozen in the ground to help a schoolmate; a group of tourists on a suis generis guided tour; a man who quit his job and travels to reunite with his mother. An evocative fable to warm the heart.

films.t: Vitrival – The Most Beautiful Village in the World
films.syn: Vitrival is a quiet village where you’d imagine that not much would happen and people would live in harmony. At least, that’s what the two local policemen, cousins Benjamin and Little Pierre, would like it to be. The truth is stranger and more bizarre than that. On the one hand, the harmless proliferation of phallic graffiti . On the other, the unexplained suicides that are taking place. But peace remains, time passes and our heroes do their best. Pierre and Benja are police officers in the small village of Vitrival, where everyone knows each other and crime is the rarest of occurrences. However, a mysterious wave of suicides and the appearance of sexually explicit graffiti begin to torment the local population. This forces Pierre and Benja to begin an investigation through which we experience an intimate portrait of Vitrival, its rituals, its inhabitants, its problems and the changes brought by the passing of time. Using real locations and non-professional actors, Noëlle Bastin and Baptiste Bogaert try to capture with an almost documentary-like lens a particular way of life, and despite the seriousness of the themes that traverse the film, the duo’s gaze is filled with humor, levity and tenderness. Nabil Aouad

aw: Special Jury Prize Canais TVCine

films.syn: Two men, long-time loserish friends, go for a walk with fateful consequences through the Michigan forest. One wants to get to their destination quickly, the other wants to enjoy it and make stops, whether necessary or not. The underlying idea is that there really is no turning back. They’ve made a pact and they’re going to go through with it. At least, that’s the idea. Ah the male dream of making a pact with a friend where we go into the forest without a map to ███████████████ where one of us drags their feet the whole time while the other just wants to get it over with as quickly as possible. Joel Potrykus returns to IndieLisboa with Vulcanizadora but already is a festival veteran with Ape (2013), Buzzard (2014) and The Alchemist Cookbook (2017). Speaking of Buzzard , 10 years later, Joshua Burge and Joel Potrykus return to their Buzzard characters to fulfill a pact that I will never reveal. In fact, I’d like to make a unilateral pact between myself and whoever is reading this to not to miss out on an excellent opportunity to get to know or revisit one of the most unique filmmakers in American independent cinema. (Rui Mendes)

Songs of whales, bird calls of Cory’s shearwaters, transatlantic letters, radio signals. Water Tongue reflects on the many forms of communication on Earth. Mariana, who is Azorean, and Stella, who is in Lisbon, communicated over long distance. Water tongue. Would it be women communicating with whales, or children guided by prophetic dreams? Mariana lives in Azores, Stella in Lisbon. Separated by an ocean, they meet again in the archipelago to listen, gaze and create a polyphonic orchestra composed of multiple voices, human and non human. Together, they dive into the land and the sea, where whales sing, letters travel and ways of feeling and communicating are reinvented. (Catherine Boutaud)

Living alone in the highest mountains of Portugal, Carlos has spent years writing letters to his beloved late wife, suspended in a time that no longer exists. His solitary world is disrupted when a filmmaker, on a quest to find a mysterious lake, stumbles upon him. What begins as a chance encounter soon evolves into a deep, yet fleeting friendship. To her, Carlos slowly reveals the depth of his grief, his memories, and his inner abyss. In their shared moments, the boundaries between their lives blur, offering both a glimpse of healing amidst the shadows of longing. A huge surprise, this debut feature by Kopal Joshy, an Indian filmmaker residing in Portugal. A journey to the abyss of Covão dos Conchos in Serra da Estrela, an enigmatic place prone to conspiracy theories, but which is in fact a functional engineering work from the 1950s. This leads to the discovery of another abyss – Carlos, a solitary hermit in the mountains. A simple, disarming film rooted in intimacy and sharing, with tremendous sensitivity. As Kopal finds her abyss, Carlos finds a confidant for his grief, and the symbiotic relationship that forms becomes the vehicle for expressing a deep longing. (Carlos Ramos)

Binka Jeliaskova makes her solo directorial debut with this love story set in Nazi-occupied Bulgaria, inspired by the author’s experience in the Partisan resistance, here mirrored in her experience of armed struggle in contrast to the blossoming of love. Winner of the main prize at the Moscow Film Festival, it was a blockbuster success in Bulgaria. The opening film in Mark Cousins’ documentary series Women Make Film , it’s considered the first Bulgarian feature film directed by a woman..

Tired of poverty and hunger, 31 young Cape Verdeans, including one woman, embark on an adventure to Cuba in a secret operation to receive military training to free the country from the clutches of colonialism.

An oasis of beautiful plants and flowers in the middle of an ocean of weeds is put to the test when a storm threatens to infest all the work done by the Gardener. Can he fight off the elemental forces testing him?

films.t: What Have I Done to Deserve This?
films.ot: ¿Qué he hecho yo para merecer esto?
films.syn: A Pedro Almodóvar film from the crazy 1980s in which the Spanish director brings us one of his protagonists who he positions as an everyday heroine. Almodóvar likes to explore the chaotic inner lives of women, including those who work as housewives. In this movie, actress Carmen Maura is one of those women, who is addicted to amphetamines, lives with a husband who doesn’t love her, has two sons involved in bad stuff, an unbearable mother-in-law, and her best friend and neighbor is a sex worker. What follows, nobody deserves that. This film will be screened exclusively with Portuguese subtitles.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Cinema at the Pool)

films.syn: In the village of Dine, in Trás-os-Montes, Portugal, solitude deepens when, under cover of night, dogs bark outside and confirm that the cave has been stormed into. Judite Lopes lives in the village of Dine, in Trás-ós-Montes. The fiction of a cave disrupts her daily life. And it’s beautiful how Francisco Moura Relvas and Rita Senra combine so much complexity in such a simple and precise gesture. It’s in places like this that some of the most beautiful moments in the history of cinema have come about. (Miquel Escudero Diéguez)

films.t: Where do Birds Go When it Rains
films.ot: A dónde van los pájaros cuando llueve
films.syn: Juan is on the beautiful mountain of La Sarna trying to make a documentary when two events lead him to confront serious topics: on the one hand, the discovery of a violent event related to the place, and on the other, the progressive loss of his sight. The birds that inhabit La Sarna, in Colombia, carry multiple meanings. For the Andean culture, some of these birds absorb bad luck by confronting it; others believe that certain species embody evil, seen as bad omens for some communities. Amidst the legends and folklore of his country, and facing an illness in his optic nerve, Juan Sebastián Sisa draws an intelligent connection between his own loss of vision and the historical obscuring of a violent event that marked his land. A symptom that transcends not only his country’s collective memory but also, in a way, could resonate throughout Latin America in a whole. (Pedro Gonçalves Ribeiro)

“Where do you call home?” was the question faced by nearly 3,000 Spanish children exiled in the Soviet Union during the Spanish Civil War. This film tells the story of Angelita Perez, who lived in Russian boarding schools from ages 4 to 24 until completing her medical studies. It’s a tale of resilience, love, and identity, intertwining past and present. It also explores the bond between a mother and daughter through shared songs and stories. The title is the legitimate question that acts as the film’s premise and the answer is 73 minutes of the adventurous life of the filmmaker’s mother. Looking at today’s world with wars on our doorstep, dictators emerging at every corner, and an attempted culture of silence promoting individualism, this seems to be the film that saves us. I’m not saying this because the film contains answers, but because its 92-year-old protagonist doesn’t seem to be afraid of anything, not even the future. Separated from her family when she was just 4 years old, Angelita and her sister (along with around 3,000 other Spanish children) head for the USSR at the end of the 1930s because of the Civil War. The narrative is built on the memories of the matriarch, a collection of surviving objects, songs in Russian, and a journey through the lands of Ukraine and Kazakhstan to Siberia and then Moscow. A 20-year journey that culminates in a return to an unfamiliar place, to relatives with whom she has lost ties and to building a new life. If this film is about the mother, it is also about the daughter, a filmmaker and artist, who looks at this life as if it were a map that had to be built from Guernica, the objects are rehabilitated and used, transformed, the photographs come to life through the stories. From the film-maker’s daughter to the protagonist’s mother. A film constructed in puzzle format, almost like a game, in which the pleasure of listening is equal to the pleasure of watching. A film about future time. (Miguel Valverde)

¡Caigan las rosas blancas! wants to deconstruct. Deconstruct ideas of gender, ideas of what is taboo, ideas of what cinema is. The plot centers on Violeta, a director who has been hired to make a mainstream porn film and decides to run away with her friends to find inspiration. What awaits them is the adventure of a lifetime.

The Serbian director’s feature debut is a tribute to his late mother. Stefan Djordjevic deals with this death by mixing fiction and fact, images he filmed of his mother and a meeting, in the present, of the whole family. While working on a project that pays tribute to her, they talk (and don’t talk) about the good, the bad and the painful. In the mix is a lost dog that will become part of the family and the grieving process. The interlocutor in the title WIND, TALK TO ME is the wind itself. The response arrives in the form of a poetic film that steers clear of sentimentality through a steady camera and a sensitive stitching of remnants of images and sounds. In his debut, Stefan Djordjevic works with archival footage from a project originally conceived as a documentary about his mother. After her death, this material is re-signified and interwoven with new images to construct an intimate reliquary: a cinematic gesture from a filmmaker-son in search of the answers his mother—now a character—left scattered like whispers in the air. Around his camera orbit nature, family, affections, and memories—fragments of life the wind insists on returning. Lucas Camargo de Barros

At his first practice with the new football team, Jonas meets Niklas. After a party, they end up at Niklas’ house. Cuddled up, the two friends fall asleep. Their closeness does not go unnoticed. The team wins the next game, but the distance between them seems insurmountable. Youth football training sessions are, for many, the only moments of physical interaction between boys, who find in sport a way of showing their emotions. Winning or losing as a team, playing well, committing and fighting for others are ways of demonstrating qualities that otherwise have little room to exist. Football, perhaps more than most men’s team sports, allows you to express emotions that would otherwise be difficult to express. Fragility, however, is not always understood in these environments where the team is one, but each boy his own. “Winners” takes us from a football training session to a party and back to training the next day. That night, two team-mates get physically close. Back on the pitch, this closeness is rendered meaningless by the codes of the game. Affection and tenderness have their own manifestations on the pitch; off it, everything is questionable. (Margarida Moz)

aw: Novissimos Prize - Honourable Mention

films.syn: Hanka visits her lonely grandfather and everything is a trip back in time, including the act of eating homemade preserves. But to talk about the past is also to confront the present. A train journey, a schnitzel, and expired pickles serve as the starting point for a narrative that oscillates between the themes of the old and the new, the past and the present, between what moves and what remains unchanged. Winter Monologues is a poignant film that portrays the life found in banal gestures and all that they contain: what has already passed and what could have been. But above all, it is a story about the affection shared at the table, during mealtime, where romantic love carries a duality: it is part of the grandfather’s memory and an unknown in the granddaughter’s future. In the end, we are left with a beautiful reflection on what remains and what is preserved over time. And a truly familiar reality: the love between granddaughter and grandfather is nurtured, not by grand gestures, but through the sharing of food and small pieces of wisdom. A reminder that, as Patti Smith says, “love is a banquet on which we feed.” (Jéssica Pestana)

Suzana is stuck in the past, unable to get over the loss of a loved one and live her life without that hurt. Days and nights and nights and days. The days go by and the grief is still going on and draining away. If this film were a record, it would be that record that we keep, our little secret, that we take off the shelf when we’re down, that we play whenever we’re sad, and that seems to momentarily heal us, to listen to alone, in the darkness of our grief that won’t go away, until one day a light comes on, which it always does. Luiz Afonso Morêda’s film manages to create an atmosphere of deep melancholy that will stay with us for longer than its 14 minutes. (Carlos Ramos)
Sometimes you’re at home with a friend and you tell them that if you don’t leave you’ll be late and the response is a crazy, unexpected and utter frenzy.

The audience is sitting in their seats, waiting for the performance to begin. Someone fiddles with their cell phone to turn it off, someone coughs in anticipation. Finally, silence and everyone paying attention. But is everyone really paying attention?
