The second part of a trilogy of films, which started with Youth (Spring) and continues with Youth (Homecoming) , in which Wang Bing follows the same characters over time — young people who have come to Zhili, an industrial city, to work hard and try to achieve their dreams. This part sees tensions rise between workers and management over pay (including the lack of it).

The film that punctuates the trilogy of films that began with Youth (Spring) and continued with Youth (Hard Times) , in which Wang Bing follows the same characters, in every facet of their lives, over a long period of time. In this final chapter, we see the culmination of their struggle for survival in rural China as a new year is celebrated.

This is the opening part of a trilogy of films, which continues with Youth (Hard Times) and Youth (Homecoming) , in which Wang Bing follows the same characters in every facet of their lives (whether at work, in their day-to-day professional lives or their friendships and love relationships) over a long period. Here, the director spends a year in Zhili, an industrial city where young people try to work hard to achieve their dreams.
Kissing is very unpleasant. Lips turn vibrant pink in anticipation and it’s a horror. Léo makes fun of the couples he sees until his own lips start to glow pink. Is it so blergh to kiss?

films.t: Zizi (or Praying to a Fabulous Tree)
films.syn: A movie that combines fiction and reality to tell the story of an Indigenous woman, the director’s grandmother, and the tree she planted, whose fruit is the jackfruit — and both are seen in the same way, as something undesirable. To return and to confront the corners of our childhood. Felipe M. Bragança comes back to Indie with a short filmed in the backyard of his grandmother’s in Queimados, Rio’s suburbs. As he describes, the film works like a prayer — not only for her but also for the jackfruit tree that shaped his youth. With unique representations and origins, Jaca and Zizi are now ghostly figures, blurring the notion of a family tree and dissolving the boundaries between ancestry and imagination. By intertwining memories, spirituality, and fable, Felipe creates a universe where the past reinvents itself and the invisible manifests. And between shadows and lights filtered through the garden trees, we are confronted with an intimate and mystical Brazil, where the land, the tree, and the family spirits become one body. (Pedro Gonçalves Ribeiro)

Just as it was never proven who the Zodiac Killer was, so was Charlie Shackleton unable to move forward with the big screen adaptation of the book The Zodiac Killer Cover-Up: The Silenced Badge by Lyndon E. Lafferty, who believed he knew the identity of the elusive criminal. But that didn’t stop Shackleton from making a movie-about-the-movie-he-would’ve-made, in a cinematic evocation of the true crime genre. Zodiac Killer Project is imaginative, intriguing and a masterful deconstruction that includes the most beautiful sunset.

(as)sento is a video that reflects on human presence without showing the body. Through images of seats displaced from their usual context and a subtle sound construction, it evokes human action and impact on the spaces we inhabit. The video creates an atmosphere of suspended time, where suggestion matters more than evidence. In this short experimental film, we return to family outings, picnics with cousins, vacations in the countryside and by the lake, and those long summer days that seemed to go on forever. Large gatherings of family and friends can be seen in this film where, despite the suggestion of so many people, no one is actually visible. What the film shows us is a choreography of chairs, carefully arranged, in which each scene transports us to a joyful memory of our lives and our free time, those moments where there is no room for routines and where every instant is marked by sharing and laughter. It is almost magical how the sound design and the compositions created with outdoor chairs craft the stories that the screenplay allows us to write when it chooses to sketch only the perfect setting. (Margarida Moz)
In a drought-stricken Portuguese estate, landowners and servants recount the same story from irreconcilable perspectives, revealing a fractured world on the edge of collapse.

The assignment seemed simple: to follow a fire brigade patrol on a night shift. The siren sounds because an elderly woman is locked inside her apartment — and perhaps it should have stayed that way, given her transformation into something far from human. Soon the entire building appears to be heading down the same path, and the camera keeps rolling. A film that proved hugely influential and unexpectedly crossed Spain’s borders.

When grandma’s dog dies, granddaughter Luna helps with the burial. But what happens when you’re dead and buried underground? Grandma evades the answer, so Luna is tempted to see for herself what’s going on down there.

In the 60s, Edviges Pisco wrote a diary about her experience as a school teacher in the village of São Brissos, in Alentejo. Inspired by her diaries, the film portrays the present day in the region, where the echoes of the past still resonate. The alchemy of cinema as a device linking past and present emerges here through the writings of a schoolteacher in an Alentejo village during the 1950s and 60s. A Memoir of Antecipation articulates memory and image in order to interrogate the persistence of gestures, spaces, and living conditions. The intimate observations inscribed in the diary resonate in the present, revealing a subtle continuity: a harsh existence shaped by human geographies and landscapes that seem to resist time. The film suggests a superimposition in which differences dissolve and continuities quietly assert themselves. The first short film by João Sarantopoulos, A Memoir of Antecipation constructs, with remarkable restraint, a possible archaeology of the present. In its candour and apparent simplicity, it reveals a quotidian that traverses time and endures. (Susana Santos Rodrigues)

Just before going into hibernation, the hedgehog realizes that one of his spines is missing, and he treasures them dearly. It turns out to be lodged in Lena’s dog’s bottom, which means the rescue mission is unlikely to be simple.

In an abandoned rural Romania, where most people have emigrated to Germany, the four seasons pass while the river remains by the house. It is a place Lavinia promises to beautify, to make comfortable—we hear her tell Dani, who is 14. A mother who, despite her emotional instability, impulsiveness, awkwardness with feelings and a turbulent relationship with her ex-boyfriend, only wants a better life for her son.

films.t: A Small Fiction of My Mother in Beijing
films.syn: In the second chapter of the Mommy trilogy, Dorothea Sing Zhang unveils the solitary daily life of her mother, a star of Chinese opera. The mostly silent, echoing backstage spaces become a mirror of the emotional distance between them. Hybrid in form, as its title suggests, this film moves between genres while staging the filmmaker’s displacement as she turns to a subject that should be inherently close: her own mother. Observational throughout, the gaze approaches what it films with a curiosity shaped by a certain distance, as if everything were still to be deciphered – from rehearsal routines and moments of rest to the voice messages sent by mother to daughter, as well as the opaque Beijing in the background. The result is a subtle bond of estrangement between the mother and the space she inhabits. And if the daughter’s silence prevails throughout, the film itself can be read as a response. More than that, it is a love letter. (Pedro Gonçalves Ribeiro)

For Azaa and Shagai, the search for a new home is little more than a diversion from an impending divorce. Trapped in the infernal traffic of Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia’s bustling capital, their argument comes alive. Like other Asian metropolises, Ulaanbaatar, the capital of Mongolia, is a dynamic hub of economic and political growth, driven by the intense exodus of the country’s rural population. In the midst of this city expanding both vertically and horizontally – with its tall buildings, chaotic traffic, and densely populated outskirts – we follow Azaa and Shagai, a young couple with a daughter, as they search for a home and try to rebuild their life – and their relationship. Between new and uninhabited apartments, demanding career paths, and emotional wounds from the past, tensions build under the weight of urban life and each person’s existential emptiness. And even so, at the very epicenter of the city’s frenzy, we glimpse brief moments of intimacy and reconciliation. A hug in the car, in the middle of traffic, symbolizes the possibility of rediscovering one another, of the love that can still exist amid the noise, responsibilities, and haste of daily life. A South Facing Window offers a sensitive portrait of the ongoing tension between family bonds and the pressures of modern life, revealing in each individual the search for identity, meaning, and connection in a world that does not wait for us. (Jéssica Pestana)

If a box of photographs, letters and VHS tapes hadn’t been found by Sergio Oskman beside a trash container in downtown Madrid, the life and work of the Modlins might have gone unnoticed by the world. Elmer and Margaret devoted their lives to seeking artistic recognition — he as an actor, she as a painter. They eventually ended up in the Spanish capital, withdrawn from society alongside their son, quietly shaping their own story.

In a new daily life, Abril, a trans woman, chooses her mother Helena as her primary caregiver for a facial feminization surgery. With maternal gestures, Helena cares for Abril with the same gaze she had when her daughter was little. This moving documentary immerses us in Abril’s daily life at a crucial moment in her transition, as she is accompanied by her mother, Helena, through a decisive phase. It confronts us directly with striking images of her facial feminisation surgery, as well as the subsequent recovery period, taking us out of our comfort zone. Sensitive and carefully crafted, the film reveals a deep bond of love and trust within a truly welcoming family. (Catherine Boutaud)

aw: Novissimos Prize

films.syn: Saura, Filipe, João, Beatriz, Rita, and Marchana have a language of their own, shaped by the growing pains of childhood and the uncertainties of adult life. During the summer, Saura and Filipe, once deeply connected, begin to drift apart. As they try to understand what still remains between them, their language also begins to change, and with it the group of friends they share. In summer, anything can happen. New friendships are formed, love is found, people dance, go to the beach, soak up the sun – and then what? What feeling remains when the spark fades, when what was certain yesterday is completely uncertain tomorrow? Rodrigo Braz Teixeira, who previously directed the short film Miraflores , returns to this world where he feels at home: the time of great doubts, of the places around us and the uncertainties of adult life. A couple, Saura and Filipe (he returns from the short film), gradually drift apart whilst trying to understand what is happening to them. He is insistent, she defiant. She is worried, he is inattentive. And this dynamic keeps spinning until it reaches an unbearable stalemate where it’s make or break. Braz Teixeira knows how to film people and landscapes; he knows that the time he spends with them allows us to feel part of their circle, to dine with them, to laugh at what they say and, ultimately, to understand their world too. And then there is Lula Pena, in a fleeting yet powerful appearance. Filmed with a consistently delicate touch, Teixeira launches himself, with this debut feature film, into the contemporary whirlwind of an intimate realism. (Miguel Valverde)

An ace, a card, a feeling yet to be revealed… In Ace, two friends live on opposite banks of the Tagus River, bound by a closeness that begins to reveal itself as something else. Amid this encounter, one of them discovers a feeling that has yet to be named. The film explores this latent passion through subtle gestures, in which every detail carries hidden meanings and suggests more than it reveals, building an atmosphere of anticipation and suspense. (Liedson Carvalho)

In a tradition dating back to the dawn of humanity, Costa da Caparica was born through the Arte-Xávega. Today, a community of fishermen adapts this fishing technique to the modern world, in a choreography between machine, waves, and Man. On the beach, amid the rhythm of the waves and the whirring of engines, an ancient choreography unfolds: the Arte-Xávega. The departing boats cast their nets in an invisible arc, only to return bearing not only fish, but the beginning of a collective ritual. On land, men and machines work together to synchronize their movements. Everything depends on a fragile balance: the rhythm of the sea, the weight of the net, the precision of every gesture. Each crew moves as a single body, in a dance where no one can falter. Between the past and the present, Arte-Xávega continues to take place, not as a memory, but as a living practice, between tradition and adaptation on the Costa da Caparica, which we know more as a beach and a place for fun, and much less as a workplace. After all, as the 1967 archival footage reminds us right at the beginning of this film, greatly undervaluing this collective effort, “The old fishermen, going about their work, add a picturesque touch to the bustling beach.” (Margarida Moz)

António, an absentee father, is in charge of feeding his daughter’s old cat while she’s on vacation. When the cat doesn’t show up, António convinces himself that something bad might’ve happened as he stumbles on small clues. Do these signs corroborate his beliefs or is António projecting his worst fear, facing death? Cat sitting turned into an existential thriller. What wouldn’t an absent father do for his daughter? He agrees to look after a cat whose habits he doesn’t know and whom he’s never cared for; he doesn’t know what to do with it, nor how to find it. The cat’s disappearance is the premise for a film that speaks to us of absences (we never see the daughter, we only hear her) and the fear of death. Will a father who has never looked after his daughter know how to look after a cat? And if something has happened to it, what will happen to him? This double mirror, in the form of an existential thriller as described by the directing duo André Santos and Marco Leão, will make us laugh until we are left with doubts, a whirlwind of emotions, just like life that never stops, always heading towards the end. The duo, returning to the short film format, offers us the melancholy of their earlier, more intimate films, in a unique portrayal of a situation, delivering a mature and intelligent direction, and allowing the great actor Miguel Guilherme to shine, who here offers us yet another of his brilliant performances. (Miguel Valverde)
América is a ten-year-old girl living in a remote village in the Andes whose dream is to buy a bicycle so she will never be late for school again.

This is the debut solo short film by young Austrian director Angelika Spangel. In An Accident , there’s trouble of every kind: three youths stage a car crash, pigs suffocate, and a fire remains unexplained. While three boys simulate a car accident in the fields and a group of children plays risky games in the village, a father and his son discover the pigs on their farm dead. In contrast to the monotony and tedium of everyday life, any event seems capable of triggering something greater. We wait for the drama to unfold, as the characters reveal feelings of guilt and shame. With admirable direction, Angelika Spangel draws a genuine and intense portrait of a place that looks familiar to us (Catherine Boutaud)

Suneil Sanzgiri’s work has been shaped by an ongoing investigation into the histories of anti-imperialist and anti-colonial struggle in the Global South — rooted in his own family genealogy of resistance in Goa under Portuguese occupation. Here, he writes an impossible letter to Sita Valles, an Angolan doctor of Goan descent who, in the aftermath of April 25, left Lisbon to join the MPLA. A film that unfolds through shifting cinematic techniques and anchors itself in a mutable aesthetic, in an attempt to grapple with what struggle truly means. How can we unearth the solidarities that time and colonialism sought to erase? The director traces a latent mapping of anti-colonial movements uniting Asia and Africa under the former Portuguese yoke. Following the trail of revolutionary Sita Valles — born in Goa and killed in Angola —, the director reveals deep connections between struggles that, though seemingly disconnected, echo on the same frequency of resistance. Through an immersive visual approach, where 16mm film is literally buried and retrieved from the earth, the film operates as both an archaeological and narrative excavation. Sanzgiri bypasses what seems invisible or impossible to track, reconnecting the power of Afro-Asian solidarities. (María Angélica Contreras)

Did you know that from the top of a pineapple you can grow a new pineapple, and so on, forever? Funny Sri Lankan animal friends grow a pineapple and dance. A bright and colourful reflection on the infinity of nature.

Two Black figures — a police officer and a university president — are interrogated by white state officials. At stake is their alleged complicity and collaboration with an oppressive, racist system; ultimately, the plans devised for the institutions they lead have, in the eyes of the State, fallen short. An essay film that probes every corner of its own cinematic language. A radical experiment in disjunction. What happens when the image of a fictional police officer is haunted by the voice of a key figure in contemporary academia? Through a conceptual device that juxtaposes conflicting archives and dialogues, this short film dissects the stifling gears of structural racism. It is a hall of mirrors where language becomes a rhetorical trap and institutions reveal their machinery of domination. Nothing exposed here is strictly new, yet the way the editing shows these layers of authority is mind-blowing. (María Angélica Contreras)

Those last days of summer break, a window about to close — don’t go, Summer. Outside, charcoal strikes the first notes of the barbecue. Balthazar’s cousins are getting ready for the big night, while his older brother pretends he doesn’t exist. That leaves Tom, the one he texts with — the only one who doesn’t remind him that he is thirteen. A summer barbecue and the apparent ease of family life. Through a single long take that builds a stifling pressure, we follow Balthazar’s journey during an afternoon where every second creates a knot in the throat and the stomach. Without any cuts to offer relief, the camera pursues the tension as night falls: everyone still treats him like a child, except for Tom. (María Angélica Contreras)

Like a letter addressed to bittersweet, thorny stability, À pied d’œuvre (winner of Best Screenplay at the Venice Film Festival) begins with a gesture that has been voiced millions of times: one day I’ll leave everything behind, one day I’ll be free. But this successful photographer takes the phrase literally and sets out in search of his freedom: writing. Paul gives up comfort, embraces precarity, and takes a job on a construction site — a guarantee that he will have the time to devote himself to his next novel.

A theatre having national as part of its name, at the top of a square, reflecting a country’s history. But which one? This is a voyage through the various narratives about D. Maria II National Theatre, forged through the intentions of the several regimes that intended to convey their own ideologies within the theatre’s mission. This is also the story of those who fought against it, opposed the institution and became part of it. How can one become heir of these stories, even if never having set foot inside. Auto da Casa do Inferno could serve as the theme to describe the saga of the D. Maria II National Theatre and the company that steered its destiny for the longest period – Rey Colaço-Robles Monteiro. But the story begins even earlier, in the 19th century, and the film directed by Tiago Bartolomeu Costa and Joana Cunha Ferreira (produced by Midas Filmes) seeks to understand why the theatre was built in that location, defining a square, for which country it was built and for which people it was meant. If it seems impossible to make such a film without resorting to filmed interviews, this film proves the opposite. It is a film entirely constructed from archive footage, evoking our memory of a time when such moving images did not yet exist, yet it also draws upon literature and the other arts within the theatre performance. And like snake charmers or storytellers from the oral tradition, the filmmakers lull us into a trance. We are transported into that theatre which once had bench seating, all sort of people and survived a fire, but which, above all, had a programme that never stopped, even when the playwrights were censored, or when the actors could not work because of their political convictions. And what is this place that is a renowned place, which witnessed all the city’s achievements, the political movements, the changes of regime? Perhaps the explanation lies in the fact that when they ‘tried to kill it’, the company moved to the Coliseu and staged the show without any set design, save for the sheer desire to be on stage. A film not to be missed. (Miguel Valverde)

That time of day has arrived: time to stretch one’s legs and switch on the television. A penguin wants nothing more than to watch his favourite show in the comfort of his armchair. But a pigeon, newly moved into the building, is determined to throw the best party in the neighbourhood.

From the window, a bird observes the world outside. Soon, what it sees seems overtaken by what it imagines, a clear reminder that the gaze is almost always defeated by reverie. A film about the possibilities of music, through the flute of Amina Mezaache and the longing for freedom.

Luxury swimming pools and overheated teenagers trespassing have always gone hand in hand. This time, however, “beware of the dog” hardly suffices: cornered by the water, the youths come face to face with three fearsome beasts. Next door, tradition holds steady — a group of friends from another generation welcomes the arrival of summer. Yet despite the screams and desperate cries for help, no one seems to hear. On the eve of St. John’s Day, everything is bound to turn bizarre. It’s the eve of Saint John’s Day, and we’re under the scorching blue sky of Mallorca. A group of young people find a deserted mansion, and the heat invites them to take a dip. Everything’s great, were it not for dogs attacking them, preventing them from leaving the pool. They’re trapped in the small symbol of luxury they wanted to dominate, for an afternoon. What kind of dogs are these? To whom do they answer? Far away, a group of wealthy people gather for a party that becomes increasingly grotesque as the day progresses. Ion de Sosa’s film is reminiscent of the films of another Spanish director – Buñuel. This is a social satire about an anesthetized, alienated, and above all, bored high society, intoxicated by privilege and empty status symbols. But retribution can take many forms, and it’s just around the corner. After all, we’re trapped in the belly of a horrible machine, and the machine is bleeding to death. Or that, or in a pool surrounded by rabid dogs. (Bruno Pereira)
With a banjo tucked under her arm, a young woman walks through a long train in search of self-understanding. In each carriage, an encounter; with every meeting, new realizations.

The cosmos needs Barbarella. Always in revealing outfits, the futuristic heroine sets out on a mission to defeat a villain. But much happens before she gets there. A science-fiction classic by Roger Vadim, the film stands as an important milestone in the careers of both Jane Fonda and the director himself. It’s time to watch it — or revisit it — with your feet in the water.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Cinema at the Pool)

films.syn: Strange lights are said to be falling from the sky. When a reporter arrives in a neighbourhood on the outskirts of Medellín, four marginalized youths who live there steal his camera and begin documenting their lives of violence and solitude — perhaps because, all too often, despair finds its outlet in delinquency. The debut feature by STILLZ, best known for directing music videos for artists such as Bad Bunny, with a soundtrack by Arca. Stillz turns away from the stratospheric success of Bad Bunny and Rosalía’s music videos to turn his attention to cinema, Barrio Triste is his first feature film, produced by Harmony Korine’s EDGLRD. We’re in Medellín, where locals speak of lights in the sky descending onto the street, and a journalist has his camera stolen by a group of young people. From now on, the film belongs to them; no one was telling their story, so they might as well steal a camera and tell it themselves. The film, like its characters, hides immense empathy behind a facade of violence. Being young is complicated enough as it is, much more so when no one seems to care about you. Nihilism with a glimmer of hope, however faint, and all of this set to an incredible soundtrack by Arca. Raise your hand if you’ve never thought that a light should appear from the sky to take us away from here, it doesn’t matter where, as long as it takes us far away where we can reinvent ourselves. (Rui Mendes)

aw: Grand Prize for Feature Film City of Lisbon

films.syn: Whenever a light flickers on in the darkness, insects lose their heads. On a back road by the edge of a forest, the ritual remains unchanged — and a family of vampires dwelling in a nearby cave begins to scheme over the different fates awaiting those creatures.

The Mayflower Dog Show is unquestionably one of the most important events in America. A film crew follows the backstage preparations of each champion dog and their eccentric owners. The tricks, the rivalries, the superstitions. As in any respectable dog show, the strangest creatures walk on two legs.

A Hungarian family of six relocates to Vancouver Island. Jeremy, the eldest brother, is distant and withdrawn, his gaze erratic. Through the eyes of Sasha — the younger sister and a secondary character — Sophy Romvari brings us face to face with the aftershocks of this intimate earthquake. Blue Heron , her feature debut, intertwines the sounds of childhood and the slow aging of memories with the utopia of understanding imposed by adulthood. Prior to this, her first feature, Sophy Romvari made a film called Still Processing (2020), which explored the trauma that still haunted her family. In Blue Heron, Romvari is still coming to terms with it. This film revolves around an experience whose origins are unsettling and whose consequences are an open wound. Yet, in this film, the director presents us with an approach of piercing beauty. Travelling across more than one timeline, we are confronted with the lives of a mother, a father and their children, in their most tender and most confusing moments. The juxtaposition of the present and the past, of reality and fiction, is a tapestry that Sophy Romvari weaves with care and mastery. We can only applaud this debut for the way it portrays something so personal in such a relatable way. Ana Cabral Martins

How far is it from New York to Casablanca? Bouchra, a 35-year-old Moroccan queer coyote and professional filmmaker, spends hours on the phone with her mother. Between them lies far more than an Atlantic Ocean — there are silences, traumas, and deeply buried repressions. The feature-length debut by Orian Barki and Meriem Bennani employs 3D animation as a vehicle for an intimate essay on affection. In New York, Bouchra, a queer filmmaker and anthropomorphic coyote, is struggling to write the screenplay for her autobiographical film. A phone call to her mother in Casablanca serves as the starting point, both for the character and for the film itself, which is built entirely around moments like this: text messages, conversations on dates, letters, and more real-life phone calls between family, friends, and acquaintances of Meriem Bennani, who co-directs with Orian Barki. Through the film-within-a-film device, which combines 3D animation, documentary style and live action, reminiscent of Ralph Bakshi’s early career, Bouchra is absorbing, intimate, entertaining, and erotic, focusing on the complex yet deeply moving relationship between mother and daughter. Falcão Nhaga

aw: Special Mention (International Feature Competition)

films.syn: It was one night at Club Voltage, in The Hague, Netherlands, that DJ Moortje — born on the island of Curaçao — invented bubbling, after accidentally setting a dancehall LP spinning at the wrong speed. In that instant, the soundtrack — and perhaps even a way of being — of the Caribbean diaspora so present in that Central European country was born. Sharine Rijsenburg’s film traces the genre’s origins while exploring its vibrant contemporary scene, so powerfully shaped by feminist energy. Described as a propulsive and highly danceable music crafted by the Caribbean diaspora of the Netherlands, Bubblinh symbolises power, ownership and freedom of the diaspora. By explicitly forefronting the female voices of bubbling, the film shows a joyful and feminist landscape of a musical scene that perfectly embodies an emancipated way of living. Tracing the historic and cultural roots of the club music, while exploring the contemporary scene that keeps pushing the envelope, Bubblibg Baby offers us a female and feminist perspective on one of the liveliest and most joyful expressions of Dutch-Caribbean cultural heritage. (Helena César)

There are lives whose stories demand to be known. Carroll B. Williams Jr. was a pioneering forestry engineer, academic researcher, and entomologist — the first African American to be hired by the U.S. Forest Service — whose legacy within the American forest landscape is immeasurable. Mars Verrone, their grandson and the film’s director, dedicates this portrait to him. The time of the forest renders human time insignificant. Nature takes time to come into being, and it endures. People pass through nature’s time without even noticing its details, and often without caring about its preservation, so essential to life. “Buckskin” was the nickname of Carroll Burns Williams Jr., the first African American to earn a PhD in forestry and entomology and to join the United States Forest Service. His life was marked by research into the forest: its preservation, and the importance of managing its resources in the fight against poverty and for the survival of Indigenous peoples. “It’s time we learned from each other,” he would say. “Buckskin” was also a man who challenged the logic of his time, when a Black man could scarcely dream of an academic career. He lived as he dreamed, and in this documentary, at the end of his life, he reflects on what he did and how he did it, using the time of the forest to think about his own—so much shorter, so much closer to its end. The serenity of his thoughts softens the nearness of his departure. He says he has his hand on the doorknob of the exit; that he does not want to go, because he loves the life he has. But there is no anger, no protest, only a peaceful sense of loss for a good life. Echoing the Welsh poet Dylan Thomas, he is urged not to go gently into that good night, but it is already too late: the forest that welcomed him so well will perpetuate his destiny. (Margarida Moz)

The color, one might say, is that fluorescent green so typical of the jackets worn by municipal waste workers. Raphaël Kaddour’s debut film guides us through the daily life of Recypark Buda: more about the people, less about the trash. Set in a recycling center in Belgium, Buda follows the daily lives of workers on the front lines of customer service. They have to deal with constant demands, complaints, grievances, and with the fact that the customer is always right. These employees simply carry out orders from above, even when they must face the public over decisions made by others. On both sides of this confrontation, different profiles emerge: there are customers who vent their frustrations on the workers, others who direct their dissatisfaction toward the company, and those who recognize the harshness of the job. But even those who listen can only shrug – there are few alternatives for these workers. In between their shifts, the usual interactions between colleagues unfold and we see them reflect on mental exhaustion, the suffocating weight of work, ideas of “success” and the meaning of their roles. At the end of the tunnel lies the mirage of retirement – something to be enjoyed when it is finally time to die. Through shifting perspectives and fragments of dialogue, the film reveals the psychological pressure of work in our century, particularly on the production floor, and questions a system that treats employees as mere tools. (Jéssica Pestana)

After buying a tuna wrap during a rushed lunch break, Kate Renshaw-Lewis found herself wondering how that product had made its way into her hands. Inspired by the logic of a Rube Goldberg machine, Busy Bodies explores the absurdity of our global supply chain. Rube Goldberg, a North American cartoonist and engineer, became famous in popular culture for his unnecessarily complicated machines designed to achieve very simple goals. We can spend hours on YouTube watching these intricate and delightful machines, which use the domino effect and that anyone can build at home. Kate Renshaw-Lewis takes this universe and elevates it into a fascinating hand-drawn loop animation, made using inkjet and screen-printing techniques. A texture that gradually fades throughout the film, as an effect of the repetition of an assembly line. (Carlos Ramos)

films.t: Butthole Surfers: The Hole Truth and Nothing Butt
films.syn: Almost always performing in full nudity, setting guitars on fire and bringing weapons onstage was all in a day’s work for the Butthole Surfers, the legendary Texas band formed in the early 1980s after two accounting students, Gibby Haynes and Paul Leary, crossed paths. Their psychedelic rock, steeped in radicalism, chaos and unpredictability, left a lasting mark on a generation of musicians, from Nirvana to The Flaming Lips, as well as the early era of the Red Hot Chili Peppers. It took until 1996 for Gibby Haynes and Paul Leary’s band to achieve their first major hit: Pepper , from the album Electriclarryland . For many, this was the gateway into the band’s universe. But anyone who arrived here, arrived late. Before that, there had already been Psychic… Powerless… Another Man’s Sac , Rembrandt Pussyhorse , Locust Abortion Technician , and Hairway to Steven . And lingering at the doorstep is not advised. You have to step inside without fear, explore the dark basements and attics of this burning house that is the Butthole Surfers, a cult band, an underground legend, masters of the absurd and of chaos. Tom Stern fully understands the mission of making a film about the band. This could never have been a conventional film —and fortunately, it isn’t. From the parody of the ever-changing number of bassists and drummers who passed through the group, to the eventual stabilization with Teresa Nervosa and King Coffey, and the infamous 1986 show at the legendary Danceteria club in New York, we are taken on a journey through the iconography of North American alternative music and culture of the 1980s and 1990s. Along the way, there is room for the lucidity of Steve Albini, the final days of Kurt Cobain, the early films of Richard Linklater, and the supergroup P., with Flea and John Frusciante, performing at the legendary Viper Room, Johnny Depp’s club, where River Phoenix died. This is one of the most brilliant and funny North American bands in the history of music, a band that was once called The Inalienable Right to Eat Fred Astaire’s Asshole . (Carlos Ramos)

Camille (Juliette Lewis) enters a home décor store and becomes obsessed with a chair. Soon after, she swaps bodies with it and quickly realizes that everyone around her prefers this version of herself. Amanda Kramer’s film, which premiered at Sundance and is narrated by Melanie Griffith, is a dramedy with a strong physical component, repeatedly showing its protagonist trapped in space, at the mercy of her surroundings. It is impossible not to read it as a satirical commentary on the objectification of women. This film is a highly idiosyncratic experience. Amanda Kramer depicts a hyper, mega-stylised world to tell a story of absolute fetishisation: someone who desires to possess an object with every fibre of their being and, later, desires to become that object with every fibre of their being. Kramer crafts everything with a rigorous aesthetic vision and a biting, dry sense of humour that gets under the viewer’s skin. Camille’s body, whose essence (soul?) is transferred to a chair, is as present in her friends’ lives as ever, and her relationship with her own mother is better than ever. It’s not just that the writer-director manages to combine elements of literature, cinema and performance art to satirise common social behaviours for their absurdity; she also reveals the emptiness and meaninglessness in her characters’ lives. By Design is a rebellion against the objectification of women, but it is also more than that: it takes the intense desire to be desired to its ultimate conclusion, to the point where one allows oneself to be used. Ana Cabral Martins

The past haunts Emily, who carries the guilt of tragedies that struck early in her life. A youth camp, her father suggests, might offer a fresh start—looking after children and finding redemption in the midst of nature. She is warmly welcomed by a group of counsellors she quickly grows close to, but a voice from the bushes urges her to leave. Every now and then a film comes along that makes me want to rescue the term lynchian from the machiavellian clutches of the film bros. But when I say lynchian , I don’t want you to think of a mere imitation. I want you to think of a film where you never quite set foot on solid ground. Where you feel yourself floating through it, as if the film were made for your subconscious. As soon as it begins, you find yourself in a space that isn’t your own; it’s intimate, and you feel like an observer, yet you can’t help but watch. Avalon Fast creates this formal mechanism to allow us to experience the same kind of somnambulism as her main character. Emily is going through a tough time; she’s in mourning, and life is passing her by. We should all join Emily, perhaps going through a tough time ourselves, but with the wisdom that together we’ll get better. Even if it means joining a sisterhood and performing some rituals, a small price to pay for therapy. (Rui Mendes)

Loss often takes the slow silhouette of apathy. As if the gaze drifts away, as if walking were suffering and speaking a mountain to climb, Miguel and Laura drag themselves through pain in search of an embrace. Youth is an unspoken sentence. Two people missing someone. In a brief excerpt from what almost feels like a slow motion relay race of characters, one smoothly giving way to another, and so on (including returns, overlaps, and closing loops), Certas Formas seems to offer the viewer a fresco of emotions and the gestures that convey them. Avoiding a direct access to the emotions, in simple words each person establishes their state, embodying the melancholy that permeates the film in a brief and unfinished explanation. Then the clash and friction of these encounters, gentle clashes rather than violent ones, gradually reveal in the visible the particularity of how each person feels it, and even more importantly, how each person shows that they feel it. In a subtle and sensitive way, privileged moments of interaction unfold through the filmmaker’s prolonged care for attention and staging. (Vasco Muralha)

In a rural region of Brazil, a family raises and sells chickens to make a living. Their mother sends Dadá and Tato to deliver one from their coop to Seu Vicente’s restaurant, where the pot awaits as its final destination. Along the way, a special bond begins to form between Chica, the chicken, and Tato.
A very tiny fish sails in a vast underwater city. Is he too small to see the world like the big ones do?
Mr. Gnome is sunbathing in his garden when, out of nowhere, a little cloud comes around and hides the sun. He gets very angry but luckily he knows exactly what to do.

A chant from another time reveals the ancient everyday gestures of a Gypsy family, anchored by the errant couple Maria and Arménio. In the flow of days and life cycles, we find resistance and celebration. In the world of Cochena , anything goes: picking flowers, lying on the ground, looking for snails, looking at photographs, remembering those who are no longer with us and whom we miss; actions that reveal a tremendous zest for life. Maria and Arménio lead the way in this world, and we follow them on walks, through conversations and encounters, through everyday moments, confessions and reflections. We follow them through the gypsy wanderings that overflow with life, where there are bonfires, dancing and music, children and joy. A film punctuated by time, by gestures, by celebrations, by young people and adults, and by what they think and say on the spur of the moment. A film where everything flows and everything seems vital. A cinematic gaze that seeks what is given to it in an immense exchange and that stays very close to the people. (Carlota Gonçalves)

aw: TVCine Prize for Best Portuguese Feature Film

films.syn: Óscar escapes from rehab, and Mário wakes up with images that don’t belong to him — no memories of his previous life. Thus are separated the two brothers living on the outskirts of Mexico City. The latter encounters Lázaro, who becomes his mystic mentor: in the underground, countless portals open to the supernatural. Clemente Castor’s work has long explored Mexican youth and their tormented bodies — Cold Metal continues along that path. “Keep playing, keep choosing… but it’s the arrow that will decide the prize,” sings a young woman in the opening sequence of Frío Metal , by Clemente Castor. Shot on the outskirts of Mexico City, the film is driven by fortune, which guides the narrative centered on Mario, a young man who awakens without memory. From this seemingly simple scenic game, a complex web is drawn that stitches, opens, and tensions perceptions. Upon meeting Lázaro who teaches him how to enter the bodies of other people through holes in the ground, Mario’s own body becomes a matter of passage, a mediator of pains and possibilities. Yes, it is indeed too profound; too dense. But Castor’s cinema is made of this rare matter that excavates, with an intense and intimate camera, the fissures of a contemporary Mexico. In this second feature film he returns to character-actors and landscape-settings, continuing in the construction of films so dense that they seem, literally, able to be held in one’s hands. Lucas Camargo de Barros

A football team coach dies—but he is no ordinary man, leaving behind a trail of grief and disorientation. What follows is far from contractual disputes over his replacement; here, football (or its behind-the-scenes world) serves merely as the backdrop for devotion and the question of what comes next to emerge. A series of surreal encounters and situations unfolds. What wreckage does the death of someone leave in those who remain? “Show me your wound?” someone asks in the film. The context of football, often marked by codes of masculinity, spectacle and performance, is displaced into a territory of vulnerability and introspection that emerges from the process of mourning which runs through this team. Nevertheless, elements characteristic of that world persist, from press conferences to backroom dealings, but they appear decentered, stripped of their usual function. We are therefore a long way from the typical sports drama. The football club becomes a space in suspension, where the usual codes no longer organise experience and disquieted subjects are left in a search for meaning. Not coincidentally, the film’s title is a direct reference to the Sufi poem by Farid al-Din Attar, The Conference of the Birds, in which birds from all over the world gather and decide to set off in search of a king, only to discover that what they were seeking is nothing other than a reflection of their own collective being – something that resides in what they are when they relinquish the ego. The existential drift that the German-Iranian filmmaker Amin Motallebzadeh pursues with notable restraint in this debut feature is expressed through a singular grammar that moves “in circles rather than in lines”, in a visually compelling register that finds its expression in découpage, sound design, rhythm and language, often charged with spiritual undertones, while not excluding occasional moments of humour. Conference of the Birds is an immersive sensory experience and a reflection on mourning as a moment of spiritual search and a process of emotional healing. Susana Santos Rodrigues

As real estate speculation intensifies, a small tight-knit community finds itself threatened by hidden interests. A wave of pollution, measured drop by drop, is affecting a community whose water supply is being targeted by those who act in secret. The inhabitants live under this threat, which seeps into them like a poison that corrodes the memories they are gradually losing. People are disappearing; a sense of fear hangs in the air; a feeling of paralysis and apathy begins to take hold; people’s mannerisms change; their gaze drifts away. The atmosphere is heavy day and night, the fear grows; in a karaoke bar, a song without a voice spreads, answers are sought, voices fall silent. They are visited by strangers who want to strip them bare, to control them. The siege tightens; they must resist. (Carlota Gonçalves)

aw: New Talent Prize McFly

films.syn: Bunny and the viewer are locked in a relationship; yet the bed of roses, the sensual game, quickly drops its mask, unleashing violence that erupts and repeats itself relentlessly. How is an aggressor made? Bunny is a seductive and, on apparent, innocent doll. Yet, in a split second, her romantic scene turns into a psychological horror film. This disturbing animation questions the role of the abuser in the cycle of violence in intimate relationships, also bringing up the issue of emotional manipulation. A powerful work that forces us to face her. (Catherine Boutaud)

Dans un Souffle is a breath caught on ice, tracing, figure skater, Nina Pinzarrone’s fragile yet unyielding pursuit of perfection. In black and white, it traces fleeting shapes and expressions, exploring the quiet resilience behind her graceful facade. Dans un souffle is a documentary that follows the daily life and rigorous training of Nina Pinzarrone, a young figure skater. This delicate film highlights the rigour and dedication required to practise this sport at the highest level. The carefully crafted camera movements and sound design follow the young athlete like a second skin. (Catherine Boutaud)

Nothing emerges from nothing. There is always an initial spark, a stubborn impulse that gives rise to a trend. That is precisely the case with David Holzman’s Diary , a 1967 film by a young director who decides to document his daily life and turn that footage into a film — in essence, a proto-YouTuber or TikTok-style influencer. An egocentric and strikingly prophetic satire, and one of the earliest examples of self-referential cinema.

It has always been this way — and it still is: so that some may enjoy their possessions with little effort, others must exhaust themselves producing them. In the Mutoshi mine, in Katanga, Democratic Republic of the Congo — in the depths of the world — a community of workers known as the Rememberers extracts cobalt, a mineral essential to the manufacture of technological devices, under the most inhumane conditions. And yet, they endure. Led by the camera, we venture deep into the Mutoshi mine in the DRC, amidst a crowd of workers. The sensory immersion is overwhelming, almost surreal. Everything blends together: shouts, impacts, movement. A raw, visceral experience that reveals the extreme working conditions faced by miners digging for cobalt. (Catherine Boutaud)

films.t: Detective Smiley and the lost friends
films.ot: Détective Smiley et les amis perdus
films.syn: The disappearance of an activist becomes the latest case for the young and enigmatic detective Smiley. Sleeves rolled up, she crosses a less obvious France, tracing the missing man’s footsteps in a lo-fi odyssey about the B-side of a generation — and of a nation. Smiley is an unlikely detective: young, with a cool, relaxed demeanour, she devotes herself to investigating disappearances (of her friends, and of her friends’ friends) – ghosts are her kind of people. Starting from what seems like a straightforward case, the investigation unfolds through encounters, testimonies and clues that multiply and branch out, opening up successive narrative threads that never fully come together. Between Paris and more remote landscapes, the story drifts: each answer leads to a new enigma, and every figure encountered seems to carry another story with them. In the universe of this work, which combines different registers on 16mm film, the everyday and the uncanny coexist seamlessly. As the investigation fragments and reconfigures itself, Détective Smiley et les amis perdus becomes a wandering journey, covering its own tracks and setting out false starts – in the finest spirit of Rivette. (Cláudia Marques)

Old age always arrives. What we do with it is another matter entirely. Or, in this case, what others do with our old age—something Dick Johnson, a psychiatrist whose health is beginning to fail, might have wondered when his daughter Kirsten asked if she could make a film about his death. In truth, it is more a film about the many ways her father might die: a mockumentary brimming with humour that nevertheless speaks straight to the heart.
The true story of a dog abandoned in his own home, at a time when my grandfather was beginning to experience his widowhood and I was returning from London, a place where I felt more alone than ever.

Maria Joana navigates the discoveries and transformations of adolescence. She experiences her first night of independence at the local Saint John street celebration, testing her limits and confronting her inner fears — but not without consequences.

Two little girls are playing with a ball. But after a petty quarrel, they get angry with each other and take offense. Their umbrage makes them inflate like balloons, they fly all the way up to the clouds. Girls get stuck up there, with no idea how to get down and save their kitten stuck in the tree.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Cinema at the Pool)

films.syn: Four film critics, accompanied by the discreet presence of a director, analyse the origins of their cinephilia. The May 3 screening will be followed by a discussion with invited guests after the film. How is a country’s cinema defined? By its filmmakers, by the images and sounds (or lack thereof) in its films, or by what is said or written about them? Júlio Alves, in his persistent quest to understand the cinema produced in Portugal, following the magnificent Sacavém and Diálogo de Sombras , once again turns his gaze to the materiality of cinema, to the physical objects that become a machine of light and project images onto a screen for the viewer. Four film critics are invited to comment on their first images, whether drawn from memory or experience, or even from the origins of our own cinema. And the result is surprising because suddenly the critics speak of their first images as emancipated spectators, which foreshadows the fact that they will become critics in the future that is our present. Alves’s camera, ever attentive, anticipates gestures or perceptions that we will only understand later and places their memory at the service of our own memory as viewers. This is a film that reflects us back. It is me, it is you; each of us identifies with what we hear, and perhaps we can understand that going to the cinema or watching films at home, on a television or a streaming platform, is a gesture as commonplace as the meals we have eaten. But when these images become ingrained in us, perhaps the future will tell us that cinema will one day come knocking at our door. Vasco Câmara, Inês Lourenço, Ricardo Vieira Lisboa and Luís Miguel Oliveira are Júlio Alves’s guinea pigs and our alter egos. (Miguel Valverde)

Not only is he one of the central figures of the Romanian New Wave, he is also a long-standing presence at IndieLisboa, where several of his films have already screened — some of them award winners ( Aferim! , 2015). This time, the drama follows in the footsteps of Bram Stoker. In the hands of the sharp-witted Radu Jude, Dracula is thrust into the present day, into a Transylvania where bitten necks coexist with workers’ strikes Directly from Romania, of course, the director, the film, and the central figure Dracula arrive to reclaim the myth of the horrendous vampire and redefine it, this time as a convenient product. Between tourist routes and stimulants to boost libido, Dracula becomes both laborer and product of the commodification of culture, a bloody legend designed to quench the thirst of consumption and marketing. The film follows a filmmaker suffering from creative block who turns to a fictional AI software, Dr. AI Judex 0.0, to create the “perfect” film for audiences. Ingredients such as sex, violence, outrageous humor, frenetic chases, and blood, plenty of blood, are combined with little regard for narrative cohesion or artistic quality. Here, what matters is satisfying the feverish desires of the market. Through stories within stories, bizarre imagery, and delirious interludes, Jude constructs a farce that reflects the wasteland of post-auteur cinema, cultural consumerism, and the psychosis of profit. Dracula, the vampire, is as monstrous as he is allegorical: what truly sucks are the mechanisms of the actually existing system. Every scene, every exaggeration, and every narrative device signals the transformation of art into merchandise. In its late phase, everything, even historical memory and literary myth, can be properly packaged, sold, and consumed. With acidic humor, bold creativity, and a touch of controlled chaos, Dracula challenges the viewer to laugh at its contradictions and to reflect, perhaps realizing that the true horror is not confined to Dracula’s dreadful castle. (Jéssica Pestana)

The letter left no room for doubt: Lisa doesn’t want to be found. Her disappearence is also a project —to photograph football fields swallowed by time and overgrown vegetation in rural Georgia. Irakli (her father) and Levani (her best friend) set out to retrace her steps, questioning strangers, animals, and the quiet goalposts along the way. Georgian filmmaker Alexandre Koberidze’s third feature is an ultra lo-fi portrait of familial conviction in motion — and of nature’s quiet defiance. Shot on Alexander Koberidze’s own 2009 Sony Ericsson phone, Dry Leaf, which begins as a straightforward investigation of a father looking for his missing daughter in the Georgian countryside, becomes something entirely different as the film progresses. Through the repetitive nature of the father’s search, and with the help of the film’s mesmerizing soundtrack, the narrative grows increasingly abstract and transforms into a hypnotic exploration of shape, color and light. If we allow Dry Leaf’s profoundly singular spell to flow through us, it reveals itself as one of those miraculous films that confronts us to the mysteries of being, and to the world’s overwhelming strangeness and grace. Koberidze’s gaze, as usual, is boldly traversed by openness and love, and his latest masterpiece is yet another one of his tender attempts to teach us how to perceive the world as if for the very first time. Nabil Aouad
Up the stairway, two movers struggle to carry an enormous piano. Sometimes hardship gives way to discovery.

In Eloise’s Summer , a nine-year-old girl discovers the world of her curly hair and Cameroonian roots. Eloise is mixed: her mom is Belgian and her dad is from Cameroon. Though her hair can sometimes be challenging and even painful, she learns to love it and explores the endless possibilities of her hair. She captures her summer adventure in a self-drawn book.

Rob (Will Maiden) and Bethany (Charli XCX) are on holiday in Warsaw, and he carries an engagement ring in his pocket. Doubts soon begin to trouble her, as caring and devoted can also mean dull. The impulse is to run away, to chase after Nel (Lena Gorá), an old Polish friend she had lost touch with and with whom she shares an intense chemistry, to the point that both feel that whenever they are together, a volcano erupts. The IndieDate screening on Saturday, 2 May is hosted by Diogo Faro, followed by a post-screening Q&A to break the ice and spark new connections – powered by a quiz you can answer here . Then it’s on to the iconic Message Party at Purex: messages of friendship or flirtation, your call. Nothing is more disruptive than a volcanic eruption: its dramatic intrusion into an apparently quiet daily life is, by nature, haunting. As an unpredictable manifestation, it readily lends itself to metaphorical readings, particularly in the realm of romantic passion. In Erupcja, however, this axis is subtly inverted. Rather than positioning the volcano as the driving force of the narrative, Pete Ohs shifts the focus towards the ways in which affective relationships, fragile and uncertain, may themselves operate as triggering forces. The premise evokes the so-called butterfly effect, associated with Chaos Theory: the idea that an infinitesimal gesture, such as the beating of a butterfly’s wings in one part of the world, may reverberate and produce unforeseen consequences elsewhere. In Erupcja, it is precisely these minor disturbances that gradually reconfigure the outcome. This movement is mediated by a discreet yet vital narrator, whose dry humour and restrained irony prove central to the film’s construction of ambiguity. Between order and unpredictability, the work situates itself within a zone of tension where chance begins to take shape. Susana Santos Rodrigues

As a gift for his wife, Álvaro buys at auction a mirror that, at the beginning of the twentieth century, once belonged to a brothel. He installs it in their bedroom, and it soon becomes clear that anyone reflected in it is suddenly seized by an inexhaustible sexual appetite. Based on a play by the playwright Vicente Pereira, this 1985 classic by Antonio Carlos Fontoura is an exuberant dance of bourgeois moralism. From the director of The Devil Queen (IndieLisboa 2023), the film is presented in a new digital restoration.

Love, cinema and naivety. They meet randomly in the street: João is unemployed, Clara is a cinema production assistant. A boy-meets-girl story where the consummation is cinema itself. The protagonist’s world reflects that of a young generation: an inner world, melancholic, sensitive, naïve, and imaginative. A world that allows a film camera to speak. It is said that Paulo Rocha once told Henri Langlois that Portuguese cinema could be characterised by three adjectives: anarchic, artisanal and visual. Óculos de Sol Pretos is, to a certain extent, a fable—as romantic as it is analytical—on precisely this subject. A “moral tale” about the artistic condition in Portugal, a “sardonic comedy” about the misadventures of making films in this country. A film within a film (within a film), starring the clumsiest of production assistants. Inspired by many of the anecdotes shared amongst colleagues on set, Pedro Ramalhete sketches a broad portrait of the Portuguese film scene, navigating between criticism (the toxic atmosphere, precariousness, the obsessiveness, power imbalances) and passion (with several love letters addressed to Portuguese filmmakers such as José Álvaro de Morais, Manuel Mozos or Miguel Gomes). “Cinema is a drudgery,” reads an intertitle at one point, and yet it goes on. A cinephile film, where that adjective is used as an insult. (Ricardo Vieira Lisboa)

Tere’s house is filled with plants and bathed in a light of its own—an ideal setting for the first televised interview granted by Rosa, the hostess’s friend and a prominent musician. Tere’s daughter, also an artist, joins the pair, and a long, ironic debate on hypocrisy in the art world begins to unfold. Add to this the power outages, the stubborn barking of a neighbour’s dog, and other comic, persistent intrusions, and the result is the perfect recipe for an ode to the everyday as a raw material of rare excellence. In a metropolis like Mexico City, where five million cars fill the roads every day, traffic jams are a common sight. After the opening credits at a noisy and congested junction, we are taken to Tere’s flat, where the entire film is set. Tere is a cellist and composer. Today she hosts Rosa, another composer, and also journalists who are coming to interview her friend. For the most part, things go awry: technical problems, a power cut, a dog barking while the recording, and Tere’s daughter, Luisa—whose father is a well-known composer—constantly makes sarcastic remarks. In this tender comedy, Nicolás Pereda surprises us with razor-sharp and hilarious direction, as well as an irreverent and magnetic cast comprising the director’s regular actors. The mother (Teresita Sánchez) and daughter (Luisa Pardo) duo stand out, revealing how the male-dominated art world excludes them, yet, through their humour and complicity, enjoy together the beautiful harmony within the cacophony of everyday life. Falcão Nhaga

A lovely kid named “O” is very curious and busy discovering the world around. Despite all the obstacles “O” manages to gather some personal experiences and to gain some new skills. Will they prove useful? A short story told from a child’s perspective. For parents. And little humans.

A single mother, her two children, sun, beach, ice creams, holidays. The games, so close at hand, seem to be unfolding miles away. A deafening silence heralds Fanny’s despair. Fanny arrives in a small seaside town to spend the summer holidays with her two young children. From this simple premise, the film crafts, with remarkable economy and intensity, an intimate portrait of an imperfect woman, torn between caring for her children and a quiet desire to escape. Driven by a restless energy, an underlying exhaustion and a constant urge to flee, she gives the film a rare vitality – observed up close, without judgement or explanation. At the heart of this unconventional yet deeply tender portrait of motherhood lies her profound bond with her children – a constant love, even as everything around her feels precarious. (Cláudia Marques)

Yes, obstetric healthcare is also marked by severe racial inequalities. In Fiction Contract , Carolyn Lazard records a simulated childbirth performed by Jada, a Black mannequin — a staging that is at once perfectly surreal and profoundly necessary How much can a high-fidelity clinical simulation achieve? What is the value of a silicone birth? What is the purpose of this exercise when the educational component is removed? In this short film, an obstetric emergency team establishes a fictional contract: an understanding that extends to the viewer and presupposes a suspension of disbelief. By accepting this premise, a one-way mirror lets us peek into a delivery room where Jada gives birth. It could be almost anywhere on Earth, but this scene takes place at Elmhurst Hospital in New York, which serves one of the most ethnically diverse communities in the world. Jada seems nervous, perhaps because she knows that, as a Black woman, she is potentially subject to a maternal mortality rate significantly higher, perhaps because she is aware that she is the first racialized mannequin in this simulation center. When the illusion fades, we are left wondering whether the protocol was strictly followed, but perhaps some hope for the future remains. (Sara da Cruz)

Between light, metal and silver, Filme Pin turns a collection of solidarity pins into an archive at another scale, spectres of exile and international struggle against Portugal’s fascist and colonial regime. A prominent member of the Portuguese Communist Party, who was part of the resistance against the dictatorship (and took part in the famous escape from Peniche in 1960), passed away recently, leaving behind a vast collection of pins relating to the various movements of the Socialist International. The collection is presented to us by his granddaughter, who knows little or nothing about these objects and the organisations they represent. But her lack of knowledge in no way diminishes her fascination. The simplicity of Filme Pin is absolute: a dark background, a hand, each pin filmed one at a time on 16mm film, a voiceover. And, in this simplicity, it reveals itself as a play on meanings (consonance and dissonance between sound and image, between background and form, between front and back) which, through editing, uncovers the musicality of gestures. Between an ode to communist iconography and an iconoclastic exercise (decontextualisation, pictorial dazzle), the camera in Filme Pin merges with the hand, touching and manipulating its materials. Hence, that eye-ring signals the formal strategy of this haptic film. (Ricardo Vieira Lisboa)

Let’s face it: building a bed with one’s father is hardly a child’s dream activity. The boy soon allows himself to be distracted by a fire-child, who lures him into a new world where mushrooms grow at a different rhythm and birds look nothing like the ones he knows. But he will have to find his way back. There is still a bed left unfinished.

Three baby birds, one big challenge — their first flight! But as the frogs begin their peculiar performance, the sky turns into a whirlwind of improvisation. Some birds twirl, some hover, and others just hope for the best.
The little cloud is looking after a pretty flower. She loses her temper when a pesky plane gets in the way.

Fordlândia is often presented online as a “ghost town” and as a utopian project by Henry Ford. Yet the Amazonian company town, founded in 1928, was never a utopia. Nor is it a ghost town; on the contrary, it is full of life. Here, the ghosts are active historical forces: Ford, capitalism, extractivism. Following Fordlandia Malaise (2019), Susana de Sousa Dias returns to explore this well-known and much-discussed “ghost town”, “utopian city” or “mystical city”, founded by Henry Ford, where the ruins, archives and testimonies ‘speak’ once more. An evocation that reveals voices and new narratives, a film that showcases indigenous archaeological discoveries, awakening and questioning ghosts, and projecting the evils and virtues of this feminine land that overflows from the fabric of memory. Fordlandia Panacea activates a place, creating a universe that propels images and propagates sounds and voices that unravel threads of history which intersect, re-intersect and expand time. (Carlota Gonçalves)
As Anna wanders through the snow, she meets an unexpected playmate.

A fortune teller lays out the cards and AP’s fate is sealed: a curse that is here to stay. What do you do in circumstances like these? You run. You search further ahead. You ride a motorcycle. One thousand dollars and the body of a little lamb — no more, no less — that’s all AP needs to break free. Along the way, the misadventures pile up, becoming ever stranger, more excessive, provocative and, above all, trashy. After all, the city where it all leads is called Trashtown A sex worker, a curse, tarot cards, a psychic, and a motorbike – that’s all it takes for a transformative journey through Trashtown. Along an erratic, almost episodic path, Fucktoys builds a universe where absurdity and desire coexist freely, without hierarchies. A trashy, queer world without moralism, one that John Waters has already introduced us to in other works, but here filtered through a female perspective that shifts the gaze: the body ceases to be merely an object of shock or provocation and instead becomes a territory of agency, vulnerability, and reinvention. Somewhere between the grotesque and the intimate, the film rejects any easy redemptive reading, opting instead for a chaotic, sensory approach that mirrors the protagonist’s own emotional instability. The result is a punk road movie that presents the decadent and inevitable side of capitalism, while also functioning as an essay on language, identity, and resistance. Art, sex work, and spiritual practice converge, allowing vulnerability, improvisation, and surrender to become vehicles for transcendence, empathy, and transformation. Fucktoys offers no easy answers; instead, it invites us to inhabit discomfort, recognize complicities, and rethink hierarchies between body, desire, economy, and spirit. (Jéssica Pestana)

Born in the favela, it has spilled into major avenues and taken over every corner — street parties, underground dances, and upscale nightclubs alike. Funk, more specifically funk putaria, is now Brazil’s most popular music genre, proudly raising its anti-prudish flag and foregrounding the body — particularly the female body — as a site of resistance, desire, and self-assertion. Funk U All, the new film by Ana Rieper ( I’ll Raffle Off My Heart , IndieLisboa 2012), brings funk to the center of sex, or sex to the center of funk. Featuring artists such as MC Carol, Valesca Popozuda, Deize Tigrona, MC Rebecca and Tati Quebra Barraco, Massa Funkeira delves into the world of Brazilian funk and celebrates this genre that has taken national radio by storm, bringing this style from the Rio de Janeiro suburbs to the whole of Brazil and beyond, breaking down social and economic barriers. The film portrays an important parallel between funk and sensuality, between funk and sexuality, and explores gender, pleasure, sexism, and the relationship with the body, whilst giving voice to the desires, successes and dreams of women in an environment that has always been dominated by men. Without moralising, Massa Funkeira reveals how, through the body, dance, lyrics and the experiences of artists, funk expresses resistance, desire, pleasure and personal affirmation. A celebration of a musical genre as the vital force of Brazil’s suburbs and of the country’s urban Black culture. (Helena César)

aw: IndieMusic Prize - Special Mention

films.syn: This is not just another film about Artificial Intelligence. Valerie Veatch’s proposal is to return to the Stone Age of this plague that has invaded our daily lives — to understand its origins and anticipate its trajectory. Through an in-depth investigation, shaped on screen as an essay, Ghost in the Machine is bold, provocative, and calls for reflection. The May 2 screening will be followed by a discussion featuring guest speakers.

Mounted on his Gravity Racer, a vehicle born in his garage, a four-year-old boy takes on the steepest hill in his neighborhood. And now? Has what he imagined turned out to be far more dangerous than he ever expected?

The bond between siblings is a system of its own: it can be as enigmatic as it is candid. Hal and Harper share their own semantics and semiotics, born and raised in Los Angeles. But when their father announces that his girlfriend is expecting a baby, the troubled childhood that Hal and Harper never quite allowed to resurface suddenly moves to centre stage. A series by Cooper Raiff, the first four episodes of which can be seen at IndieLisboa. Canais TVCine series preview. Hal & Harper is a tender, quietly devastating miniseries about the fragile architecture of family and the ways love can both sustain and undo us. At its centre are the messy, profound bonds between siblings. Set in Los Angeles, it follows Hal and Harper – two deeply codependent adult siblings – as they navigate relationships, friendships, and the emotional residue of a complicated childhood. When their father announces the arrival of a new baby, brother and sister are forced to confront both their past and the uncertain shape of their present, trying to not desperate about the future. Created, written, directed by and starring Cooper Raiff as Hal, alongside Lili Reinhart (a truly unforgettable and extraordinary Harper) and Mark Ruffalo (their loving and haunted dad), the series unfolds as an emotional rollercoaster – by turns chaotic, funny, and deeply moving (and at times bringing you to tears). The bond between Hal and Harper is symbiotic and visceral: a source of comfort, but also constraint. Shot in just 50 days from a 300-page script developed over six years, this 9-episode miniseries favours subtle gestures over melodrama, capturing the unspoken tensions that shape family life. At the festival, the first four episodes will be screened, with the remainder to be available on TVCine channels. A moving exploration of memory, identity, and connection, Hal & Harper lingers long after the final frame. (Alexandra Ferraz)

films.t: Henry is a Girl Who Likes to Sleep
films.syn: More than a love letter to Henry the cat, this film drifts into a drowsy performative exercise of life together — gestures, silences, sighs. Mostly horizontal in stance, it moves at a snail’s pace, as if morning never quite ends. What would we be without them? This film is a letter to Henry, with whom the narrator shares a horizontal life and an immense desire to sleep. Henry is a cat. Henry is also the girl who writes the letter and who finds in the furry creature the projection of a need for comfort and tenderness: “I want a human to rub my head against, and whole days spent under my blankets.” One sleeps so as not to have to exist: “I do think going to sleep is one of the very best things for people who are unhappy.” Sleep here is not laziness, it is not carelessness, nor is it linked to sin; it is intimacy and comfort; it is a body that curls up like a cat to overcome vulnerability and everything else. Like a snail that retreats when the outside world is all a threat, the narrator also wants to curl up in her blankets and withdraw into herself. This letter addressed to Henry seems, after all, an attempt to overcome the fear of feeling in the form of a declaration of (self-)love to a cat. (Margarida Moz)

aw: Special Jury Prize (International Short Film Competition)

films.syn: What is it that grows while decomposing other organisms? Microfungi are natural biodestructors, essential to the recycling of dead matter and the continuity of nature. In this essay film, we watch them grow under the microscope while art conservators attempt to preserve humanity’s collective memory. The metaphor speaks for itself. Holy Destructors, the second feature by director Aistė Žegulytė and cinematographer Vytautas Katkus, continues their research into the intricate relationships between humans and other species. Here, they let us into the world of the microfungi who regulate everything that exists by feeding on it, creating new life out of decay and grief. Alongside wondrous images of these workers toiling away, we look over the shoulder of human remains’ conservators, partake in a grim Easter rite, and look lovingly into the icons of Christianity, all examples of the funny and immensely touching attempts at preserving the relics that we use to make a little sense of the destruction happening all around. If death regulates the world, we obsessively spend our lives trying to regulate death, rejoicing in strange tasks such as the ones we witness throughout this joyful memento mori. Holy destructors, filled with wonder and curiosity, is an invitation to indulge in our rituals of upkeep with a healthy dose of letting go. Leonor Castro Nunes

films.t: Home is where the heart is
films.syn: Mia’s past could be called trauma. Deep drawers, filled with objects and fragments of a childhood scarred by her father’s sexual abuse. A film that both recreates and redirects — a place where healing is not arrival at the shore, but an exploratory, intentional drift. Revisiting childhood should always be accompanied by beautiful and colorful memories, but for some, recreating the past is like falling into an abyss filled with ghosts. In this film, the house that should have been the cradle of infancy is reconstructed in all its spatial details, where the most heinous episodes fit. In Home is Where the Heart Is , the past is not merely remembered; it is laid bare in all its horror through a performance that uses virtual reality to reconstruct the house where Mia lived through an abusive childhood. Every detail of the structure, every object that fills it, is a vestige of violence, attempts at disembodiment, and silences. “I had the feeling that something precious just broke. That’s exactly how I felt when I passed through the door of that house.” The memory of a broken home redefines the adult in subtle ways that link violence to love and reproduce it in the search of affection and understanding. We need to rebuild this house in order to tear it down to the sound of Wim Mertens’ music, which vocalizes emotions when all words have already been spoken and what remains is revolt and action. (Margarida Moz)

In the middle of the night, she grabs her car and hits the road. A desperate woman is determined to sell her own version of an energy drink to a mysterious online buyer, at any cost. Strange, decadent and darkly funny, the film offers a possible portrait of contemporary America. I’ve always had a small regret, I didn’t learn “stuff” during covid, I guess I just existed. I’m not going to lie and say I’ve never felt some envy for all the people that learned a new “stuff” during the lockdown. Watching Homemade Gatorade reactivated that envy in me. Life just seems better if I learned to produce my own homemade gatorade, find some sketchy people online to sell it to, drive more than six hours through the night and eventually explore holes people have in their ground. Imagine all the stories we could tell if we lived the homemade gatorade life. (Rui Mendes)

In an old movie theater, the oldest question of all: how do I know if I love someone? Life has moved with his mother to the Times Theatre, in downtown Manila, and finds himself stumbling through the tentative first steps of love. Everything within this setting matters: the films, the venue’s fading grandeur, and the quiet wisdom of its projectionist — their confidant. It’s in the title: Honey, My Love, So Sweet offers us, above all, sweetness. JT Trinidad plays with light and shadows to paint the innocent picture of the discovery of love, through the eyes of a queer child – Life. Much like Life, this film is also guided by curiosity and intuition in the creation of a charming and tender atmosphere, occasionally contrasting with the vibrant life of Manila.
