The research method chosen by Life is infallible and universal to any geography and stage of life: looking for answers in films. In this search, Life quickly discovers that, like this old Cinema and contrary to what films want us to believe, love can also be decadent and perishable. (Sara da Cruz)

A choreography of people and kindred creatures moves toward a bizarre tower. As if under a spell — a hypnotic occurrence — the group is unable to stop, estranged from command over their own faculties. Yet there is someone who seems to vibrate at a different frequency. You’ll feel the urge to head out and dance after watching this gripping animation. The journey takes us to a remote tower in the desert, where a group of characters falls victim to a mysterious “dancing plague.” What begins as a rhythmic movement quickly escalates into a collective mania, an uncontrollable fever taking over every body. In this contagious universe, line and color merge in a hypnotic ritual with the power of rhythm. (María Angélica Contreras)

The obsession with wellness has reached every species. In a luxurious retreat that markets relaxation to restless birds, a budgie attempts to rediscover himself. For reasons he cannot quite explain, all he truly wants is to return to the safety of his cage. O Hotel Oblique encontra-se, possivelmente, a meio caminho entre uma fantasia de dominação do mundo e o mecanismo de escape de um periquito que só quer descanso. Ou será liberdade? Neste breve filme de animação, embarcamos numa viagem surrealista marcada pela incerteza, estranheza e humor. Com um tom desconcertante, acompanhamos a ave protagonista em busca da consquista do seu espaço pessoal. Merlin Flügel lembra-nos de que os pássaros também sonham. E alguns são particularmente bons a encontrar o caminho de volta para casa. (Sara da Cruz)

Sexual fetishes of white men toward Asian women have persisted for centuries — burdened with the macabre and racist promiscuity they inherently carry. In 2021, however, when Robert Aaron Long murdered eight women in Atlanta in an attempt to suppress his own desire, a new circle of hell was reached. Through a series of letters, Dutch–Japanese filmmaker Kiriko Mechanichus addresses the killer directly. Why? More than a portrait of a real crime, How to Catch a Butterfly unfolds as a personal and provocative essay on desire, power, and representation. The film takes a crime as its point of departure to expose the persistence of western fantasies surrounding asian women – often perceived as submissive – and the dynamics that emerge from them. By inscribing her own body and voice into the narrative, the filmmaker rejects this projection and asserts a subjectivity that resists homogenization. This gesture is not merely performative but critical: it confronts the tendency to dissolve singularity into a collective, consumable image. The film operates as a field of inquiry, invoking and reconfiguring codes associated with pornography as a system for the production of desire. By exposing these categories, it reveals how certain bodies are framed, eroticized, and hierarchized according to logics that exceed the individual level. Through multiple layers, the intersection of misogyny and racism emerges: the female body is simultaneously objectified and racialized, inscribed within a typology that limits its agency. Without seeking to explain it, the film shifts the focus to the regimes of representation that make it possible. The result is a critical work that invites the viewer to confront not only what they see, but the conditions that shape their own gaze. (Jéssica Pestana)

aw: Grand Prize for Short Film EMEL

films.syn: It’s winter and there is no rain. Sofia returns to her grandmother’s house. In the mountains, she finds a land where only the Wind lives. All that’s left of the house is dust and ashes. In the attic, Sofia finds pieces of lives other than her own. That’s where the house listens. A camera peeks through windows and stirs up ghosts in a film that breathes; Lillian Gish, the young Letty, fresh from Sjöström’s earthy The Wind , watches us. Here, cinema acts as a witness and sparks the imagination. Night comes to lull the bodies to sleep, lighting fires in the foreground that crackle and send up flames. By day, one must look to the sky, clear the air, listen to music. Sofia returns to her grandmother’s uninhabited house; the atmosphere is heavy, there are boxes waiting for her and crumbling walls; there is dust, there is ash. A film that breathes like a lung of wind, moving through textures, shadows and sounds, where the windows never cease to peer out at ghosts. (Carlota Gonçalves)

From 1922, Häxan is regarded as one of the most significant horror films of the early twentieth century — and on top of that with a mockumentary twist. Yet it is much more than that: by combining historical facts with folk traditions, the film throws open a window onto the evolution of witchcraft through the centuries and, of course, onto the persecution women have faced throughout history. — with musical accompaniment.
A grandfather dies and tries to leave his home. Unfortunately, his family don’t want to believe that he’s gone for good. Every time he tries to run away, they take him back to them.

films.t: I Am The Film Motherfucker, But I Am Real
films.ot: أنا يلا بعمل الأفلام اللي إنت بتتفرّج عليها، بس في الحقيقة
films.syn: A found-footage collage emerges from five archives in post–Arab Spring Egypt: an activist in exile, the recruitment of a group of cadets from a military academy, a television series, and other fragments of a generation born of a failed revolution. The film reclaims propaganda — so deeply performative — in which the athletic male body is staged as the ultimate agent of the authoritarian state led by President el-Sisi. Activist Wael Ghonim, a computer scientist and former Google executive, was a central figure in the Arab Spring in Egypt in 2011. In this film, he also appears as the central figure, years later, in exile, caught between lucidity and the mental collapse of someone who witnessed all the dreams of a revolution crumble into a new autocracy. What we see is a fascinating and overwhelming archival work that exposes the aestheticization of violence, the cult of the body — even in children — as a war machine, repression turned into entertainment, and historical revisionism, all promoted by President el-Sisi’s regime. A denunciation and warning about the propaganda machine serving an autocrat, in Egypt as in all other autocracies around the world, or those on that path. (Carlos Ramos)

films.t: I Built a Rocket Imagining Your Arrival
films.ot: Fiz um Foguete Imaginando Que Você Vinha
films.syn: Rosa lies inside an MRI machine. She is asked to think of a happy memory, something she doesn’t have. It is time to create one, by returning to her childhood, when her mother was arrested and accused of murder. And there they are, in a realistic reverie, travelling in an old hot dog van along the dirt roads of northern Brazil. Janaína Marques’ feature debut is a guided tour through a mind in turmoil, its landscapes and its wounds. A mother and daughter, on the run through north-eastern Brazil, driving a hot dog van after an armed robbery, arrive at a hotel where the sign reads, ‘The Rabbit Hole’, in blue and red neon: this is Rosa in her imagined wonderland, when, inside an MRI scanner, the technician asks her to recall a happy memory. I Built a Rocket Imagining Your Arrival proposes a therapeutic journey through the subconscious to rediscover, or invent, these memories. We witness the reunion between Rosa and her mother, Dalva (at times older, at others younger than her), who was imprisoned for many years after killing her neighbour’s husband. Janaína Marques takes flight with a sensitive and captivating debut feature film, which, with almost no male characters, tackles the themes of domestic violence, femicide, motherhood, love, and reconciliation honestly. Soul and heart in the form of a film. Falcão Nhaga

I first met Jay at Kanaal40, a bar located in Amsterdam’s Warmoesstraat. I worked behind the bar, Jay worked as a security guard at the door. At the threshold of the club, Jay found a sense of security: a space to express themselves and explore who they want to be. Even after the bar closed its doors, the experience continued to shape Jay’s life in deeply personal ways. Jay worked as security at the door of Amsterdam’s Kanaal40, a cultural space that combined a bar, restaurant, club, and platform for the so-called “micropop culture”: small cultural scenes, niches, and very specific communities. While inside, diverse artistic expressions and people intersected, the door served as a boundary between the outside world and this ever-changing universe. It was at this threshold that Jay found something deeper than just a job. The position at the entrance became a space for observation, belonging, and discovery, where they began to explore their own identity, influenced by the inclusive and experimental energy of the place. The film follows this process of transformation, painting a portrait of Jay and Kanaal40, where the director also worked and where the two met. Through cutouts, assembling, layering, and juxtaposing of images and drawings, this animated documentary conveys a sensory experience and reveals Jay in all their complexity. (Margarida Moz)

films.t: In the Darkness of the Night – Director’s Cut
films.syn: Free Admission. Tickets can be collected on the day (Culturgest, from 6.30 pm). Maximum of two tickets per person A roadside strip club run by an entire family — and, as always in João Canijo’s cinema, a family with more beneath the surface than it first appears. It is time to return to In the Darkness of the Night (2004), one of his most significant works, presented here in the director’s cut — in essence, the film’s original version, running 17 minutes longer than the one premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in 2004. A tribute screening dedicated to one of the masters of national cinema, who passed away this past January.

June 2006, Stockholm. Two men enter a bank wearing helmets and carrying weapons. It was this event that Ruben Östlund, the multi-award-winning Swedish filmmaker, drew upon for this short film, which would go on to win the Golden Bear at the 2010 Berlin International Film Festival. The film reconstructs a failed bank robbery, shot in a single take and choreographing more than ninety participants.

Radu Muntean, one of the most distinctive voices of the Romanian New Wave, returns with his latest short film. In a remote forest, an ornithologist gathers material for his research. While reviewing the footage from his cameras, he comes across a feral child. What now? Shall we play hide-and-seek? Radu Muntean, one of the most established directors of the Romanian New Wave, returns to IndieLisboa, this time with a short film. The premise is simple – somewhere in a lost forest, a solitary ornithologist collects material for his research. We don’t know if he lives in a post-apocalyptic world, or if there are simply no more people, but one night, while reviewing the images from his cameras, he comes across a wild child. With a deliberate pace and a palpable tension only a few can achieve, Muntean deconstructs the thriller structure until little more than a skeleton of distant sounds and human fears. Welcome back, Radu. (Bruno Pereira)

Fallen, seemingly unconscious, a man goes unnoticed on a busy street. An insect crawls into his head, and drowsiness quickly disappears. He is now a man seized by terror, turned inside out by his own fears. After Howling (Best Short Fiction Film Award at IndieLisboa 2023), Japanese filmmaker Aya Kawozoe returns to the festival.

Old videotapes reveal what memory has made impossible to forget: Shayma’ Awawdeh was six years old when the Second Intifada erupted in Hebron, Palestine. Children play atop tanks and rubble as we hear Shayma’s voice, speaking to her mother. In Intersecting Memory, Palestinian filmmaker Shayma’ Awawdeh attempts to reconstruct memory through a personal archive of images from the Second Intifada, opening onto a collective experience of historical violence. The footage from old tapes, together with the film’s voice-over, creates a tension between the clarity of childhood memories and the possibility – or necessity – of forgetting as a defense mechanism, or even a form of survival. The images do not exhaust themselves in their documentary value: filtered through memory, they become something else – a space where the visible coexists with what is fragmented or omitted. In the encounter between image and testimony, the film gains intensity, reactivating the collective imagination through a first-person voice that restores affect and presence. Susan Sontag argued that constant exposure to images of violence can produce a kind of collective numbness. Today, we are confronted with such images, but rarely with the duration and depth of the trauma attached to them. In this sense, the film acts as a gesture of memory’s continuity, reminding us that the resistance of the Palestinian people is by no means recent, while also testing the limits of this numbed gaze. The result is a film that is both emotional and political: the story of a nation inscribed on the faces of Palestinian mothers, who have endured – and continue to endure – countless massacres, protecting their children as best they can from the horrors imposed upon them. (Jéssica Pestana)

A tomato — a simple tomato — from the moment it is planted until it rots. Winner of the Silver Bear at the 1990 Berlinale, this short film by Jorge Furtado is one of the most significant Brazilian films of the twentieth century. Charged with acidity and irony, the filmmaker exposes consumer society and its inequalities.

films.t: it’s not the sun who is moving
films.ot: it's not the sun who is moving
films.syn: Free admission. Luis Macías’ spatial metaphors It’s not the sun who is moving Luis Macías 6 x 16 mm film projector installation, colour, loop 2026 The installation It’s not the sun who is moving proposes an abstract contemplation, where the immobile reveals its own invisible choreography. A dissonance arises between the illusion of what we perceive as constant and what is really changing. Motionless… we gaze upon the suns. What is yet to come? This immersive, multi-room installation, in which film projections of the sunrise, sunset and full moon footage recorded through a system that rotates image by 360° unfold across three spaces, invites the audience to move freely among them and engage in an immediate relationship with the celestial bodies over the course of a single day. — At a time when watching films (and series) has become a solitary habit shaped by streaming platforms and an exhausting abundance of choice, many of us nonetheless find a consolation from the weight of everyday life in this lone, convenient, screen-bound ritual. Therefore, it is not surprising that expanded cinema live performances are often audiences’ favourite once they get themselves exposed to this shared, in-person experience that transforms viewing from a flexible act, prone to distraction, into a spatial, collective and engaging one. Emerging in the 1960s alongside experimental film and performance art, between intermediality and media convergence, expanded cinema practices continue to be on the forefront of the novel audiovisual expressions, evoking unexpected emotional responses and creating memorable impressions. This uniqueness is the result of the real-time blend of technique and creativity, a kind of a skilful exchange with the machine: devices become instruments, the filmstrip or pixel a material, the audience and performer(s) together with space active parts of the work, offering a form of art that is ephemeral and unrepeatable. This performance is part of a series of six analog live performances by Luis Macías, presented across the member festivals of the European Short Film Network throughout 2026. The project is realised in cooperation with THIS IS SHORT and curated with the support of 25 FPS Festival. An expanded cinema installation with free admission, to see at Palácio Sinel de Cordes in collaboration with Trienal de Arquitectura de Lisboa during the first day of Open House Lisboa.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: European Short Film Network)

films.syn: In Ivar , the debut film by Norwegian filmmaker Markus Tangre, puppets are placed within a framework of everyday social realism. Anne notices a sudden change in her husband’s scent, and the night turns into a moment of self-questioning. In Ivar, we enter the mind of a woman trapped in a long-term marriage. Her husband is no longer the man she fell in love with – or perhaps he has begun to reveal exactly what he always was, now that she has stopped idealizing him. An ordinary, even banal man, but now examined through the increasingly meticulous and unforgiving lens of a wife who can no longer stand him. And under that lens, the banal becomes something else – abominable, repulsive, hateful. Love has died, and passion has long been buried in the swamp of routines, silences, and, worst of all, the hideous little habits of a person once loved. She desires nothing less than to be struck by a burning passion, the kind that upends an entire life. But not with her husband. Meanwhile, he is perfectly happy, leading the easygoing life of a man who sincerely believes everything is fine. He drifts along, sluggish and content, completely unaware that, inside his own wife’s mind, he is brought to trial every night – judged, condemned, and duly executed. Between her fantasies of a longed-for rupture and the very real dryness of everyday life as a couple, a vast abyss opens up – one that is as uncomfortable as it is comical, filled with boredom and estrangement. The marriage drags on, stubbornly alive. (Jéssica Pestana)

Four children guide us from the entrance to the visiting room of a prison — a place they go twice a week to see their mom or dad. Prisons aren’t built with children in mind, yet in Belgium, over 16,000 kids have a parent behind bars. I’d love to see you gives a voice to the children of prisoners and shows how they end up in a situation they never chose.
A film about the joy of community and creating together. As performed by ducks.

In modern-day Lisbon, two art students drift through a weekend of escapism and late-capitalist burnout. Sofia and Amandine’s toxic friendship is put to the test when Amandine crosses paths with Guilherme, a pretentious artist, at an independent exhibition. Kiss and Be Friends is an acerbic comedy exploring intimacy, identity, and a generation driven by irony, anxiety, and Instagram. The city is Lisbon, the protagonists are two young women—one Portuguese, the other French—the lingua franca is English, the setting is gentrified, the milieu is artistic and academic, the tone is satirical, the characters embody a range of stereotypes, and the result is a biting comedy that portrays a city going through a transformation. From start to finish, Kiss and Be Friends defies its title. In fact, the narrative structures and situations suggest we are dealing with a romantic comedy, where the foreign and the traditional meet in an exotic setting. But this romantic façade is, in a systematic (and even cruel) manner, stripped away with every interaction, every duality, every game of manipulation or pretence. This is not a film about love and friendship, or rather, it is so by contradiction. Ana Baldini and Roly Witherow dissect the superficiality of human relationships in a city (and a society) that operates according to notions of utilitarianism, producing a moral tale about the value of authenticity. (Ricardo Vieira Lisboa)

In a Polish folktale, a young possessed woman has lived for centuries inside the mysterious Kontrewers Stone. Zuza Banasińska — who presented work at IndieLisboa in 2024 — draws on this ghostly figure to set fiction and reality simmering in the same pot. Her 102-year-old grandmother, confined to her bedroom and gently waving toward death, encounters — and becomes enchanted by — the relic (or by the haunting presence that inhabits it), in a lucid affirmation that communication is far more than words. In Kontrewers , legend has it that a young woman committed murder with a stone. Since then, the stone has never stopped growing. The soul of a girl trapped in a stone that continues to grow speaks to a 102-year-old woman. Believing she has found her mother, she begins an unsettling dialogue that spans the entire film. Obliterating space and moving freely across shots of the most varied origins, this cosmic dialogue, in a mixed-media approach that surprises at every turn with its unexpected cohesion, creates a journey through textural raccords , exploring both the violence inherent in this story and the violent history of these textures. Beyond the cruelty, the film seeks this synthesis in great tenderness: the filmmaker’s delicate interest in this story and in her own grandmother, the vision that allows her to delve into this approach. (Vasco Muralha)

Located between Salamanca and the Portuguese border, in a harsh and mountainous landscape, lie Las Hurdes — a kind of village-from-nowhere, a place where misery and aridity are briefly interrupted by the arrival of a film crew. Luis Buñuel’s third film, based on an ethnographic study by Maurice Legendre and shot just a few years before the outbreak of the Spanish Civil War, portrays the traditions and resilience of a people living in an unforgiving land.

films.t: Last Night I Conquered the City of Thebes
films.syn: António and Jota return from the front with their friends, looking for an ancient Roman thermal bath. They joke with each other recounting past tactical glories. The baths have appeared after a long time spent under the water of a reservoir, and people of all ages curious about the discovery come to spend the day. But there is something mysterious about these thermal waters — as if the baths influence the mood of the men, giving them the courage to say things they have never told anyone. José Tolentino de Mendonça, in his book The Mystic of the Instant, challenges us to not only think of time horizontally, meaning as a narrative succession of instances, but also vertically. Vertical time is not chronological and repeats itself unto eternity, it is the universe’s daily breath: the passing from day to night, the movement of the stars, the falling of rain. And cinema, which literally records time, is the art most uniquely capable of bringing us closer to this breath. In the extraordinary debut of Gabriel Azorín, the focus is precisely on the articulation of this verticality: we see two stories set in the same location, a Roman thermal bath, but separated by 2000 years. In both stories, fragile men confess their tender yearnings to their close friends. They are under the same sky and stars, bathing in the same baths, separated by time, but mysteriously folded into each other. In the leadup to the premiere of his film, Azorín wrote that “every film presents a conflict between the linearity and circularity of time. Cinema has a unique way of presenting itself as both a fleeting and permanent experience, reminding us that life is ephemeral while sheltering us in a habitable and eternal temporality.” Confronting us with the vertical or circular nature of time is to remind us of its passing, and in the words of a recently departed giant, “I despise stories, as they mislead people into believing that something has happened. In fact, nothing really happens as we flee from one condition to another… All that remains is time. This is probably the only thing that’s still genuine — time itself; the years, days, hours, minutes and seconds.” Nabil Aouad

The sea is ailing. It is unclear whether this is a recent affliction or the accumulated toll of decades of human exploitation. Three desperate, forgotten fishermen turn to dynamite fishing as their cure. A catastrophe in every sense of the word. An unknown disease appears to have decimated much of the plant and animal world, whilst three amateur fishermen struggle to survive. Under these extreme conditions the film prompts us to reflect on our relationship with the environment and with one another. This dystopian scenario resonates with us and does not seem so far away. (Catherine Boutaud)

films.ot: Lenas Hof: Das Huhn will fliegen
films.syn: The hen is supposed to lay eggs, just like the other chickens. But the swallows in the air have awakened a completely different longing in him: she wants to fly!
The squirrel’s nest is warmly padded for the cold winter with all kinds of stolen goods. But then a flood breaks out and forest animals flee to Lena’s farm. The squirrel would like to help them…

On a dimly lit plain, where life is scarce, the Organoid spends its days in a simple existence. At a certain moment, it begins to sense a threatening presence around it. It decides to flee and the confrontation happens. Life of the Organoid is a film that presents the life cycle of an unlikely and bizarre organism. The visual narrative follows a seemingly strange and purposeless being – described as a mass of “flesh” with legs and a small, primitive “head” – as it eats, drinks, sleeps, defecates, and even reproduces. What at first may seem simple or even absurd gradually transforms into a reflection on movement, behavior, and the experiences that are part of any form of life, or life in its raw state. Daan Lucas creates a singular visual universe that blends humor, estrangement, and a curious sense of contemplative observation of existence. Through animation and an almost visceral aesthetic, the director brings the viewer closer to something both repulsive and fascinating, creating an ambiguous relationship with the creature. What initially appears grotesque begins to take on a certain familiarity. The organism’s repetitive gestures and basic needs become recognizable, almost human, suggesting that despite its unusual appearance, it shares with us the fundamental impulses of survival. (Jéssica Pestana)

Things cannot always go our way. Two characters connected by their hair explore the world around them. As they come to accept that they may want different things, the strand of hair stretching between them grows longer.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Cinema at the Pool)

films.syn: At the edge of time, in an unknown realm, a primitive man comes face to face with a creature from outer space. A most singular intertemporal encounter.

films.t: Look, She Has Her Eyes Wide Open
films.ot: Regarde, elle a les yeux grand ouverts
films.syn: In the 1970s, the MLAC (Mouvement pour la libération de l’avortement et de la contraception) was a key organization in the fight for the right to abortion and contraception. Filmed over several years, the film follows several women in a non-hospital setting, offering a portrait of remarkable intimacy and profound collective historical significance. This screening marks the international premiere of a new digital restoration presenting, for the first time, the film’s full-length version of this militant work.

Sometimes, the hardest step in a day is the first one. In Loose Sleep , our hero fights a battle against himself: is it worth it to leave the comfort of the duvet and live life outside? By means of a fragmentary narrative, built on dreams and associations, this short film follows the protagonist’s speculation on activity and passivity, the passage of time and the (dis)advantages of being awake. Between the bed, the flowing water and the nature beyond, there is a movement that flows through the film and drifts freely in a certain aimless current. Rodrigo lets himself go, gets up and lies down, and the rhythm of the images enters a flow that seems to generate a dreamlike current of gentleness, sounds and sensations. Loose Sleep sets the images free, allowing them to be imprinted on the film and projected into further dreams, awakening a world that stirs to the “possibilities beyond the bed” in a constant ebb and flow between in and out. (Carlota Gonçalves)

What Jodie Mack does with images seems to elude the realm of concrete things — or at least to grant it another temporality, another light, as if unfolding within a dream, through a singular and wholly experimental montage. In Lover, Lovers, Loving, Love , the British filmmaker composes a loving and erotic choreography among flowers and petals rescued from her own garden. The return of experimental filmmaker Jodie Mack to the festival ( The Grand Bizarre , IndieLisboa 2019) unfolds through poetry, romance, and a continuous dance of flowers. All films are meant to be seen in a cinema, but some only truly make sense when experienced that way. This is one of them. In that space, the film rises to another level, that of a shared, almost ritualistic sensory experience. There is love, life, sex, and death. The film is beautiful, beautiful, beautiful. A beauty that multiplies across each of its parts, until it spills into a psychedelic explosion of floral textiles. (Carlso Ramos)

aw: Silvestre Escola das Artes Prize for Best Short Film

films.syn: Following the acclaimed Sun Dog (2020), this is the second film by Dorian Nour Jespers, a young Belgian filmmaker with a certain flair for the absurd. In Loynes — which premiered at Cannes’ Quinzaine des Cinéastes — a corpse goes on trial in 19th-century Liverpool. A nameless body with no known past is put on trial before a boisterous court in nineteenth-century Liverpool. Kafkaesque at its core, Dorian Jespers’ second short film proposes – among other layers – a reflection on time itself. The accused body is lifeless, yet “to be dead does not mean not to be”: a ghost is created, crossing years and spaces to prevent its own story from being erased. Strange, absurd, and ironic, Loynes is a project that unfolded over many years, evolving from a feature film into a video installation. In its final form, the film brings together drone images and some striking VFX, along with a camera inside the courtroom that seems perpetually searching for something, perhaps guilty, clues, or a voice capable of explaining what is taking place there. It is also a mirror of a society endlessly seeking itself, haunted by the ghosts of its own past. (Pedro Gonçalves Ribeiro)

Gerd Osten was an important Swedish film critic who ultimately turned to that profession after numerous failed attempts to become a filmmaker. In Mamma , Suzanne Osten—her daughter, who unlike her mother would go on to become a filmmaker and a central figure in her country’s cultural life—tells the story of a woman (clearly based on Gerd) who, between the late 1930s and the 1940s, persistently tries to make films in a Sweden occupied by Nazi Germany.

films.ot: C'est arrivé près de chez vous
films.syn: A pair of filmmakers become fascinated with Ben, a serial killer who seems to them the perfect subject for their documentary. His everyday life proves to be bloody, and with camera in hand the film becomes complicit in his macabre crimes. A cult work, controversial upon its release, it reflects on the ethics of the media and the elasticity of their limits.

films.t: Marcel the Shell with Shoes On
films.syn: Everything about Marcel is adorable: the tone of his voice, his shoes, his hopefulness. The tiny shell lives with his grandmother in a bright and comfortable apartment, yet his heart cannot rest: under mysterious circumstances, the two lost contact with the rest of their family. Their course is about to change. A filmmaker passing through the Airbnb where Marcel and his grandmother live posts a short film about the endearing shell online, and it quickly goes viral. The odyssey begins.

With an aesthetic rooted in hand-painted imagery, Me And You and Smoke is an imaginative and sensitive animated film, marked by a distinctive sense of humor. As a fire breaks out, a boy’s obsession with his love interest ignites and grows out of control.

Umata, Africa, 2093. The landscape is enchanting, even though, many years ago, a bloody war here destroyed generations. Kuve’s journey is driven by the desire to make a film about the consequences of that conflict, and it is in this process that he meets Mumbi, an aspiring actress who tries to dissuade him from using Artificial Intelligence in his work. From that point on, it is the film, it is love — it is everything at once.

The eerie chant of a decaying choir of cherubs heralds a utopia. A machine — not quite a machine — unveils its own vision of paradise. Merrimundi is the latest film by Niles Atallah whose recent work has delved deeply into post-apocalyptic aesthetics. According to the Doomsday Clock, in December 2025 we stand 89 seconds from the end of the world. What we will find there may echo what we see in Merrimundi. Pure delirium and chaos in a post-apocalyptic setting where multiple languages are spoken and from which a space of rebirth and creation also emerges. Niles Atallah delivers a film we can almost touch. A sensory feast and creative impulse that expands the imagination and broadens horizons. Between musical, performance, and collective hallucination, Atallah’s puppets are steeped in the spirit of the Quay Brothers and Švankmajer. (Carlos Ramos)

Jacques Tati is one of those incomparable names when it comes to cinema. This film is among his most brilliant gems; it is here that Mr. Hulot is born. The master of comedy brings him into the world and immediately places him in the most sandy of settings: a seaside resort where the character proceeds to spread chaos. Holidays always demand their share of mishaps.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Cinema at the Pool)

films.syn: Alex witnesses his best friend being attacked, but an intimate secret keeps him from speaking up. Guilt consumes us, and so does fear. When young Alex witnesses his best friend being violently attacked, all he can do is run away and remain silent, like a victim of a hidden demon – which, in his case, is the concealment of a secret that makes him, in his own eyes, guilty. Monstro is a film about teenagers who are growing up, just as their bodies and desires are. That is how they see themselves, but the parks have many eyes and conceal many fears. This is a film about the discovery of courage, anchored in Nuno Baltazar’s solid direction and in the masterful work of composition, art direction, colour and sound. A film of extraordinary moments, monumental silences and raw emotions. (Miguel Valverde)

films.t: Monty Python and the Holy Grail
films.syn: The years go by, but Monty Python endure. It’s never too often to return to the most iconic comic sextet in British history. And, being the good Britons they are, in 1975 they turned their attention to the legend of King Arthur and the quest for the Holy Grail. One of those comedy classics that goes well with just about anything. The film is directed by Terry Gilliam and Terry Jones.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Cinema at the Pool)

films.syn: From 1970, presented here in a newly restored version, Ester Krumbachová’s film—by a key figure of the Czech New Wave and co-writer of the essential Daisies , by Věra Chytilová—revolves around Ona, a forty-year-old single woman whose life has not turned out quite as she had hoped; a marriage would be the bare minimum. She then recalls an old flame who, in his present form, happens to be the Devil. If at first this does not seem to trouble Ona, the conversation soon takes a different turn.

If only words could soften the distance between people. Unfortunately, that is not always the case. Such is the situation for Thomas and Carla, whose relational rift deepens after Carla is involved in a car accident while travelling with her dance partner to view a house in the countryside. Allow me a bit of hyperbole when I say that nothing in the world is as complicated as the relationship between two human beings who have decided to tie the knot and build a life together. Okay, what about brain surgery, you ask? Yes, it’s complicated, but there’s training for that. However, no one trains us for when the person we’ve chosen to spend the rest of our lives with is crying—we can talk and, above all, we can listen, but it’s a special kind of helplessness. No matter how much we feel we’re helping, it’s impossible not to feel inadequate. And when nothing seems to work, how about a hug? A hug can heal a lot of pain, but sometimes it’s not enough. We want to overcome the physical barrier and embrace the heart directly. But how, when no one trains us? Angela Schanelec is back at IndieLisboa after Music (2023) with the magnificent My Wife Cries , which shows us that cinema is truly a machine of empathy. There is no conventional training for relationships, since we are all infinite combinations of personalities, but cinema has everything we need to learn. Just as when we see someone we love crying, if we watch closely and listen carefully, perhaps we’ll learn something and come closer to embracing someone’s heart in the same way that cinema constantly does for us. (Rui Mendes)

aw: Silvestre Prize for Best Feature Film

films.syn: Based on the legend of NABIA, the goddess of rivers and waters in Galician-Portuguese mythology, a wordless allegorical narrative unfolds, celebrating the integration of human cycles into natural cycles, to the extent that harmony allows. Nabia was the name given by the pre-Roman Iberian peoples to the goddess of fertility, health and abundance, often regarded as a water deity or associated with mountains and forests. Nabia proposes a re-examination of this mythical figure through an iconoclastic haze that lies somewhere between the codes of silent cinema (the aspect ratio, the rejection of dialogue, the instability of focus, the predominance of wide shots, the pictogram-like quality of the images) and the distorting explorations of Alexander Sokurov’s cinema. The result is a period fable touched as much by mystical fantasy as by the soaring montage of dreams. Humans and animals dominate this strange territory where artifice and paganism question the meaning of the ‘natural’. Sabrina D. Marques infuses every image (every gesture, every glance) with a dreamlike quality, completely dissolving narrative conventions and allowing us to sink, slowly, into this amniotic slumber. Until, at last, a child cries and the world begins anew. (Ricardo Vieira Lisboa)

films.t: Newport and the Great Folk Dream
films.syn: There was a time when music festivals were defining spaces. The Newport Folk Festival, in Rhode Island, was as much about music as it was about activism. Set between the 1963 and 1966 editions of the event, this film unveils a new generation of American folk music, marked by the rise of artists such as Joan Baez, Johnny Cash, and Bob Dylan. In 1965, Dylan shocked the world by performing three songs with an electric guitar, abandoning his acoustic approach in a moment that would become etched in the history of music. According to the prevailing myth, an enraged Pete Seeger rushed, an axe in his hands, to cut the power supply. He had to put an end, once and for all, to that betrayal, the disgrace of seeing the young once prophet of folk music converted to the perversion of electric music, of rock ’n’ roll. The venue was the Newport Folk Festival, the year, 1965. That’s the place and time we return to in Newport and the Great Folk Dream . We return not to confirm the myth, but to discover the truth. And the truth is far more complex, interesting and revealing than the myth, which cast Dylan as the scapegoat for something that, in truth, was beyond his control. Assembled from the 100 hours of footage shot by Murray Lerner, director of Festival (1967), between 1964 and 1967, featuring an impressive gallery of legendary names (Johnny Cash, Mississippi John Hurt, Son House, the Staple Singers, Dave von Ronk, Odetta, Pete Seeger, Bob Dylan, Joan Baez), Newport and the Great Folk Dream tells the story of a folk utopia, brief and unsustainable, giving way to the world of rock ’n’ roll and its attached counterculture that, in this film, looms before us as surprisingly contemporary. (Mário Lopes)

Lia is a shy girl who works in a convenience store. Although she asked to be transferred to the night shift to avoid serving customers, she discovers that the night clientele is even stranger. Amid distorted faces, jarring noises and awkward movements, and unsettling encounters, this animated short film explores the different forms fear can take: fear of others, fear of taking up space, fear of confrontation and of being seen. Lia works the night shift at a convenience store to shield herself from constant public exposure. She quickly discovers that at night, customers are even stranger and more unpredictable, as they embody her fears and ghosts. But do they also carry her kindness? (Margarida Moz)

films.ot: Nie ma duchów w mieszkaniu na Dobrej
films.syn: Siblinghood is a bond like no other. Jana, Nastka, Franek and Benek are four siblings on the threshold of adulthood, each grappling with their own anxieties and tangled stories — one believes they are haunted by a strange little monster, another faces troubles with drugs, while another tries to clear the fog of love. One thing is certain: within this web, no movement is ever truly isolated.

The trio of filmmakers met at the École des Beaux-Arts de Montpellier, where they soon founded a research collective exploring the intrusion of reality into online video games. After several films delving into this relationship, they arrive at Normal Planet , where a virtual museum welcomes visitors embodied by extravagant avatars. For about a decade now, this trio of filmmakers has been exploring, between research and cinema, the ways in which experience and perception of reality are shaped in virtual worlds. In Normal Planet , they imagine a day in a crumbling virtual museum, inhabited by curious avatars delivering disarming and often biting commentary on the artworks. A very polite frog controls the entrance with a metal detector; a festive dinosaur mistakes a horse-riding orangutan in a painting for Louis XIV; a group of kawaii teenagers in TikTok mode animates the space with lively discussions. Amid rooms overrun by vegetation, canonical works and crudely rendered surfaces, a flow of conversations unfolds that is as absurd as it is revealing: they discuss nudity in paintings, contemporary modes of art consumption, the way video games shape our perception of landscape, and the impossibility of “undoing” an action in art as one would on a screen. At the same time, the virtual bodies glitch, distort, and pass through surfaces, as though testing the limits of that world. Guided by the gaze of a fish, Normal Planet becomes a playful essay on the museum as a space of projection, where the virtual and the real contaminate one another and aesthetic experience is continually reinvented by its visitors. (Cláudia Marques)

It is autumn, and a squirrel busies itself preparing its stores for the coming winter. In the process, it discovers a missing nut — only to come face to face with a brazen crow. What follows is a wild chase through the forest.

For as long as she remembers, Francisca lives with an inexplicable and uncontrollable aversion to belly buttons. Nothing makes her more anxious than this simple part of the body and the shapes in the world that resemble it. When therapy isn’t enough to solve her cherished phobia, Francisca turns to other types of methods — without any scientific basis and not recommended for anyone who suffers from the same condition.

For Bear, Nikki isn’t just his childhood friend — she’s the love of his life. But confessing his feelings becomes a puzzle of its own: shyness, and the fear of hearing “no.” He turns to a drastic solution — buying a One Wish Willow, a vintage toy from the 1960s that grants a single wish. The problem is that once a wish is granted, there’s no undoing it, and Nikki’s unconditional love soon begins to reveal a sinister side.

When I look at my love, he looks at the boy in front of him, but we only see each other’s backs. Never the face. Because we’re not all dancing together. We’re in pairs. And in this dance, my love doesn’t exist. I drag him into it, but only his back. And it was his back that I fell in love with. His broad back, dressed in the most beautiful costume in the world, which is all the costumes he wore. A whispering voice tells us a story of love and heartbreak. In the image, against a black background, a succession of photographs forms various compositions. They are almost always night-time photographs marked by the sharp glare of the flash. Miguel De’s camera is particularly attentive to the details of rural kitsch: plastic flowers, motorbikes wrapped in tarpaulins, worn carpets, religious iconography, barbed wire and, of course, the world of folk dances and costumes. But what could easily be a condescending gaze is, touchingly, a display of affection. The context of folklore serves as a catalyst for a naive hyper-romanticism that possesses the disarming power of its confessional tone. This, and of course, the play on gender roles defined by tradition, challenged by the love story between two young men. The handkerchief becomes a symbol of desire, with the red embodying the ardour of lust. The narratives the camera invents in each photograph shatter the continuity between sound and image. Until, as in La Jetée , the stillness of the photograph gains movement through the power of a single glance. (Ricardo Vieira Lisboa)

films.t: Oh Be a Fine Girl Kiss Me
films.syn: Shot in 16mm film and smartphone, Oh Be a Fine Girl Kiss Me blends historical fiction and autobiography in a meditation on life’s choices and constraints, as well as on the systems and categories that shaped modernity. The narrator is made soul to communicate with us the memory of a past life in her reincarnation as a nun. Time flows with the images to reach the words that narrate her story alongside three other nuns – the “Machines of God”. They were summoned by the Vatican Observatory to map and catalogue the stars in the sky. The images shift through colour, movement, flickering, constellations of light, objects, figures and real people: the nuns. Fiction, facts and autobiography intersect; different timeframes cross paths; centuries are traversed, and this entire micro-universe concentrates and intensifies to articulate thoughts and reflections that travel in a time machine. (Carlota Gonçalves)

After the Fall of the Berlin Wall, Olinda — a city on the outskirts of Recife, Brazil, whose fate was then overseen by the country’s first communist woman mayor — became known as the first city in the world to bankrupt a McDonald’s. “A McFilm by Douglas Henrique,” the credits read. With fries sauce, by the way. What do the Cold War, Brazilian municipal elections and a few Big Macs have in common? Through an impressive work of archival research, Douglas Henrique resurrects, with humor and irony, the near-mythical Battle of Olinda, when two women from opposing political parties vied for control of the “unofficial capital of Brazil.” Between electoral strategies, collective imaginaries and promises of progress, we uncover the mechanisms behind the first-ever bankruptcy of a McDonald’s restaurant in the world. It is the early 2000s, yet the escalation of violence in public debate already proves inescapable, revealing what now shapes the course of global politics. (Pedro Gonçalves Ribeiro)

Olívia, 12, her little brother Tim and their mother are forced to leave their apartment and move to a new neighborhood. To shield Tim from this upsetting situation, Olívia has him believe that this is all part of a film in which he’s the main character. Through laughter, tears, magic and the solidarity of new friends, they will find out that they are the heroes of their own life.
A brave mouse helps the fallen stars return to the sky.

Maxwell Alexandre was born and raised in one of Rio de Janeiro’s largest favelas, Rocinha. At 28, he burst onto the contemporary art scene, and his works are sold for exorbitant prices. His success hides a painful wound and reveals a structurally racist system. Films are constructed in many ways, and Pardo is Paper is no exception. Its director, a French filmmaker with a degree in mathematics and a background in political science from Chile, began his cinematic journey there. And perhaps for this reason, his creative territory lies outside the cinematic elite, yet close to the artist. To the person who works daily and turns their movements into art, even when the noise inherent to their origins seems to bar them from entering a museum. The artist Maxwell Alexandre was born and raised in one of Rio de Janeiro’s largest favelas, Rocinha. And with that, his destiny seemed set, at best for street art. The film shows the artist’s absolutely relentless working process – he never stops working – and, at the same time, we follow the preparation of an exhibition in Paris, at the Palais de Tokyo, perhaps one of the most elitist venues in the world of contemporary art. What is the artist’s place and what is the work’s place, ask the artist himself and his director? This is a portrait full of doubts, questions, and even contradictions. For if the art world is structurally racist, the fact that the artist becomes part of it and has a place within it places him in the position of an impostor. And his works on brown paper speak to this very point: his protagonists are not the museum visitors, but those who work there, particularly in the most precarious jobs. How does one maintain the coherence of one’s discourse whilst being part of that system? Hence, this film does not take the stance of wonder, but rather that of social consciousness, power structures, representation and racial hierarchies. (Miguel Valverde)

In Roswell, New Mexico, aliens are everywhere — they’re the local mascot, the identity of this small town that claims to have witnessed the crash of a UFO in 1947. More than a search for answers, this is a film that carries us in its pocket and hurls us into the surreal. Annabelle Amoros (Special Mention for the Silvestre Award for Best Short Film at IndieLisboa 2022 with Churchill, Polar Bear Town ) returns to the festival. The exquisite humor and singular style of Annabelle Amoros lead us to Roswell, the town where UFO obsession drives the rhythm of daily life. While the director digs for information and asks the locals awkward questions, the film takes an unexpected path. But is this a documentary? Halfway through, things get funky. The narrative shifts and certainties dissolve, plunging us into a new dimension in the New Mexico desert. (María Angélica Contreras)

Between the 1970s and the 1990s, the government of the Federal Republic of Germany produced a series of educational films designed to present a wide range of professions in meticulous detail. In OVERWORK , Céline Berger breathes new life into this archival material. In a 16mm film worn by time, images of nature appear. First trees, then animals. From the very beginning, an opening rhythm can be heard in the soundtrack. We enter the world of work, found footage from instructional films by the German Employment Agency. The image seems to follow the sound, but still relaxed. Without us being able to immediately pinpoint the moment of change, we are thrown into a vertiginous rhythm. The image fits into the manual gestures of each job, the rapid cuts create immediate associations between images, and the sound times these movements. In the flow, the sound follows the image as much as the image follows the sound. A collage of the gestures of the trade that seeks to uncover all its hidden rhythms (and the clashes between them). (Vasco Muralha)

A life told through scraps of paper, in just 14 minutes. The new film by don hertzfeldt — the American filmmaker nominated for the Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film with World of Tomorrow (2016), which also screened at IndieLisboa — is a frenetic exercise, darting between the concrete and the abstract, between colored pencil and blue ballpoint pen, and bursting with inventive energy. What does the trail we leave on paper over the course of a lifetime say about us? In a vertiginous flow of marks, words and drawings, Paper Trail reconstructs an entire life through fragments of paper alone – from childhood scribbles to school exercises, notes, forms and signatures – tracing the evolution of handwriting and identity. Using animation techniques developed for the film, don hertzfeldt turns the act of drawing and writing into pure movement, condensing time into a hypnotic and deeply affecting audiovisual experience. (Cláudia Marques)

films.t: PARA VIVIR The Implacable Time of Pablo Milanés
films.ot: PARA VIVIR El implacable tiempo de Pablo Milanés
films.syn: As a tribute for posterity, Fabien Pisani opens the drawers of the private life of the influential Cuban voice Pablo Milanés, nueva trova founder. From there he draws archival footage, weaving it together with interviews with the singer himself, family members, and artistic collaborators (Chico Buarque, Fito Páez). It is the portrait of a brilliant generation of musicians whose words today reveal their disillusionment with a revolution they now consider to have failed. It is standing in the present time, through the eyes and feelings of Pablo Milanés in the final stages of his life – having moved to Spain for medical treatment, yet always longing for his island – that the entire journey of the singer-songwriter is revealed; the man who, at the turn of the 1960s towards the 1970s, changed the face of Cuban music. They called it “nueva trova”, a new song for the new country that had sprung from the revolution, and it found in Milanés its greatest interpreter, singing of his people’s struggles and demands, lending new poetic depth to the Cuban son, embracing other South American musical expressions and drawing inspiration from jazz. Directed by Fabien Pisani, Milanés’s adopted son, Para Vivir is an intimate portrait of a larger-than-life figure, admired by artists as diverse as Chico Buarque and Harry Belafonte—two of those interviewed — while, in the same movement, guiding us through the story of revolutionary Cuba. The singer of Para vivir lived through the revolution, supported it, questioned it and opposed it whenever his conscience compelled him to do so. (Mário Lopes)

aw: IndieMusic Prize

films.syn: The absurd walks in through the front door, and the house itself becomes the protagonist. In her debut film, multidisciplinary artist Matea Radic draws on hand-drawn animation, family photographs, and a distinctly personal sense of irony to return to war-scarred Sarajevo, the city she left behind as a child. What does attachment really mean? A roughly drawn animation, in a middle ground between the confident strokes of art naïf and the more deliberate crudeness of a certain school of independent comics. This vision, hovering between the sweet and the grotesque, is used by the filmmaker to explore the contradictions and fears of living in or visiting Sarajevo, her hometown. This exploration takes place within a realm of a never obvious symbolic, associative surrealism. Tomatoes appear and recur, for example. Snails, bombs, and shifting spaces are all central elements of this film. But none of these elements carries a single, oppressive meaning. With a dark and disconcerting humor that is far warmer than nihilistic, Paradaïz invites us to rethink the concept of home. (Vasco Muralha)
It’s a scorching summer, and Pat and Mat prefer playing table football indoors. Even then, they’re hot, so they invent all sorts of ways to cool down.

films.t: Patty Is Such a Girly Name
films.syn: Originally from a remote Greek island, Daphne, a teenage judoka, moves to Athens to pursue her Olympic dream. Soon, all the obstacles inherent to this new life begin to rise before her: the pressures of competition, a coach with a hidden past, and confusing feelings she had never known before. A coming-of-age story set in the uncharted waters of sexuality, intertwined with the web of interests and lies behind the scenes of the sporting world.

After losing their home, a father tries to protect his son from their new reality. In Pequeno País, a father struggles to protect his son from an inescapable reality: the loss of their home in a city where evictions are becoming increasingly common. Amid the streets of Lisbon and the invisibility of those who survive there, he does everything he can to ensure his son can continue his studies, hiding the difficulties and the weight of his own downfall. In a silent gesture of resistance, he refuses to let his son work and bears the harshness of daily life alone. The film reveals, with intimacy and urgency, the fragility of those living on the margins and the strength of a love that insists on being greater than adversity. (Liedson Carvalho)

Precarity as a unifying force. A German waitress and an Iranian YouTuber despair for different reasons, yet in this film—almost caricatured in its inevitability—all roads lead to Rome. That is to say: it was written that their ill-fated destinies would meet. What follows is a mountainous odyssey in search of ghosts. The original German title echoes something like “Longings in Sangerhausen”, a small town that is the birthplace of the Romantic poet Novalis and also one of the strongholds of the far-right in the country. The ghosts of July are, therefore, ambiguous feelings that run through the particular political cinema of Julian Radlmaier, which here takes on more affectionate contours. In this fable that moves across centuries and spectral hopes, we are guided by Ursula and Neda, an East German waitress with a broken heart and an Iranian YouTuber with a broken arm, both trapped and lonely in precarious lives. The winding paths of chance bring the two together in an unexpected ghost hunt in the mountains. While stone swallers attempt to grapple with xenophobia and other perversities, Radlmaier constructs a romantic adventure film about an unlikely friendship and the longing for another life. Lucas Camargo de Barros
Somewhat anguished, caught in that lonely feeling incapable of resolving anything, a small mouse makes a decision — perhaps as an odyssey of self-discovery — to climb an enormous mountain.

Documentary film(mast)er Jan visits the (playing) drunk slave HD. Playing Drunk is the new film by Jan Soldat—a German filmmaker who has devoted his body of work to exploring sexuality, intimacy, fetish, and, ultimately, love — and marks his return to the festival after being featured in the Focus section at IndieLisboa in 2015. A filmmaker sets out to film a (self-proclaimed) sex slave “playing drunk.” Playing while drunk? Pretending to be drunk? The exchange is not mutually erotic. The subject agrees to present himself sexually, without revealing his intentions. The director seeks to document. The director also doesn’t seek to interact from the outset: the documentary vision he pursues does not allow it, nor does the constant, thoughtful work of framing the shots (done on the spot and with little time to accommodate the subject). But what happens when the slave decides to rebel against his contract? And what happens when the impassive gaze is frustrated to the point of having to interact? The master-slave relationship, which was already traditionally deconstructed in the initial proposal, progressively collapses from this central figure who dominates, distorts, and orders the film (its rules, its conditions, and its form). (Vasco Muralha)

Everything happens on the screen. In Ploo , an elderly owner of a vector-technology shop confronts the idea of death with the precious help of a moth. The human condition, too, is a matter of mathematics. In Ploo , John Frickey takes us on a not-so-linear journey between vectors and pixels. In constant narrative and stilistic leaps, we find the human being chasing infinity while trapped in loops, like a moth to a flame. This film, despite being full of poetry and nostalgia, quickly forces us to accept that there are things beyond our immediate perception and understanding. Nothing like vibrant animation, humor, and some mathematics to remind us of our ephemeral nature. After all, the credits can only roll when there is an end in sight. (Sara da Cruz)

On a forest home trip with her classmates, ten year old Marlene is struggling with her early pubescent, changing body. She feels ashamed of her boobs growing. Therefore, she avoids to shower with the other girls and hides her evolving body under large sweatshirts. When the other kids start making fun of an oddly developed tadpole at the forest home museum, Marlene is weirdly identifying with it and decides to set it free.

In a distant past, Léon and Elvira, itinerant artists, make a living hopping from town to town. In Covarronca, harassed by the Commissioner, they are forced to spend the night out in the open. That’s when they meet Stubbs, a Cambridge student, with whom they find shelter in the home of a painter at odds with his wife. Meanwhile, a curse sends them into the 21st century, where the future of social security and of a rock band are at stake. Some look at the night and see stars; others see far more than that. Here is one of the most improbable delights, in the box of surprises that is Providence and the Guitar, the fourth feature by João Nicolau, very freely adapted from the eponymous 1978 story by Robert Louis Stevenson. The adventures and misadventures of Léon and Elvira, a pair of itinerant troubadours in the 19th century, form the backbone of this period comedy built around the small frictions that a life devoted to art inevitably brings. In parallel, the film is intermittently traversed by another present: Léon plays in a punk rock band called Desgraça, while Elvira is a militant of the Total Left. Separated by time yet aligned in condition, they confront variations of the same dilemmas. Then as now, artistic life emerges as a fundamental practice, marked by persistence and stripped of mystification. More than a calling, it is a form of political resistance, a gesture that endures even when faced with structures of power, whether in a medieval or contemporary setting. At the centre of it all, word and song operate as engines of enchantment. This playful dimension, so characteristic of Nicolau’s cinema, achieves here a particular precision, unfolding in a picaresque humour expressed through rhythm, body and performance. The multidisciplinary filmmaker also co-writes the songs, in collaboration with João Lobo, who oversees the musical direction. These are songs that seem to demand a life beyond the film, perhaps even an album release, for the delight of all. “Go and spread the word. To those who are worth it and those in need.” (Susana Santos Rodrigues)

aw: Prize for Best Direction for a Portuguese Feature Film

films.syn: A group of convicts is subjected to the harshest punishment: crossing a desert with no water or provisions in exchange for the promise of freedom — all while being pursued by particularly brutal military forces. Invited by the U.S. government, a television crew documents the ordeal. The film ran in theaters for only four days before being banned by the Nixon administration, which claimed it presented a distorted image of the United States, strikingly resonant today.

films.t: Quentin Blake’s Box Of Treasures: Mrs Armitage on Wheels
films.ot: Quentin Blake's Box Of Treasures: Mrs Armitage on Wheels
films.syn: The primary goal is to visit her cousin Angela. Yet more often than not, the journey and its misadventures surpass the destination. Mrs. Armitagem and her dog, Breakspear, set out to invent a bicycle: and that is their grand adventure.

The hotel breathes. It rustles. It waits. Yessica is the only one who hears it, the only one who sees what’s writhing beneath the surface. Today, she takes action. From Gonçalo Almeida we have seen the recent, multi-award-winning Atom & Void , in which, through the journey of a spider, we are able to sense the end of the world. Almeida has a remarkable ability to create other worlds within our own, without resorting to artificiality. He uses the composition of sound and image to create living organisms that can be objects, animals or people. In his new film Quietness , the hotel is one such living being in search of its own space. It breathes, gives orders, moves slowly amongst the tourists and staff until Yessica hears it, and from this point the film unfolds into a realistic phantasmagoria, in which nothing frightens us, yet everything is worrying or unsettling. Once again, in just a few minutes, Almeida manages to pull us out of the safety of our cinema seats, making us glance to the side just to check that everything is alright. As one of the new voices in Portuguese cinema, this filmmaker, born in Santiago do Cacém, is getting better and better and is well worth watching. (Miguel Valverde)

Raw Material was filmed over a year in the Interior Douro region. Through testimonies from local communities, the film reflects on different, at times conflicting, notions of value in relation to the landscape and how practices of cultivation, preservation and extraction benefit and impact the people who live there. A film that explores ideas of what is contained but not immediately visible within the land. Rocks as an alphabet, the raw material that writes the text and composes the book of the soil, or, more precisely, the history of the Earth. A history intertwined with our own. In Raw Material, James Newitt observes the layers that make up this living archive, examining both the exploitation of natural resources (such as lithium extraction) and the forms of intimate relation between the bodies that inhabit the territory. Between agriculture, geology and mining, labour and affective relations, Newitt chooses to listen without exposing: testimonies, whether from surveyors, geographers or rural inhabitants, appear almost always without a face, shifting the focus towards matter, rocks, mineral particles, tools and sound. By capturing the extractive gesture alongside a possible sense of communion, blurred boundaries emerge: someone unwell confuses their body with the soil and calls not a doctor, but an engineer of the land. Positioned between the experimental and the documentary, the film constructs a space of sensitive excavation which, little by little, reveals an unsettling portrait of the region and of the materiality that constitutes us. (Susana Santos Rodrigues)

The promise comes from Albert Brooks himself in the comedy-laden prologue: Real Life will be the next big step in documentaries about real family life — a claim made in full awareness that, six years before its release, the An American Family (1973) series of PBS had already become a phenomenon. Here, the family in question is the Yeagers, from Phoenix. Brooks and his crew move into their home, cameras at the ready, and promptly begin to sow chaos.

An adult woman heads to Disneyland Paris dressed as Snow White. As she approaches the gates, she is stopped by security, who prevent her from entering on the grounds that there is already a Snow White inside the park. The tourist is confused: isn’t this Disneyland? Aren’t people supposed to dress up as the characters?

Through improvisation, we emerge into a visual and aural experience, where we follow a musician. Reflection, Improvisation is a film that introduces Gabriel Ferrandini, one of the biggest names on drums in Portugal. We follow his work from rehearsals to the production of his new album. In Black and White, Reflection, Improvisation follows the making of an album featuring duets between drums and saxophone. With a jazzy rhythm, the film explores improvisation as a form of creation. Sound, silence, and repetition intertwine in an intimate and ever-changing process. (Liedson Carvalho)

In the early hours of May 13, 1948, the village of al-Ma’in, in the northern Negev desert, Palestine, was invaded by Israeli troops, and its inhabitants were expelled. Among them was the Palestinian historian Salman Abu Sitta, who, through a years-long collaboration with Forensic Architecture — a multidisciplinary collective that uses architectural tools and techniques to investigate human rights violations — reconstructed the land where he was born using 3D technology. In this return to al-Ma’in, a Palestinian village occupied in May 1948 and almost entirely destroyed by the Haganah, the paramilitary organization of the Jewish population that would give rise to the core of the Israel Defense Forces, the memory of a place that Western history wants to make irrelevant is recovered. Forensic Architecture is an interdisciplinary research group from Goldsmiths, University of London, that crosses architecture, human rights, journalism, art and law, which here joins Salman Abu Sitta, a defender of the Palestinian right of return, to rescue his village and show the world that his native village was a small oasis, with roads, buildings, orchards and above all a local population that had long existed there. It is with forgetfulness and invisibility that the right to occupy territories has been justified: Israel insists on the ancestral legitimacy of occupying places where there are no physical traces of its people having existed there. The power of the biblical word does not need to override the historical evidence of the presence of the Palestinian people in that territory. It is, therefore, to prove that the Israeli occupation displaced villages and pushed their inhabitants into a now devastated land strip, that this group of researchers recovered archives and aerial images and reconstructed in a 3D model the village of al-Ma’in, which was combined with Abu Sitta’s testimony. The film follows this process and as the village comes back to life, the past gains stories, smells and small moments, and memory goes from word to evidence. The truth shines in the enthusiasm of Salman Abu Sitta, who seems at peace with what he sees. Al-Ma’in may be destroyed, but now we can see that it exists. Perhaps now the Palestinian people can return home, even if only to this one. We shall hope! (Margarida Moz)

films.ot: O Rio de Janeiro Continua Lindo
films.syn: The streets of Rio de Janeiro overflow with samba — it is Carnival. Ilma writes to her son, whose whereabouts have long been unknown; in her letter, she sends news of her country, itself faded or perhaps never truly found, a victim of a history of colonization that continues to breed oppression. Every celebration carries its reverse side. In the heart of Rio’s Carnival, a mother searches for her missing son. She writes a letter on behalf of all the mothers who have seen their sons and daughters murdered by the police. This political short film is marked by a powerful spirit of resistance and resilience. It is a cry for justice and a condemnation of the crimes committed against the black population in the country. (Catherine Boutaud)

In the village, he became known as the Soldier. He arrived with a document identifying him as the heir to an abandoned farm. It was there, sometime in the seventeenth century, during the Thirty Years’ War, in this German Protestant settlement, that he gradually earned the trust of the locals, presenting himself as a hardworking and devout man. Yet it is all part of a grand illusion — one that soon begins to surface in dangerous ways. Actress Sandra Hüller won the Silver Bear for Best Leading Performance at the Berlin International Film Festival. There’s more freedom in pants , Rose says. Set against the backdrop of the early 17th century, somewhere in Germany, a mysterious soldier, Rose, appears in a secluded village. Quiet and with a face disfigured by a scar, this stranger declares himself the heir of an abandoned farmstead. Over time, he becomes part of the community in a quest for acceptance rooted in deception. The tale of one who, defying her birth as a woman, lived as a man. Through precise framing and emotional austerity, Rose explores the violence of social structures and the fragility of selfhood. Sandra Hüller ( Anatomy of a Fall , The Zone of Interest ) is splendid in her portrayal of Rose, with striking echoes of Joan of Arc. Based on true events, Markus Schleinzer’s film is both an unsettling study of identity and belonging and a tremendous achievement in cinematic language that leaves an indelible mark on the audience. (Alexandra Ferraz) “A few years ago, a historian friend of mine called me to wish me a happy birthday and told me about an interesting German court case she associated with the date. Exactly 250 years before I was born, on the same day, a woman had been executed in Halberstadt, Germany, for pretending to be a man and being found guilty of sodomy. She is considered the last woman in German legal history to have been executed for this crime. At that time, sodomy was defined as same-sex love between men, bestiality, and penetration with an object. This birthday greeting was the beginning of a lengthy research project in which I studied hundreds of women from different centuries who, for various reasons, had put on pants to publicly present themselves as men. Even if only for a short time. There were many reasons for this: easier access to work, escape, crime, the hope of avoiding rape, the hope of avoiding forced marriage, the hope of living a more self-determined life, the hope of gaining access to education, lesbian desire, transsexuality, patriotism, exoticism. I also came across a handful of female soldiers in knight’s armor and female pirates. However, the resulting screenplay does not follow a single biography, but represents a conglomeration of my imagination and individual fates that I encountered on my journey with the subject. There’s more freedom in pants , Rose says at one point. That’s exactly what connects all of the women’s fates that I’ve encountered.” Markus Schleinzer

For a long time, nothing good has happened in this small fishing village in Cornwall. But fortune may be about to change. “The Rose of Nevada”, a vessel lost at sea three decades ago, mysteriously reappears — with only one chance left: to return to the water, so that fair winds may once again blow through this community. Yet on its second return, the new crew comes face to face with the past. Time has slipped back thirty years. Throughout the course of his career, Mark Jenkin has developed an extremely singular filmmaking practice: He shoots his films on location in a small fishing village in Cornwall, mostly works with people who originate from the area, acts as his own cinematographer, and exclusively uses a 16mm Bolex camera, exploring with great interest the grains and textures of the filmic stock that he uses. This practice gives birth to the unique language of his films, a language which in his latest film finds its most sublime form. He also further cements himself as one of the defining chroniclers of modern day fishermen, documenting with immense tenderness their shared pain. Enormously moving and beautiful, Rose of Nevada is one of the year’s must see films. It stands as the director’s most essential homage not just to fishermen but to the Cornish people at large, to their dying way of life, to their hidden magnificence, to the eternal nobility of their bodies and souls. Nabil Aouad

The new school year brings challenges for 14 year old Sana. She is starting at a new school where she will learn all the ins and outs of the world of baking. In the evenings she is training hard for her very first international boxing match. In a couple of weeks she and her team mates are invited to fight at the Olympic Center in Pisa. How will she cope, combining these two big passions that are both demanding a lot of her? Will she manage to juggle both and succeed in finding her footing?
The hierarchy begins in the elementary school playground, the center of life at that age. The tumultuous episodes of early friendships can last forever.

films.t: Rua (This is not a movie, it’s a comet)
films.ot: Rua (Isto não é um filme, é um cometa)
films.syn: A journey through the universe of musician and composer Vítor Rua, from pop-rock music to opera, passing through repetitive-minimalism and improvised music. “Minimalism united will never be repeated!” – the challenge that kicks off this documentary about Vítor Rua, alluding to Telectu, the duo formed by Rua and Jorge Lima Barreto in the early 1980s, one of the first groups to claim affiliation with so-called repetitive minimal music. A first-person film in which Vítor Rua shares countless captivating episodes from his unpredictable career, as unbelievable as they are realistic, as utopian as they are plausible, featuring plenty of archive footage, as well as various testimonies from Edgar Pêra, Fernando Alvim, David Ferreira and Chris Cutler. From his journey in minimalist music, through the production of operas, as part of the duo Telectu, as a founding member, guitarist and principal composer in the first line-up of GNR, or as one of the musicians and producers on António Variações’ first album, this is an extraterrestrial journey, beyond Mars, through terrain unknown to mere mortals but deeply natural to Vítor Rua. (Helena César)
Summer, 80s. Rui Carlos and his friends spend their afternoons playing football. When the ball gets punctured, he is left alone to deal with the responsibility and challenges of adult life.

It snowed! Lou and Marius are playing in the street, building a snowman. But Mom calls them back home. Marius has to practice clarinet, and Lou has homework to do! Pfff! … Lou opens her notebook and begins her exercises. Marius plays a few hesitant notes, but… incredible! Outside, the snowman has moved!

In 1988, at the last major public performance of communist Yugoslavia before the outbreak of war, Sonja Vukićević — one of Serbia’s great dancers, also known for her anti-Milošević activism — performed a historic solo before a packed stadium. In a gymnasium in present-day Belgrade, we watch her return to the field: her body as an archive of collective memory. Maurice Ravel’s Boléro is a work with a distinctly feminine perspective, as it arose from a commission by the dancer Ida Rubenstein, renowned for her expressiveness and boldness on stage, who starred in its premiere in Paris, in 1928. Since then, it has often been choreographed and performed by leading figures in the world of dance and, particularly in the 1980s, underwent various reinterpretations and witnessed significant moments in history. Filmmaker Marta Popivoda, a leading filmmaker focusing on women, returns to the archives to recover the performance of the dancer Sonja Vukićević (a well-known anti-Milošević activist), who in 1988 performed a historic solo to the famous Boléro before a sold-out stadium in the former Yugoslavia. The date is historic for Serbia, as it precedes the war, yet at the same time, it marks a moment of affirmation of a body within a space and within history. The performance evokes the deepest desires, the effort, the life that resides within a body, and the materialization through movement of that which is the secret each person carries within their own body.
