Between 1988 and the present day, Vukićević’s body activates the evocation of this very collective memory, because ultimately the syncopated, uniform and repetitive movement of this work—which was composed for its transformation through the various instruments of an orchestra—returns to us a body whose movements are the synthesis of that very construction. (Miguel Valverde)

At night, somewhere in an old farmhouse, by the light of an oil lamp, a whistle sounds, the curtain rises and a show with talking puppets begins. Biblical fables are performed, such as The Story of the Creation of the World .

The son lives on the streets; the mother walks the avenues in search of traces. The only proof of life are the graffiti he leaves on the city’s walls — which she begins to document. Then, as if that paint were a letter, she takes up the spray can in search of a reply. A woman has lived for years in Stockholm with no news of her son. The only traces of his existence are scattered across the city in the form of tags he leaves on walls – signatures she has recognised since his childhood and which, to her, feel like an echo of his voice. These signs of life are her last refuge: she begins to follow and photograph them with devotion, assembling a photo album that becomes an intimate, obsessive archive of loss. Keeping her identity playfully concealed, the film observes her quiet, persistent gestures, until she finds an unexpected way to respond – and perhaps to reconnect. Blending present-day images with fragments of the past, this tender and moving film about maternal love casts new light on the potential of graffiti – even in its rawest forms – as a gesture of presence, memory and communication. (Cláudia Marques)

films.ot: Stallion y la Bola de Cristal
films.syn: Behind closed curtains, in the murky bedroom of a young man with ambitions of sorcery, unfolds the second short film by Catalan Christian Avilés — a filmmaker deeply interested in the hidden spirituality of adolescence. Christian Avilés’ cinematic universe pulses with magic, in theme and in form. In this second film, a queer character, seen as a “freak”, pours desire into the phone pressed to the chest, into dreams and poems devoted to the one longed for. The sentence “I belong to desire” captures not only the confinement of a small room, but the fiery hunger of a youth burning for a life that blazes. It’s both a film and spell, drawing viewers in, enchanting, and awakening the memory of love experienced with almost unbearable intensity. (Pedro Gonçalves Ribeiro)

The man, almost a myth, who in 1914 was born Herman Poole Blount in Birmingham, Alabama, soon became Sun Ra – a solar figure at the heart of the twentieth-century free jazz movement; an Egyptologist who, in that cradle of civilisation, discovered Afrofuturism; a philosopher who founded his own cosmogony and channelled it through a keyboard. Through testimonies from members of his Sun Ra Arkestra and archival recordings, Christine Turner unveils the galaxy of this trailblazer. A film, a meteor, a journey through time. It is no surprise that the movie starts with ‘Over the Rainbow.’ Not only because the standard changes into something else at the hands of the man born Herman Poole Blount, but also because this a song that speaks of a place where the dreams we dare to dream come true, something that meant a great deal to Sun Ra, who was born into this world (coming through Saturn, obviously) in 1914, in Birmingham, Alabama. A jazz genius, the creator of an Afro-futuristic mythology that brought together Ancient Egypt, science fiction and the Civil Rights movement, he was not just an agent of musical revolution. ‘The possible has been tried and failed, now it is time to try the impossible.’ From this sentence, Christine Turner drew the title of the documentary. With the participation of members of his Arkestra, historians and researchers, with illuminating archive footage, from music on stage to Sun Ra walking through the pyramids of Giza, ‘Sun Ra: Do the Impossible’ is a revealing dive into the universe of one of the most fascinating and surprising musicians of the 20th century. (Mário Lopes)
What do dogs love to do most? Roam freely and make new friends. Tatarang is no exception.

A love story between two men — that was always the premise. But barred from filming it in his home country, the director was forced to reinvent it elsewhere, in another geography, with a different protagonist. The celebrated fusion of reality and fiction. Cinema as an act of discovery — and love. Prevented from making the film he had once envisioned, a director recreates it in another country, under entirely new circumstances. The care required by this transformation leads both creator and new actor to question how the story can unfold and what paths it might take. Through a reflective-meta lens, viewers are invited to envision the scenes that were only ever written on the page, weighing the possibilities of the version that never existed against the one that now comes to life. Amid all the changes, one simple gesture seems to be the heart of the story: a kiss shared between two men. (Pedro Gonçalves Ribeiro)

In a performance hall, five businessmen attempt to close a deal. Yet whether it’s the increasingly disturbing turn of the conversation or the sinister manners that begin to surface, something feels off — an absurd comedy by Richard Hunter. As mild as a fever or an intrusive thought, this is a surreal comedy about five businessmen trying to do business. The key word here is “try,” because communication isn’t easy. Conversation topics range from the great questions of humanity—like discussions about the different shades of color that asbestos can appear in—to more mundane themes, but always delivered at a frantic and mind-blowing pace. Anything goes to prevent any business conversation from even happening. Who could imagine that the corporate world could be so much fun? (Bruno Pereira)

films.ot: Esse olhar que é só teu
films.syn: Two women share the same space, in another time. As we contemplate the gaze of both, a question arises: why is one of them probably the most well-known Portuguese woman in the world, while the other has been almost erased from our history and collective memory? In this film-poem, I summon an image in an attempt to decipher the enigmatic gaze of filmmaker Bárbara Virgínia.

Camille is a teenager with Down syndrome whose greatest wish is to join a semi-professional dance company. On the day of the audition, she and her sister Agathe come to realise that, after all, nothing changed.

Sentences are projected, but no reply ever comes. Movements are cold and unhurried — so that nothing can catch anyone off guard. Everything is calculated. Everything is plastic. Everything is exactly as it must be. Father, mother and daughter comply with what is written in their script: a façade-family performing a choreography they call home. In The Apple Doesn’t Fall… we catch a glimpse of someone’s domestic life. In this house, a faulty light is enough to expose all the flaws, despite the collective effort to look good in the picture. In spite of the absurdist language, it becomes clear that there are always strict rules under someone’s roof, especially when the law dictates that each roof can cover only one child. From this only child, we see life summarized in episodes marked by the weight of loneliness and where repetition and resentment are constant. The choreography and the frequent oscillation in rhythm are not enough to divert attention from the violence in the silence, which sometimes reveals indifference, sometimes the weight of expectations. What remains of this façade when you take down the fourth wall? (Sara da Cruz)

aw: Special Jury Prize (International Short Film Competition)

films.syn: A family from Lugo, Spain, owns the confitería Ritz, an institution in the Argentine city of La Plata. It is here that everything unfolds, through a series of strange, funny and melancholic events that suggest a succession of tableaux rather than a conventional narrative sequence—very much in keeping with Lucía Seles’ cinematic language. Lost characters drift through the story, caught in a quiet despair shaped by their inability to communicate. Lucia Seles is a self-proclaimed graphomaniac, and in The Bewilderment of Chile, we are taken on a tour through her observations on many subjects, but maybe most of all, our insatiable need for someone to understand what we really mean through our clumsy words. Between the feverish editing style, the cast of characters who gravitate around a pastry shop in El Plata and amp up the feeling of the film to telenovela heights, and the written notes which appear on the screen right next to the subtitles, one could very well go crazy, if not for the subtle control the director has over everything. And it is in this gesture that Seles’ impulse of recording all that surrounds her shapes itself into a touching way of trying to make sense of all of this electricity and confusion. The Bewilderment of Chile is a demanding sensorial experience, but one that perfectly mirrors and honors this contemporary fragmentation of the self and reassures us that we are worthy of being looked at. Leonor Castro Nunes

Three students travel to Maryland to shoot a documentary about the legend of the Blair Witch, concerning a witch who supposedly vanished in the forest only to return and haunt the town. As their research unfolds, the friends lose their way and the circumstances grow increasingly sinister, everything documented by their cameras. The 1999 film by Daniel Myrick and Eduardo Sánchez became a classic of horror cinema, a global phenomenon that established a new paradigm for the found-footage subgenre.

For a long time now, Amadou & Mariam have travelled from Bamako to the wider world. This film follows their journey across different geographies and places where they gather musical ideas and weave them into their instruments. The final stop is a major concert in Mali and one last album — a film that brings us within inches of their creative process while also featuring testimonies from some of their closest collaborators: Damon Albarn, Chris Martin, Manu Chao, Tiken Jah Fakoly and Vieux Farka Touré. The story of Amadou & Mariam – the world’s most famous African duo – from the streets of Bamako to the Glastonbury Festival, in an electrifying blend of blues, soul and rock with traditional African rhythms from Mali. A story that is also, or above all, a love story between two blind people, united by music and life, who have become global icons, transcended borders and brought worlds together. Against a backdrop of adversity, hope and joy, there are tours taking place all over the world, awards, collaborations with Damon Albarn of Blur, Chris Martin of Coldplay and Manu Chao, a deep bond, years spent living in France, several albums released and a homecoming for a major concert. (Helena César)

Long thought to have vanished, the relentless Countess Báthory is forced to abandon the calm of the shadows. In present-day Vienna, she joins forces with her subordinate Hermine and her nephew Rudi Bubi, a vegetarian vampire. In that city, on a journey of baroque exuberance and lurking fangs, they relentlessly search for the whereabouts of a book capable of extinguishing all evil in the universe — something that, truth be told, would not suit them at all. A film by Ulrike Ottinger, starring Isabelle Huppert. And we begin with a tale of she-devils. Through a canal beneath the city of Vienna, a formidable vampire navigates in search of the red elixir of life. Isabelle Huppert, as beautiful as ever with her pale, delicate skin, plays Baroness Báthory, who, with her devoted maid, is searching for a book that will solve all the world’s problems; for this reason, they try at all costs to ensure it never sees the light of day. The great Austrian filmmaker Ulrike Ottinger returns with a baroque, tragicomic universe, featuring hilarious characters and fantastical moments. The cast also Includes Conchita Wurst, best known for winning the Eurovision Song Contest with “Rise Like a Phoenix”, and she emerges suddenly in the film when, at a certain point, she performs this song, which has already become an anthem for the Eurovision world. A film of metamorphoses and transformations, these extraordinary characters bring to life a Dantesque adventure, with a high degree of sophistication and a relentlessly fast pace. (Miguel Valverde)

A woman and a man on vacation in Pico Island, in the Azores. The adversities of this journey, set in constantly changing nature, trigger arguments that conceal deeper issues within the characters and their difficulty in connecting.

It’s Carnival, and at school there’s a parade to choose the best mask. This is a portrait of a Romani family in which a mother prepares her two daughters for the big event: Amanda, the youngest, fears that things might not go as planned.

films.t: The Circular Universe – Jocy de Oliveira
films.syn: Few artists can claim the historical significance of Jocy de Oliveira. A pioneer of electronic music in Brazil — carrying a weight comparable to such towering figures as John Cage and Karlheinz Stockhausen — she was also a brilliant pianist, performing as a soloist under the direction of Igor Stravinsky. In his film, Dácio Pinheiro gathers her legacy while keeping a clear gaze on the present — a time in which the Brazilian composer, now 90 years old, continues to create experimental opera. Jocy de Oliveira turns 90 in 2026 and continues to create. Dácio Pinheiro offers her an early gift with this film, a historic recognition of the work and life of Brazil’s pioneering electronic music artist. A contemporary of figures such as John Cage, Karlheinz Stockhausen, Luciano Berio, and Igor Stravinsky — with whom she interacted, influenced, was influenced by, and collaborated — Jocy has forged a singular path. This is a film in the spirit of discovery within IndieMusic: works that introduce us to lesser-known artists who are urgent to know. Those who remember the film Electronica:Mentes (IndieLisboa 2020), by the same director, which depicts the rise of electronic music in Brazil from the 1960s onward, will recall Jocy de Oliveira’s dazzling presence: pianist, composer, performer, opera creator, and much more, always defying labels and experimenting, one of the emerging figures of that era. Her artistic freedom and radical creativity inspired Dácio Pinheiro to dedicate this film to her, now fully under her own name. A fragmented, poetic, and circular film, just like her work. Jocy de Oliveira turns 90 in 2026 and continues to reinvent herself. (Carlos Ramos)

While the dealer hasn’t arrived, eight jazz musicians nurse their hangovers and play. An awkward filmmaker records what he imagines to be an honest testimony of a small human collective cramped inside a New York apartment. The feature debut of Shirley Clarke, a key figure in the independent cinema of the second half of the twentieth century, is based on Jack Gelber’s play of the same name and repeatedly asserts its distance from reality.

Bea, a 50-year-old woman on the verge of divorce, calls the emergency line to report a break-in at her home. Denís, a 25-year-old trans man—adrift between precarious work and the pull of nightlife—is still there. What begins as a scare soon gives way to curiosity, and the weekend unfolds as an unexpected journey of mutual discovery.

When the fish dies, the mother’s depression breaks the surface. The daughter dances to keep the world afloat. In this animated poem, a fish dies before a mother and daughter. It is nature exercising its logic, as a heron in flight catches the solitary fish and returns it lifeless to land. An emotional abyss unfolds, seemingly transcending that moment and evoking human impotence in the face of loss, whether of an animal or of reason. The mother fragments into shadows, tenebrous replicas of herself, calling her to the lake, insisting that she succumb to sadness. The daughter, without words sufficient to recover her mother, chooses dance as a plea, evoking the bond that unites them, in a fragile and desperate gesture to hold onto what is slipping away. La Mort du Poisson is a choreography where music breathes for those who can no longer speak. An intimate lament, where mourning is not merely ritual, but a mirror: the place where the child discovers that loving also means accepting the limits of others, and finding her own center in movement. (Margarida Moz)

An unlikely family is born. In nineteenth-century Edinburgh, two schoolteachers open a boarding school, dreaming of laying the foundations for an independent life together. Soon after, an aristocrat decides to enrol her “illegitimate” fifteen-year-old granddaughter, and the newly built world of Miss Pirie and Miss Woods begins to crack — especially when the grandmother suggests that Jane should spend the summer there as well. The school year resumes, and everything spills over. Edinburgh, 1810. Marianne Woods (Clare Dunne) and Jane Pirie (played by the film’s co-screenwriter Flora Nicholson), two teachers, embark on their dream of an independent life together and open a boarding school. Soon after, a wealthy aristocrat (Fiona Shaw) enrolls Jane Cumming (Mia Tharia), her “illegitimate” 15-year-old grandchild. An accusation follows, leaving the teachers fighting for their lives and resulting in a legal battle that would scandalize the establishment. Based on true events, this is the premise of The Education of Jane Cumming by Sophie Heldman. The courts took ten years to reach a decision, and the documents were sealed for a century. But instead of focusing on the legal battle, this tender film explores the female universe hidden within the original court records. Before Sophie Heldman, The Children’s Hour (1961) by William Wyler first explored this case. Adapted from Lillian Hellman’s 1934 play, the film stars Audrey Hepburn and Shirley MacLaine as the teachers. However, Sophie Heldman’s film takes its inspiration from the 2013 study by Lillian Faderman, Scotch Verdict: The Real-Life Story That Inspired The Children’s Hour . The Education of Jane Cumming allows us to journey through echoes of films such as Céline Sciamma’s Portrait of a Lady on Fire and Jane Campion’s The Portrait of a Lady . As Sophie Heldman said, “Miss Pirie and Miss Woods are early feminists who carry the seed of future emancipation movements.”. This fascinating portrait captures gender pressures shaping nineteenth-century women’s lives, as well as the class forces behind their marginalization. An urgent drama about rejection, desire, and the courage to stand up for justice. (Alexandra Ferraz)

Miguel is 9 years old and obsessed with singer Mariah Carey. He goes to a Catholic school and one day his class is challenged by the nuns to sell calendars of the Virgin Mary. When he finds out that he won’t be able to keep the profits from the calendar sales like he thought, he decides to take action. After all, his favorite singer is coming to perform in his town, just like a miracle.

As far as the eye can see, a vast construction project in West Africa is tightly secured, with its guards, watchtowers and barbed wire. At night, by the fence, a man makes himself known: he tells the British contractor that he has come to retrieve the body of his brother, who died there just hours earlier. Claire Denis returns to IndieLisboa with an adaptation of Bernard-Marie Koltès’s masterful play Black Battles with Dogs .

Iceland’s icy beauty conceals a turmoil of lava. Earthquakes are becoming increasingly frequent, and Anna, Iceland’s leading volcanologist, fears the worst: a volcanic eruption is approaching that could destroy Reykjavík, yet no one seems to take her seriously. But this is not the only upheaval she faces: a Danish photographer enters her life, complicating her marriage and putting her family at risk. The Fires is based on a popular Icelandic novel and replicated the book’s success at the country’s box office.

A great idea is not necessarily an intricate web or a complex labyrinth — a great idea is one that works. Here it is, courtesy of John Smith, who in 1976 premiered a film that answers a desire we all share: what if a sentence could trigger an action in a person and/or an object? The Girl Chewing Gum is precisely that — the voice of the British filmmaker seemingly commanding the fate of a busy London street.

The absurd, the unusual, but also the tedious and the banal — anything can become a film. Why shouldn’t concrete, a kind of antithesis to colour, imagination and ideas, be fertile ground? John Wilson, a comedian best known for the series How To with John Wilson , makes his feature-length debut with a bold premise: after attending a Hallmark workshop on how to write and sell a television romantic comedy, he decides to replicate the strategy in a documentary about concrete. John Wilson in attendance.

Metal detector in hand, the Hunter roams through forest and city in search of treasure. It is his way of life, his calling: the summons of Lord Gold. Along the way, however, he finds everything; his home resembles a museum, or a shop filled with objects rescued from anonymity. Where are you, Mr. Gold? Where are you hiding? We hitch a ride on a motorbike journey with the Hunter in search of lost treasures. A punk road movie with a raw, vital energy. Where are you hiding, Mr. Gold? My metal detector with green neon lights will find you. The power and value of things lie in the meaning we give them, not in their intrinsic worth. (Carlos Ramos)

Lorenzo’s ear feels different. It was after a boat accident that the ringing began — and never left — growing louder and more insistent, seeping into the fabric of his everyday life. Through medical appointments and less conventional therapies, this is his search for relief — for something that might restore silence. After an accident, Lorenzo begins to hear a persistent ringing that profoundly alters his relationship with the world. As the sounds of everyday life begin to unsettle and challenge him, he drifts through medical appointments, therapies and unexpected encounters, in search of relief or understanding. At the heart of the film lies a simple idea, emerging from a medical diagnosis: the less we listen to the outside world, the more we hear what is within. From discomfort to curiosity, the film gradually reveals his growing attentiveness to sound – to what comes from without and what resonates within – shaping a delicate sensory experience, between familiar noises and newly perceived frequencies. With a gentle rhythm and subtle humour, El oído absoluto traces a path of listening and openness, where strangeness gives way to an intimate form of reconciliation with the world. (Cláudia Marques)

films.ot: O INTRUSO, a partir dos textos de Jean-Luc Nancy, María Zambrano e da minha autobiografia
films.syn: The Intruder is a video essay rooted in the experience of a heart surgery. Inspired by texts by Jean-Luc Nancy and María Zambrano, it superimposes clinical, personal, and emotional images to form a dense visual archive. Accumulation and rhythm shape a non-linear narrative in which memory, body, and time are reconfigured through voice and heartbeat. The heart is the active organ and the centre of the narrative, presented in a dizzying whirl of words and images set to a frenetic, highly philosophical and musical rhythm. The heart, the ‘noble viscera’, the ‘breath of life’, the mysterious element that dwells within us, the unfathomable that lodges within our innermost being, the ‘dark cavity’, the ‘thirst for intimacy’, the ‘indivisible’ – all take shape in a delirious spiral in The Intruder . An archive of images from science, art, the natural world and the personal and private world unfolds whilst reflecting on the body, memory and time. A stream of thoughts beats fearlessly and flows out like a sensitive, blood-like current, setting the rhythm of a world that is thought and reimagined, between the brain and the heart; the emotional graph is variable, the beat constant and the call intense. (Carlota Gonçalves)

First we giggle. Then we repeat syllables and words. Until something magical happens: we combine them and create something new. No longer just imitating, we begin to say something about the world around us. These are our first sentences, precious and unrepeatable. Based on the book of the same name, this short film brings together sentences that were spoken for the very first time.

After all, what remains beyond the records and the books? What is left beyond the debris of the people we once were — and wished to be? Al Cook is a man alone, a blues musician frozen in time and, soon enough, lost in space. An aggressive real estate company wants to demolish his house, and the memories through which he lives are now at risk. What melody remains for him then? The Italian-Austrian duo Tizza Covi and Rainer Frimmel return to the festival after winning the Distribution Award in 2010 with La Pivellina .

In a spa surrounded by mountains of salt, guests relax and sunbathe, while workers collect the glowing crystals under the sun. Children run off, escaping the watchful eyes of adults, and a woman drifts through this landscape in a haze, detached from reality. As night falls, the space transforms, shaped by the desires of those who pass through. In a spa, there is space to savour languor, for bodies to stretch, to immerse themselves, to settle into floating baths. There is a slow movement, spreading through the air; the scattered voices of guests drift away, whilst the light reflects off the chalk-white walls and the shadows cast figures and sounds. A child wanders off, a body withdraws, and the night, laden with mystery, weaves an atmosphere of whispers and desires. By day there is light and labour once more, there is abandonment and bodies moulding themselves to the mountains of salt where they gather. Here, weight seems to float enigmatically, and the salt crystals cast an intense, magnetic glow. (Carlota Gonçalves)

aw: Prize for Best Portuguese Short Film

films.syn: On the 50th anniversary of the Carnation Revolution, I made a documentary about Álvaro Cunhal. Now, on the centenary of the 1926 military coup, it seemed only fitting to make one about Salazar. Conceived as a diptych, the film brings together figures such as the housekeeper, the cardinal, the minister of propaganda, the nurse, and the shoeshiner, who—through their memories—recount stories we all believed had not been forgotten.
The Red Planet is under attack. Its inhabitants are forced to leave. They land on the Blue Planet, where people are not particularly welcoming…

Only the city remains—only it is capable of holding her. After an unexpected breakup, May, a Korean woman living in Berlin, searches for signs of healing as she wanders through streets and gardens. At every corner, she is carried back to her Seoul, a jumble of times and places and a lingering sense of not belonging. It is within a new routine, in the mundanity of everyday life—nights of clementines on the sofa, dance classes—that May keeps going. For her first feature film, director Lan-Xi Ruan has chosen a Korean protagonist, May, who is going through something very similar to her own experience: that of being an expatriate living in Berlin. She is lost, on the one hand, amidst memories of a house, a familiar space, a home that no longer belongs to her, and, on the other, immersed in the immediacy of her life and all the moments that make it up: a dinner that turns into a break-up, a living room where the intimacy of friendship is lived out, a forest where she feels the freedom of nature, or a walk where she encounters an ex-lover and acts out her fantasies of confrontation. The director films all this with a charm, a clarity and an elegance that is difficult to describe, but palpable on screen. The events are subtle, yet they reveal clues to May’s inner life. These everyday moments, which we as viewers can glimpse without being detected, are also entertaining (sometimes anecdotal, sometimes playful), because even amidst the melancholy, humour shines through. Ana Cabral Martins

The Red Spectacles is the first installment of the “Kerberos Saga”, a trilogy conceived by Mamoru Oshii — best known for his work in animation, particularly Ghost in the Shell (1995) — imagining a Tokyo dominated by a Nazi Germany that emerged victorious from World War II. Kōichi Todome is a former officer of Kerberos, a paramilitary unit clad in seemingly invincible exoskeleton armor, who returns to his country’s capital only to find it in an even darker state than when he left. A noir classic presented in a new 4K restoration.
The fat wolf lived with a round but completely empty stomach. One day, by chance, he discovered a hidden talent to finally fill his belly.

ap.sel: Officially selected (section: Cinema at the Pool)

films.syn: The age of video surveillance has not only taken over our avenues; it has trespassed into the natural world. Today, we live online, in a reality where we can choose to follow a family of owls 24 hours a day. Will this bring us closer to truly knowing these wild animals? Or does it push us even further from understanding what inhabits their gaze and consciousness? Is this an excess of control — or simply monitoring? At one point in the film, a viewer in a livestream chat of an owl’s nest remarks: “every time you think you understand something about them, they undermine it again.” It’s a simple observation, but not an insignificant one. In The Shining Tapestry , surveillance cameras quietly trace the daily life of a family of birds. Watching it soon gives way to something else: the act of looking, bringing a confrontation with nature’s mysterious gaze. Such attentiveness feels increasingly rare, yet it carries a quiet force. It is a reminder of life’s beauty and an opening toward other ways of imagining coexistence, among humans and with the surrounding world. (Pedro Gonçalves Ribeiro)

Returning to the place where one grew up is to expect that everything will remain the same—people, roundabouts, scents. Danielus, an emigrant in Norway, comes back to sell his parents’ house, but his stay becomes prolonged in a gesture of surrender to the solitude that memory demands of him, a rediscovery of a place that no longer belongs to him, in a daily life infected by several surreal elements. The first feature film by Vytautas Katkus, a filmmaker who has already presented several shorts at IndieLisboa.

One of Britain’s most influential hard rock bands sets out on a tour across the United States to promote their latest album, Smell the Glove . Joining Spinal Tap on the road is Marty DiBergi, a filmmaker and devoted fan determined to shoot a documentary along the way. Rob Reiner’s feature debut is a defining mockumentary, anchored in the quirks of the greatest bands of the twentieth century and the oversized egos of their members.

These are fascistic times — in discourse, in images, in intimacy. Vika Kirchenbauer questions the actions (and inactions) of the German state in the face of escalating violence. Drawing on observations and recordings from the past three years, this is a deeply personal essay, irregular in rhythm — like the very cadence of thought itself.

A country house and a double date. It begins cordially, politely — of course — until alcohol starts laying down its own law, loosening tongues and inhibitions. In its wake come old conflicts between siblings and spouses, tensions, resentments, and the you-never-told-me-this revelations long left unsaid. Welcome to the Passive-Aggressive Olympics. In Tres , four friends spend a weekend at a country house, but the idyllic retreat quickly turns into a battlefield defined by indirect barbs and direct attacks. Argentine director Juan Ignacio Ceballos builds an atmosphere of stifling tension where social courtesy is nothing more than a mask about to slip under the weight of biting comments. What begins as a getaway between friends quickly escalates into full-blown aggression, driven by a masterfully developed script and sharp dialogues. (María Angélica Contreras)

A good son returns home. Robbie comes back to his small town in rural New Jersey, where his mother still mourns the sudden disappearance of her daughter, Noelle. Determined to uncover what really happened to his sister, the young filmmaker retraces her steps, interviews local residents, and searches tirelessly. And his persistence begins to bear fruit. Found footage is to horror what autotune is to pop music – like it or not, it’s here to stay, and that’s a good thing. But be warned, for every Future or Charlie XCX there are a thousand Rebecca Blacks. Which is to say, for every Rec or Blair Witch Project, there are a thousand The Devil Inside. Well, this film is something else entirely. Directed by Robbie Banfitch, who brought us the magnificent The Outwaters, Tinsman Road takes its time to establish a routine and a connection with the viewer, and realizes that what makes the format work is the naturalism of the performances, the way mundane moments can be transformed into something truly horrifying. Robbie returns to his family home in New Jersey to try to support his mother and try to unravel the disappearance of his sister, Noelle. Consumed by grief, the mother wanders the house at night, as if possessed herself, and sees signs of her daughter everywhere. It’s a film that demands patience, like (some) good things in life. (Bruno Pereira)

On an interstellar journey, a group of scientists studies the last living vestiges of Earth. The artificial intelligence, Museo, becomes a portal to the crew’s diaries and a fragmented archive of humanity. On Earth, the one believed to be the last of the humans traverses a ruined planet that is slowly recovering, little by little, from the apocalypse it endured. In Leonardo Pirondi’s Tropical Fractals (world premiere at IndieLisboa), the end of the world looms. Planet Earth has fallen into ruin; its inhabitants have fled into outer space in search of something. There is a system, Museo, which opens the doors to the logbooks of a crew on the brink of extinction. And on this devastated Earth, there seems to be a glimmer of hope: a solitary man trying to find traces of something that may have survived, just as he has. In times of climate disasters and unjust wars, this film by Pirondi places us in the limbo of human existence, in our capacity to still create something and not merely destroy. A fable in the form of experimental science fiction, it brings the universe of the director’s short films to the feature-length screen and manages, with limited resources, to create a contemporary version of the end of the world. Should we believe in those who have gone, or in that prophet who remained? The film embraces the prophet, and with him, our capacity to still resist is made possible. Cinema takes many forms, and this one is truly beautiful. (Miguel Valverde)

The messy life of a young couple and their clandestine cat in a room whose rent they cannot afford. A story of love, sharing, and hope — unshakable and resilient in its innocence in the face of the unstable and disordered life of our times. Letter to an absent director. Dear Patrícia, I wanted to tell you in person that I really love your first film, Dois e Um Gato . It’s a mature film about a young couple, with childish jokes wrapped in a mature framework—or perhaps not quite—and sly laughter in poignant moments. I’ve never spoken to you, but I know your work very well and I love it so much. Perhaps you’ve worked on some of my favourite films in Portuguese cinema, and now you’ve given me—given us—this film. An ode to love and hope – don’t come in through the door, there’s always the window; we’ll take the cat and there’ll be three of us; there’s no money to pay the rent, never mind, one day we’ll pay, we just can’t manage it now. But dance with me, dance if it’s still possible, in this world or on the other side. Do you know, Patrícia, that we share the same orange lamp? It’s exactly the same as mine, it’s in the middle of the film and in the middle of my hallway. Is it the cosmos? Virtue? Doubt? Random words is what I feel like saying. Life is very unfair. Right now. The film. The other side. This side. Beside. Do we dance in the world? Well, we do. And Two and a Cat ? I don’t know if you liked Françoise Hardy, but if you did, I’ll share Le premier bonheur du jour with you; your film brought back a memory of Godard for me. And Two and a Cat ? Let’s celebrate it by showing it. Kisses from your admirer, Miguel Valverde

In this fantastical and sinister universe, the bird-people — human bodies crowned with avian heads — struggle to confront an imminent threat: their eggs are haunted. A violent, surreal, and fiercely imaginative animated film.

Arielle and Myriam contemplate and philosophize — their eyes fixed beyond, into the star-strewn darkness. They reflect on love, the sacrifices it demands, and the madness it can inspire. Two divas in a tribute to the very origins of cinema. Complementing “The Blood Countess” is this short film by Spanish producer/director Lluis Miñarro, in which two other divas of French cinema, Arielle Dombasle and Myriam Maziérès, remain in a static shot, talking with one another whilst gazing at the sky, as the world seems to pass them by. The red reflected in the tone of their conversation—provocative, sharp and wonderfully seductive—allows the viewer to enter a game of double meanings, where nothing is what it seems and even the most original form from the early days of cinema now takes on a new sophistication. “If love is always utterly mad”, then what shall I give you? An ode and a tribute to cinema. (Miguel Valverde)

So vast, yet so private. Grief is a paradoxical entity — an old (un)familiar presence, a creature of many silhouettes. In this bookbinding workshop — devoted to extending the lifespan of a few volumes — it becomes the central character. An entire film under the effect of the Goldberg Variations. It begins with the precise application of dye to water required for a paper-dyeing process, and the rest of the film that follows seems to move in the same tone of subtle diffusion. The story of mourning of one of the characters in a bookbinding course is the thread that ties together the various moments of this film, but beyond the explicitly narrative, it is a patient look at these emotions. Through carefully crafted long takes that observe both the behavior and the passage of time of the characters inhabiting them, the film seems to reveal, in this discreetly melancholic tone and under various lights, the small yet significant emotional variations of this grieving process (and of the people surrounding it). Regardless of the story attributed to it, Bach’s music in the film remains inextricably linked to calm. (Vasco Muralha)

Fisheress, beware not to catch in your nets the sulfurous Seranha! The malefic Venenus, from her mouth injected, will inflame your sleeping ecstasy and transform you forever… Loosely inspired by The Little Mermaid by Hans Christian Andersen, or rather, a delirium shaped as a queer fable with psychedelic drive and a vampiric tone. In Venenus , the Seranha rejects any logic of romantic redemption. There is no prince, nor any desire for assimilation into the human world. The body, instead, asserts itself as a site of transformation and contagion. The film begins in an apparently documentary register, suggesting a fishing community whose everyday reality is soon contaminated. Subtle sonic and visual dissonances begin to infiltrate, unsettling the apparent calm and signalling a drift into the fantastical. It is through the fisherwomen, embodied by the duo Venga Venga, that the narrative fully shifts into the realm of metamorphosis, triggered by the capture of the Seranha, portrayed by Tita Maravilha. In just over six minutes, Marie Fages achieves the remarkable feat of constructing a mythology of her own, where eroticism, the grotesque, and playfulness intertwine as forces of emancipation. Soundtrack by Menino da Mãe. (Susana Santos Rodrigues)

films.t: Vintage Glitch. Cities to end all summers and twilights
films.ot: Vintage Glitch. Cidades para acabar com todos os verões e crepúsculos
films.syn: In the distant future, the world of the eternal present is inhabited by bio-mechanical-digital-electronic beings. But one of these beings does not believe that it has always been like this and sets out on a journey of discovery in 3 stages. Such stages are made up of moving paintings, images corroded by the glitch and 2D and 3D animation, intertwined by narrator-poets and music, in a sci-fi object combining subversion, adventure and childishness. Memories of the end of time, or an account of a time in collapse? Both, we venture to say. The voice we hear is that of Bernardo Devlin; the music and lyrics are by Jorge Ferraz. The former was a member of Osso Exótico, a leading name in Portuguese experimental music, and, as a solo artist, a cult figure with an already extensive discography. The latter, as leader of Santa Maria and Gasolina Em Teu Ventre, authors of Free-Terminator (1989), left a significant mark on Portuguese exploratory rock. Also a member of the short-lived João Peste & O Acidoxibordel, Ferraz carries on his musical exploration at the intersection of electric, electronic and poetic sounds, both as a solo artist and with the multimedia collective Cellarius Noisy Machinae. It is from this collective that Vintage Glitch emerges. It is science fiction for our present days, a dystopian reflection set against the digital dioramas of Carlos M. Ferreira. The soundscapes provide the backdrop and the words, caught between the memory of what was and the unsustainable instability of the present, act as a guide through the fragmented reality that Ferraz and the collective present before us. (Mário Lopes)

In Linz Cathedral, the Hard-Chor, conducted by Alexander Koller, performs Bruckner. Sound and visual artist Stefan Tiefengraber invites us to listen to what is usually unheard. By removing the sonic source, the Austrian artist searches for what the pauses reveal — for reverberation, for echo: what remains when sound itself falls silent? We are struck by a certain strangeness and surprise in this small conceptual film. What lingers in the silent moments of a choir? Drawing from the choral works of Anton Bruckner, mainly motets characterized by polyphony and without instrumental accompaniment, Tiefengraber cuts off the voices and shows only the reverberation and decay of these divine chants across the walls and vaults of the Mariendom Linz, the largest church in Austria. The choir falls silent, leaving only the echo, accompanied by the facial expressions of the singers when they are not singing. To the strangeness and surprise is added a certain comic quality. An idea that Jocy de Oliveira would certainly not have disdained. (Carlos Ramos)

Gisberta, a immigrant trans woman, receives the news that she is HIV positive, causing her to lose all her sources of income and become homeless and addicted. In the building where she finds shelter, she is approached by an extremely aggressive young group. After discovering she was HIV-positive, Gisberta’s life turned into a living nightmare, at a time when she was already in a very vulnerable position. A trans woman, Brazilian and an immigrant, she was tortured in 2006 and then left for dead in a well by a group of young men in Porto. Since then, Gisberta has become an important symbol of the fight against transphobia and, more broadly, of the LGBTQIA+ struggles. This moving animation portrays her tragic end and pays tribute to her. (Catherine Boutaud)

films.t: We Put the World to Sleep
films.syn: The mission is secret and the ambition utopian: a film to truly bring the world to an end. We Put the World to Sleep is a work about borders — a nine-year production that offers anything but certainty: performer or character, improvisation or script, death or persistence, the real or its satellite. This is the second chapter of the “spiritual trilogy” by Romanian filmmaker Adrian Țofei and his artistic partner Duru Yücel. It’s Wednesday in a week just like any other; it’s 2 a.m. and you can’t sleep. That unanswered email is haunting your thoughts, you realize you need a distraction and you turn on the TV (or whatever the equivalent is for people younger than me) It doesn’t happen every night, but on this particular one, you catch a film that’s indescribable, like a feverish dream that you’ll have difficulty talking about it with other people. After all, that experience late at night was for you and you alone. We Put the World to Sleep brings that feeling back to me, a kind of hilarious meta-found-footage film that shakes up the genre with incredible inventiveness. We follow two actors who lose themselves in their roles; before you know it, we’re already in another layer of meta-commentary until we end up in an intense study of the psyche of serial killer Richard Ramirez. Something that deserves to be watched at unspeakable hours and with curiosity in mind. (Rui Mendes)

At a summer camp in 2007, João meets Ivo. We Were Just Brats is a possible narrative of a queer teenager who finds, in the dormitory and in the hip-hop and pop music of his world, a space that oscillates between self-discovery and punitive surveillance. At a summer camp where everyone seems a little too close for comfort, some unforgettable encounters take place. The film takes place in the summer, in the early 2000s, and amid rows of beds, stifling nights, and music listened to in secret, an intimacy grows, made up of small gestures and questions that hang in the air: “What are you listening to?”, the song itself is relatively unimportant, “Can I listen with you?” There are feelings that fit into a shared earbud, a touch, a tender and lingering embrace. But there are also desires that learn early on to hide, shaped by fear, vigilance, and the idea that certain things must not be spoken. Caught between the desire to get closer and the fear of being seen, a young man discovers that growing up also means navigating the space between what one feels and what one is allowed to feel. Summer romances are never easy, but some are harder than others. (Margarida Moz)

We already knew it would come to this: in 2194, bodies bearing a human likeness are cultivated to host artificial intelligences. Transfers between the digital and physical realms have become daily routine. An immigration officer from the Department of Embodiments arrives to interrogate a being on the verge of transformation. Set in a future in 2194, the transfiguration between the digital and physical worlds has become a common practice, and artificial intelligences can now inhabit lab-grown bodies designed in the image of humans. In this context, an agent from a department responsible for these transitions enters a facility to interrogate an entity that is about to complete its process of embodiment. Weird to Be Human , by Jan Grabowski, builds its narrative around this encounter, exploring the tension between an entity in transformation and an institutional structure that regulates and validates the process. The aseptic, minimalist setting reinforces a sense of control and distance, contrasting with the entity’s vulnerability and curiosity. This confrontation serves as a reflection on the criteria that define what it means to be human. More than a question of the body, the film suggests that humanity may be tied to consciousness, sensitivity, or even recognition by social systems. At the same time, it highlights how these definitions are shaped by bureaucratic structures that seek to classify and constrain what escapes the normative. In this way, Weird to Be Human presents itself as a visual and conceptual essay on identity and empathy, questioning to what extent being human is a natural condition or a construction shaped by rules and conventions. (Jéssica Pestana)

A movie about distorted sound reality. This experimental short film is constructed from archive footage and meticulous sound design. Alternating between black and white and colour, Búzio offers an immersive visual and auditory exploration, playing with our perception of reality. (Catherine Boutaud)

A group of teenagers gathers for a camping trip. While two of them try to define their romantic relationship, they are surprised by a swarm of fireflies that leads them deep into the forest. Where Fireflies Sparkle is a sensitive and captivating portrait of adolescence and first loves. We delight in following the two protagonists as they discover desire and explore the unknown. With a fresh perspective and an authentic atmosphere, Clara Vieira transports us to the magical world of the forest, where anything seems possible. (Catherine Boutaud)

films.t: Who’s Afraid of Zurita de Oliveira?
films.ot: Quem Tem Medo de Zurita de Oliveira?
films.syn: This film celebrates the life and work of Zurita de Oliveira — musician, performer, composer, and author — widely recognized as the pioneer of rock & roll in Portugal. She turned music into an act of defiance, forging a path at a time when there was little room for free-spirited women. Through songs and testimonies, the film reclaims her memory and transforms her previously unheard lyrics into a gesture of resistance, sung and performed by the women of today. The question in the title is a provocation that raises another question posed by director Francisca Marvão: “Why erase women from History?” Zurita de Oliveira is considered the first Portuguese woman to write, sing, and record a rock song, titled O Bonitão do Rock , released on an EP in 1960, yet she remains largely unknown to the Portuguese public. Here, Francisca undertakes a process of historical recovery (and reparation) by investigating the life of a revolutionary woman. This gesture continues the director’s important body of work in rescuing women in the artistic world from invisibility, as she had done in her previous film Ela É Uma Música (IndieLisboa 2019). Surrounded by various women musicians, some of whom form bands for the film, Francisca creates a space for artistic creation where new interpretations of Zurita’s songs are performed and original pieces are composed from previously unpublished lyrics discovered during the research. It is this dimension that transforms the film into a hybrid body between documentary, fiction, and concert, constituting one of its greatest strengths. Let us walk toward a world where no one is afraid of Zurita de Oliveira. (Carlos Ramos)

Women of the Revolution is a film that celebrates the multitude of revolutionary women: the mothers of our democracy. Through the voice, gaze, silence, and actions of each of these women, we learn about the richness of their experiences, which together give us a legacy of trust, justice, perseverance, respect, and freedom. These are women who defeated fascism, colonialism, and social inequalities in Portugal and the occupied African territories and transformed the world around them.

An obsessive exploration of the three geometric dimensions in hopes of reaching a fourth. Following Vortex (2015–2017), Grid (2017–2021) and Canto (2021–2022), Alexandre Alagôa appears to be pushing his structuralist cinema to the limit with XYZ (2024–2026). As with his earlier works, his focus remains on architecture’s capacity to define and construct spaces – following in the footsteps of Takashi Ito’s experiments in the 1980s. But whilst Vortex transformed the domestic setting into a labyrinth of screens and mirrors, Grid turned the skeleton of an unfinished building into an abyssal geometric back-and-forth, and Canto began with an anonymous alleyway in the backstreets of some suburb to construct a centripetal whirlwind of cubist effects, XYZ stands out as a radical culmination of a decade’s work. Radical in the sense of root. This is a film that explores the essential elements of cinema: the two-dimensionality of the image combined with the effect of depth through time. And, as one might expect, at the end of this tangle of dizzying variables, the analogue matrix of cinema is rediscovered: the projector and the celluloid film (in a digital film made without a camera). A disconcerting paradox. (Ricardo Vieira Lisboa).

aw: Prize for Best Portuguese Short Film - Special Mention

films.syn: A defining work of the genre, this mockumentary introduces a certain Mr. Zelig, a man who lived in 1920s America and exhibited a rare condition: a “chameleonic disorder” that caused him to transform, both physically and psychologically, into those around him. The question that remains is: what identity, if any, was truly his?

films.t: “Alternative Routes” – Viseu garage’s rock echoes from the 80s and 90s
films.ot: "Percursos Alternativos" - Ecos de Garagem: o Rock em Viseu nos anos 80 e 90
films.syn: Alternative Routes is a documentary by Rui Mota Pinto that reveals the musical diversity of a city, celebrating it and expanding its history through textual, sonic, and visual narratives that inspire new generations. It is a portrait of Viseu’s alternative music scene from the 80s and 90s, where musicians, radio broadcasters, programmers, and other music lovers are invited to confront their experiences throughout those decades. Across the country, many garages were emptied of cars to be filled with drums, basses, guitars, and amplifiers in the 1980s and 1990s. Before studios, often with no one really knowing how to play very well and without a plan, many bands started and ended in garages. What mattered was playing. Each decade has its own sound. In the 1980s and 1990s, it was that of alternative rock and its many variations. This is the story of the garage bands of Viseu, many of them local in scope, several reaching national dimension. Major Alvega, Lucretia Divina, Bastardos do Cardeal, Dead Corporation, Funny Bunny are some of them. More than a film about bands, this is a film about freedom and the act of making things with friends. In Viseu or anywhere in the world. (Carlos Ramos)
